World.title: The far-right leader pushing Germans to forget the Nazi past
World.content:
Hans-Thomas Tillschneider could soon wield more power than any other far-right figure in Germany’s postwar history to turn his radical ideas into reality.

The man leading the charge to make Germany proud again won’t say he wants his fellow Germans to “forget” the Nazi past, but that is where his ideas invariably lead.

Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, a 48-year-old lawmaker for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, was until recently little known beyond his largely rural constituency. But he may soon be in a position to help realize one of the greatest ambitions of the party’s most extreme faction: remaking his country’s postwar identity and steering Germans toward leaving behind the Nazi past.

That history “remains present in a peculiar way — yes, like a zombie,” Tillschneider told POLITICO in July on the sidelines of an AfD conference in the eastern city of Magdeburg. “It’s an undead entity. And that is not normal. That is not good.”





Germany’s much-vaunted Erinnerungskultur, or culture of remembrance, is central to its self-conception — and long served as an existential imperative. Though halting, West Germany’s reckoning with Nazi crimes and the Holocaust in the decades after the end of World War II served to help restore the country’s standing among democratic nations, making possible its membership in Western alliances. The country’s constitution was shaped in repudiation of Nazism, with safeguards intended to prevent its resurgence.

But for the AfD’s most extreme leaders — many now concentrated in rural areas of the former East Germany — the culture of remembrance has merely perpetuated what some, including Tillschneider, call a “guilt cult” designed to instill self-loathing in the German Volk, a term for “people” which is imbued with near-mystical significance on the far right. Without openly denying Nazi crimes, they argue the cultural and political reckoning with them has damaged the Volk’s identity, leaving Germans weak, atomized, and vulnerable to “globalist” forces such as the EU and the U.S., long viewed by the far-right as a corrosive force due to the homogenizing influence of its individualist, consumerist culture — at least until U.S. President Donald Trump’s arrival.

Tillschneider’s ideas aren’t new. The backlash against Germany’s culture of remembrance is as old as the effort to reckon with the past itself. But as the intellectual architect of the party’s blueprint for governing in Saxony-Anhalt ahead of a Sept. 6 election in the state — where the AfD is so far ahead in the polls it’s within striking distance of an outright majority in parliament — he could soon wield more tangible power than any other far-right figure in Germany’s postwar history to turn those ideas into reality. Tillschneider, currently the AfD’s spokesperson for culture and education policy in the state parliament, is a leading candidate to become the head of a future ministry that would oversee school curricula and cultural funding in the state.

Hans-Thomas Tillschneider speaks at an AfD convention in Magdeburg, eastern Germany on July 11, 2026. | Jens Schlüter/AFP via Getty Images

“We want to spread the joy of being German,” Tillschneider said at a pre-election AfD “family fest” on an overcast August afternoon in Querfurt, a small medieval fortress city in his Saxony-Anhalt constituency. “It’s a celebration. Celebrate the fact that you’re German.”

This did not mean, he added, that the AfD would eliminate school lessons on Nazi crimes. Rather, it would “shift the emphasis,” he said, so the Nazi past loses its contemporary urgency.

“Of course, I’d also like to see history classes on the Third Reich,” he said, “But good history classes. Good history classes convey a sense of the otherness of the past.”

‘More Bismarck, less Hitler’

In some ways, Tillschneider, a bearded, bespectacled former university lecturer, seems an unlikely figure to advance the revolution in German identity the far-right has long sought.

Born in Romania during the Cold War, Tillschneider grew up in a German-speaking minority community whose roots in the region stretched back to Habsburg rule. His family moved to West Germany when he was still a child. At university, he became interested in Islamic studies, drawn — as he now explains it — to the subject because it was foreign and unfamiliar. He later studied in Syria before earning a doctorate and publishing a book on “the origins of legal hermeneutics in early Islam.”





After moving to eastern Germany in subsequent years, Tillschneider came to depict Islam as fundamentally incompatible with German society and became a prominent figure in the so-called “New Right,” a network of radical intellectuals known for recasting old, extremist ideas in more culturally palatable terms. He also became associated with an extreme faction within the AfD called Der Flügel (“the Wing”) alongside Thuringian politician Björn Höcke, who drew widespread condemnation in 2017 for calling Berlin’s prominent Holocaust memorial, located near the Brandenburg Gate, a “monument of shame” and demanding a “180-degree turn” in Germany’s memory politics. Der Flügel was dissolved in 2020, but its members, including Tillschneider, have only grown more influential in the party since then.

Tillschneider was the main author of the AfD’s program for how it will wield power in Saxony-Anhalt. At the root are myriad measures aimed at “stabilizing” German identity by redirecting cultural funding and revising school curricula, over which states have primary authority. Tillschneider has announced plans for changing history lessons so that they are oriented toward “more Bismarck, less Hitler,” — controversial phrasing that has recently been removed from the governing manifesto. The party’s program also proposes cutting funding for “anti-German art” and developing a “patriotic tourism” strategy for the state.

Party leaders say they don’t intend to eradicate memorials to Nazi crimes but will fund and restore those that “honor the sacrifices of soldiers” in both world wars. “This support should benefit all monuments equally, without petty political judgments,” the program reads. “Fallen soldiers gave their lives to defend their country. Recognizing and honoring this great sacrifice is a first sign of a patriotic turnaround.”

Tillschneider and Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s top candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, at the party’s family festival in Querfurt. | Nette Nöstlinger/POLITICO

It’s perhaps no coincidence that such a revolution in German identity would take root in the former East Germany, where the AfD is ascendant. While West Germany was attempting to undertake a confrontation with the past, imperfect as it was, the state narrative in the former East Germany was that its people had vanquished fascism, which in any case was a product of the West. Many of the AfD’s supporters in the East believe a West German narrative about the Nazi past was imposed on them after the fall of the Berlin Wall.

But for Tillschneider, there’s another reason the revolution will begin in the East — because eastern Germans already know what it means to see a political regime collapse.

“As a result of the peaceful revolution, people have witnessed a change in systems and, as a result, have gained some distance, are more reflective,” he said at the AfD family festival, speaking in a breathless torrent. By contrast, he added, western Germans “have been stewing in the same soup for 80 years.”

‘Love for the homeland is not a crime’

As attendees queued for beer and free bratwurst at the AfD family festival — held on an arid field on the outskirts of Querfurt, beside an agricultural-machinery plant — Tillschneider took the stage before an “Our Country First” placard and declared that they had ample reason to celebrate: the establishment parties, he said, were nearing their demise.

“We’re celebrating the fact that the policies that are directed against us — which take away our freedom, which strip us of our autonomy, which impoverish us — will come to an end,” he yelled, his booming voice saturating the speakers. “On Sept. 6, for the first time, we have a realistic chance — and this isn’t just campaign rhetoric — a realistic chance to end this nightmare, to put an end to this horror!”





Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s top candidate in Saxony-Anhalt and its potential future premier, then took to the stage to a rock-star reception. Charismatic and very popular online, his quick smile belies the radical politics of the state branch of his party, which domestic intelligence authorities have classified as an extremist organization seeking “to abolish parliamentary democracy in its current form.” AfD politicians in the state, including Siegmund and Tillschneider, deny being extremists, portraying the label as state repression that undermines the democratic will of their supporters.

If Siegmund is the face of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, Tillschneider supplies much of the brains. Siegmund alluded to this during his speech, thanking Tillschneider for spending “hundreds of hours” on the party’s governing manifesto.

“I’ll need him over the next five years because we’re making history together,” Siegmund said of Tillschneider. “The sun rises in the east, but it will shine over all of Germany!”

People at the AfD family fest in Querfurt line up to buy party merchandise. Nette Nöstlinger/POLITICO

As people waited in line for hours to get Siegmund’s autograph, Tillschneider darted frantically from tent to tent, making sure things were running smoothly. “Don’t sell them for less than €10!” he shouted to a group of volunteers as he handed them a box of tote bags emblazoned with Siegmund’s face.

One of those volunteers, Gesine Sauer, a 48-year-old social worker from the area, said she agreed with Tillschneider’s ideas about making Germans proud of their history.

“People always focus on just a very small part of German history — and that has nothing to do with anyone trying to deny it, or trying to dismiss it — but German history is so much more than that,” she said. “And time and again, from all sides, we’re being forced to grapple with this question of guilt. That’s wrong, and it’s not a positive development. Instead, we should reflect on what we were once capable of achieving,” she added, going on to list German historical accomplishments in medicine and industry.

Others put it more simply. “I’d say that was all 90 years ago, and at some point we should just let the past be the past,” said one woman in her 60s wearing a bracelet in the colors of the German flag.





“With us, if you say you love your homeland, you’re stamped as a Nazi,” said one man, a 51-year-old railroad track worker, as he waited in the long line for beer wearing a shirt that read “Love for the homeland is not a crime.”

Most attendees, however, cited other reasons for voting for the AfD: economic and industrial decline; refugees receiving state support while Germans struggled to pay their bills; the government’s refusal to accept cheap Russian natural gas while sending billions in federal aid to Ukraine.

For Tillschneider and his fellow far-right ideologues, these more tangible issues are all connected to the crisis of German identity: the country’s reluctance to pursue its own interests, they argue, stems from an “anti-German” strain of thinking within the country.

“That’s why we have policies that are self-destructive in every area — because we have a cracked identity,” Tillschneider said from underneath a tent at the festival.

Tillschneider listens to Siegmund, the AfD’s top candidate in Saxony-Anhalt and its potential future premier. | James Angelos/POLITICO

He rattled off ideas for repairing the German soul: a “pride month” celebrating German cultural heritage and a festival of German music — not “Baroque music or European music,” he clarified, but “German music.”

He denied the goal was to make Germans forget the Nazi past. Yet he went on to describe a process that seemed to amount to just that.

The goal, he said, was for this history to “no longer be so urgent, no longer so intrusive, no longer so present.”

He added: “Just because something is no longer present doesn’t mean it will be forgotten.”

Nette Nöstlinger contributed reporting.

World.title: Pedro Sánchez’s Ceuta crisis just got a lot worse
World.content:
“This wasn’t a spontaneous migration movement, but rather an operation that originated in Morocco and was spearheaded and coordinated by Morocco,” center-right People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo said at a rally in Ceuta on Wednesday.

“The government knew and covered it up,” he added, calling for snap elections. “They lied to our faces.”

In the immediate aftermath of the surge, Sánchez described it as an “attack on the territorial integrity of Spain,” but insisted Rabat had nothing to do with it.

He doubled down on that position on Monday, assuring the public he had “no information from Spanish security forces or our intelligence services that would cast any doubt on Moroccan authorities,” and instead accusing Russia, Israel and “an international far-right group” of orchestrating the operation.

But according to the police report, first revealed by Spanish newspaper El Español, Moroccan agents helped orchestrate the mass entry of migrants into the exclave. El País later published a page from the document with images that appeared to show uniformed Moroccan security officers guiding groups of people toward the beach from which they could cross into Ceuta.

The document was commissioned by a judge investigating the surge and drawn up by the National Center for Immigration and Borders, a specialized intelligence unit within Spain’s National Police.

World.title: Nigel Farage’s Reform show gets a reboot
World.content:
The party knows looking credible is key. That’s why Farage will be leading the pledge-making to the public, culminating in a policy-laced but unscripted speech on Friday. Robert Jenrick, Zia Yusuf and Richard Tice — his spokespeople for the Treasury, home affairs and business briefs, respectively — will be making them too.

“It will be very serious about the problems the country faces and how we intend to fix them in the first 100 days,” the official cited above said.

Some in Reform had hoped the conference would mark the moment Farage announced an expanded front bench. Key posts like health and defense remain unfilled, despite Farage trying to demonstrate the party is no one-man band. But the party will hold off until after the Birmingham jamboree is over, instead announcing “a couple of new people” later this month and in October, according to the official.

Summer of scrutiny

Farage’s return to the limelight, which he has uncharacteristically dodged ever since his re-election in Clacton, began on Wednesday, with an interview with the BBC’s political editor.

The Reform leader has faced repeated questions over a £5 million donation from crypto-entrepreneur Christopher Harborne, as well as support from convicted fraudster George Cottrell.

Farage continued to insist Wednesday that he has “done nothing wrong” in not declaring the support in the run-up to the 2024 general election. He argued that the intense scrutiny of Reform’s funding is down to an “establishment” stitch-up, and railed against living in a “complainants’ society.” He compared his situation to the investigations faced by fellow “outsider” Donald Trump.

World.title: Wildberger fordert globale KI-Behörde nach Vorbild der Atomaufsicht
World.content:
Die zunehmende Leistungsfähigkeit von KI-Modellen bereitet Wildberger Sorge. „Es verstärkt die Dringlichkeit, hier in ganz besonderem Maße mehr Sicherheitsvorkehrungen zu treffen“, sagte er. Die Entwicklung sei „so rasant“, dass Unternehmen vor möglichen Angriffen „nie ganz sicher“ seien.

„Funktioniert nur mit Amerika und China“

Die Idee einer internationalen KI-Aufsicht nach dem Vorbild der Atomaufsicht wird seit mehreren Jahren diskutiert. Auch OpenAI-Chef Sam Altman hatte sich dafür bereits mehrfach ausgesprochen.

Nach Ansicht des Ministers können Staaten die Risiken fortschrittlicher KI nicht im Alleingang kontrollieren. „Das erfordert aber auch, dass der Dialog grundsätzlich zu diesem Thema global aufgenommen wird – und das funktioniert am Ende des Tages natürlich auch nur mit Amerika und China zusammen“, sagte Wildberger.

„Die gute Nachricht ist: Wir sind noch in der Kontrolle“

Wildberger plädiert zudem für klare Meldepflichten. Die Veröffentlichung sicherheitsrelevanter Vorfälle dürfe nicht allein von der Einschätzung der betroffenen Unternehmen abhängen. „Natürlich müssen solche Vorfälle verpflichtend gemeldet werden“, sagte der Minister.

Die Frage gewinnt derzeit an Bedeutung, weil unklar ist, ob Vorfälle wie der Angriff von OpenAI-Agenten auf Hugging Face bereits von den Meldepflichten des AI Acts erfasst werden. Experten und Politiker fordern seit Tagen mehr Klarheit darüber, welche Regeln für besonders leistungsfähige KI-Modelle bereits während interner Tests gelten.

Nach Ansicht des Ministers bleibt noch Zeit, um die Risiken leistungsfähiger KI-Modelle sowohl politisch als auch technologisch einzuhegen. „Die gute Nachricht ist: Wir sind noch in der Kontrolle“, sagte der Bundesdigitalminister. „Aber wir müssen aufpassen, dass uns das nicht entgleitet.“

World.title: How Merkel and Merz lost eastern Germany to the AfD
World.content:
This Sunday, the far right is well placed to take power in a German state for the first time since 1945.

Ulrich Siegmund, lead candidate for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, took to the stage in the central marketplace of the town of Naumburg and declared there was a new “awakening” in eastern Germany.

Ahead of a vital election in the region of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday — in which Siegmund is within striking distance of becoming the first far-right leader to govern a German state since 1945 — that appeal to an eastern identity struck a chord.

A young man beside me was hollering “Ostdeutschland!” although he was too young to have lived in the communist German Democratic Republic. “It was purer there,” he explained. “More German. Not America-Germany like the West.”





Elements of Siegmund’s new awakening sounded reminiscent of the old East, and his speech would certainly have played well in the Kremlin. He condemned the foolishness of supporting “corrupt” Ukraine and addressed the need to return to oil and gas supplies from Russia.

East Germany formally dissolved in 1990, but it did not disappear. Its struggles for identity within the sprawling German federal system, with power concentrated in Berlin, have fueled the ascent of the far right.

If the AfD does secure an outright victory this weekend, it will raise profound questions about how chancellors such as Helmut Kohl, Angela Merkel and Friedrich Merz failed to manage the post-unification transition and prevent large parts of the east from veering off on a political trajectory toward the far right.

Sausages and strongarms

In a generally upbeat line for sausages and beer in Naumburg, there were also some less cheery sorts in neo-Nazi T-shirts and regalia. One of the crowd told me the government in Berlin “sends our tax money to the Jews in Israel and [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy instead of spending it here.”

It is important to stress that the eastern political identity is not monochrome nostalgia for the GDR. Indeed, the AfD is repurposing the slogan of the 1989 demonstrations against communism — “Wir sind das Volk” – “We are the people” — for its own ends.





That taps into memories of marching for freedom in the last days of the socialist state.

“And now we will show the world again,” said Dirk Huzenlaub, a metalworker in his blue overalls, whom I spoke to on another campaign pit stop in the nearby town of Lützen

He has done well as a self- employed worker, supplying many local companies. But he adds that the “people at the top don’t want us to do well — they keep us down on purpose.” A welter of internet conspiracy theories followed, including the notion that Merz and his predecessor Merkel “betrayed us — we risk our country collapsing the way the old East Germany collapsed.”

AfD supporters gather to listen to the party’s candidate in the Saxony-Anhalt election, Ulrich Siegmund, on August 24, 2026 in Naumburg. | Gallup/Getty Images

Beyond the conviviality of the sausage line, the mood can sour fast — as I discovered when I sought to speak with Siegmund in Lützen, only to be told “mainstream” press were not welcome. I was roughly jostled aside, my arm twisted by a musclebound heavy flanking Siegmund, who sported an earpiece and a lavishly tattooed neck.

“Move or I will take you to the police,” he barked. We had a short, unproductive debate about the constitutionally guaranteed right to report freely in public places.

Another hard arm twist and shove ensued, ending with me stumbling over a curb and being dragged to a police car. No one seemed much bothered by this.





“This woman is being un-co-operative,” the minder snarled. At the next stop in Naumburg, another attentive policeman enjoined me to stay away from “Security Zone 1” — anywhere near the stage.

Then came the more chilling warning.

“It’s for your own safety,” he added. “Best remember, in that zone, the AfD are the masters.”

Merkel and the migration backlash

The last two chancellors — Merz and Merkel — have provoked a strong backlash in eastern Germany.

For Merkel, the outcome could have been more positive. She hailed from the East herself and was an active participant in the Wende, or “turn”, away from communism. She inherited Kohl’s pledge to produce “flourishing landscapes” in the “new federal states.” Forlorn towns and cities were restored, the air pollution from brown-coal energy supplies ended, and potholed roads are now smooth enough to roar along in Mercedes and BMWs.

But the East responded far more negatively to Merkel’s decision to allow a mass influx of asylum seekers from Syria and North Africa in 2015 and 2016. She signaled her empathy for that in a conversation with me in 2018, saying she understood the heartache of easterners seeing their communities empty out demographically and traditional jobs disappear.

“Of course, these disturbing personal experiences affect people and leave a deep mark — we need to understand this,” she said.





But Merkel’s responses did not go far enough for people worried about the speed of social change. And from 2015, the AfD began to soar.

The Covid era deepened divisions too: a social media campaign demanded the introduction of the Russian Sputnik V vaccine ahead of better options. That demonstrated a complex blend of attitudes which feature strongly in AfD lore to this day: Distrust of Western capitalism and an acceptance of Russia.

The veteran sociologist Detlef Pollack diagnoses a “victim mythology” western politicians find hard to combat without sounding aloof. Fully three-quarters of voters who lean towards the AfD think the unified Germany has robbed them of their just deserts, in comparison with two-fifths of the public in the old GDR.

An AfD supporter carries a tote bag featuring Siegmund that reads “Our year!” | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

Frustration came to mark the dealings of Merkel and her successor Merz in talking about the mood in the old east.

“There is no point trying to convince you [about the justification for accepting over 1 million refugees],” she said at a rally I attended in her final election campaign in 2017 in the industrial town of Bitterfeld as a hostile mob booed and blew horns to stop her being heard. Backstage she shook her head, clearly furious.

The more she was lionized as a Gloriana of international liberal democracy for her robust dealings with U.S. President Donald Trump, the more alienated she became from socially conservative easterners. The AfD also learned from the MAGA movement how to unite multiple strands of thought into campaign messages, interwoven with slugs of fake or exaggerated stories.





The arrival of Merz, a western politician not armed with a vast array of communication skills, together with struggles of the wider German economy — like the symbolic hit of massive projected job losses at the VW plant in Wolfsburg close to the old border — have taken a further shine off the lure of the Federal Republic’s prosperity model.

Falling behind

An assessment from the Halle Institute for Economic Research noted that, after the 1990s, the “initial catch-up momentum came to a halt. Since then, the East German economy has mostly grown even more slowly than the West German one.”

It blamed the “lack of productivity of East German companies,” as well as a protracted brain drain and a low rate of business formation. A German defense official, granted permission to speak confidentially to POLITICO, added: “Overwhelmingly, the new defense industries which will drive prosperity and security are based in the old Federal Republic. That gives the east less interest in arming against Russia — it’s a double hit we need to address.”

Merkel has demanded more “courage” to “fight for democracy,” channeling her own brand of 1989 nostalgia. These messages embolden the AfD’s opponents, including churchgoers now rallying as they did against the regime in 1989. Problematically, though, her appeals can also come across as “Bevormundung,” with eastern Germans feeling like they are being treated with haughty condescension.

People, including supporters of Antifa, protesting near an AfD rally in Naumburg on August 24, 2026. | Gallup/Getty Images

Merz warns that a far-right government in Saxony-Anhalt would mean “foreign investors steering clear of the state in future” and that the state “will face considerable problems.”

Whether that scare tactic proves persuasive remains to be seen.

(For his part, Siegmund has shed the miserabilist mantras of other AfD luminaries. “My God, the women are great-looking in this town,” I hear him announce to giggling selfie-seekers in Lützen. “Better not tell my wife.”)

Merz also does not exude much personal interest in the East, other than seeing it as a problem to be kept at bay. Very few of his Cabinet hail from that part of Germany — though the party cites the rise of a new generation of eastern Germans to the next tier of ministerial posts. That may need to accelerate soon to combat the rising mood of alienation.





Arriving on a whistlestop visit on Monday to support Sven Schulze as his party’s candidate for minister-president, the chancellor condemned “people who trade on anger.” He did venture out among voters — something many leading politicians avoid.

Saxony-Anhalt is a small state in population — with just over 2 million inhabitants. But it is also the cradle of the Lutheran tradition of challenging the mighty — a theme that the more historically minded rally-goers raised with me.

As Siegmund puts it: “Even if we don’t get there [to an overall majority], we are not going away.” That too was a stubborn cry from the streets in late 1989. And in 2026, it spurred huge roars of approval through the marketplace in Naumburg, drowning out the counter-protests.

Siegmund is within striking distance of becoming the first far-right leader to govern a German state since 1945. | Hannibal Hanschke/EFE via EPA

On Sunday, the AfD will be put to the test.

So too will a German political establishment that won unification, only to lose much of its grip on people power.

Anne McElvoy is a former correspondent in East Germany and author of The Saddled Cow, East Germany’s Life and Legacy.

World.title: Inside Kallas’ fightback against plans to tear up the EU’s diplomatic service
World.content:
Kallas’ allies fear that an overhaul intended to make EU foreign policy more effective could instead give President Ursula von der Leyen’s Commission greater control over the work overseen by the high representative.

“If I have somebody above me who is actually deciding, then it doesn’t work,” Kallas told journalists Wednesday after a debate with EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland.

One diplomat, referring to the Franco-German plans, said: “She [Kallas] wants to delay the whole process because she doesn’t want to be subject to von der Leyen.” Another said “she wants this whole thing to go away.”

The pushback is taking shape through Kajsa Ollongren, the EEAS’ new secretary-general, who has been touring EU capitals to discuss reform proposals with national governments.

Ollongren will brief staff on the findings from that tour at a town hall meeting with the EEAS this week, where Kallas will formally introduce her, according to the officials and an EU diplomat.

Ollongren is also expected to propose the creation of a “council of elders” task force to reflect on possible internal reforms, one of the officials said.

World.title: Milestone: Giorgia Meloni's right-wing government becomes Italy's longest-lasting since WWII
World.content:
Giorgia Meloni's hard-right government will become the longest-lasting in Italy's postwar history on Friday, a notable record that belies considerable challenges ahead of elections next year.

 

In a country once a byword for political instability, Italy's first woman leader will have been in charge of the same administration for 1,413 days, one more than the late Silvio Berlusconi managed during one of his four stints in office.

"It is certainly a point of pride," Marco Osnato, a prominent lawmaker with Meloni's far-right Brothers of Italy (FdI) party, told the AFP news agency of the milestone.

The record is likely to boost the prime minister's image as Italy, which has had almost 70 governments over the past 80 years, gears up for a national vote in 2027, analysts say.

With FdI constantly topping opinion polls, it might seem Meloni is on track for a repeat of her 2022 win.

But recent events have complicated the path to re-election, said Lorenzo Pregliasco, of the YouTrend polling institute.

This year Meloni was undermined by a justice reform referendum defeat that showed voters there "may be an alternative majority" to the coalition currently in power, Pregliasco said.

Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni during a round table meeting during the NATO summit in Ankara, 8 July, 2026 AP Photo

Success?

The drubbing also raised questions about the government's record.

With plans to strengthen the powers of the prime minister and increase regional autonomy, the reform was one of three flagship coalition pledges that the government has so far failed to deliver.

And critics say results have fallen well short of expectations in other areas too. The government, which enjoys an ample parliamentary majority, has failed to tackle the structural issues that many believe hold Italy back, they say.

"This stability was not capitalised upon," said Chiara Braga, the leader of the centre-left opposition Democratic Party's parliamentary group.

"It did not lead to any significant improvement in people's living standards or business competitiveness."

Supporters of the "No" vote celebrate the outcome of a constitutional referendum that cancelled a justice reform approved by Parliament in Rome, 23 March, 2026 AP Photo

Italy's economy is forecast to grow a lacklustre 0.6% in 2026, while real wages have been virtually stagnant since the early 1990s.

Unemployment has fallen from above 7% to around 5% percent ver the past four years, but the number of economically inactive people, those who could work but are not looking for a job, remains high.

"This government has primarily sought to survive" by "doing as little as possible," said Tito Boeri, an economist at Milan's Bocconi University.

Supporters counter that the administration has cut taxes and increased tax revenues, brought fiscal discipline to the highly indebted nation and won Italy a more prominent role on the global stage at a fraught geopolitical time.

"When it comes to foreign policy, Italy has never been so central, particularly in Europe," Osnato said, noting that from a hardening of migration rules to energy policy Rome was now considered a driving force in Brussels.

'Nothing has changed'

Politically, Meloni's coalition risks bleeding voters to Roberto Vannacci, a former general who regularly bashes migrants and LGBTQ+ people.

His newly-created Futuro Nazionale party polls at around 7% and could emerge as a kingmaker next year.

But support for the ruling alliance, which includes the far-right League of Matteo Salvini and conservative Forza Italia, is buoyed by perennial infighting within the left-leaning opposition and increasing abstentionism, analysts say.

Voter turnout in 2022 was about 64%, a record low, and fell below 50% for European elections in 2024.

EU Parliament member and former Italian army general Roberto Vannacci speaks in Rome, 14 June, 2026 AP Photo

"A sizeable share of voters is really disappointed and angry," said Giovanni Orsina, a political scientist at Rome's Luiss University.

Italy's chronic issues have led many to believe that "no one can solve their problems," he added.

In August, Meloni was loudly booed at a sporting event in Taranto, a southern city home to a giant steel plant plagued by economic and environmental challenges that the government is struggling to keep afloat.

Surveys show that the cost of living, a deteriorating public health system, security and immigration are among Italians' top concerns.

Such trends were in plain sight in Tor Bella Monaca, a working-class eastern suburb of Rome dotted by rundown apartment blocks, cash-for-gold shops and discount stores.

Governed by Meloni's party, the district regularly ranks among those with the lowest voter turnout.

"Nothing has changed in Italy over the 45 years I've been on this planet and nothing will," said Maurizio, an IT worker who preferred to give only his first name.

Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni addresses to the lower chamber of parliament in Rome, 9 April, 2026 AP Photo

He is tempted by Vannacci but will not vote next year, he said, lamenting the lack of a long-term vision for the country.

Others were more upbeat.

"People expect to see improvement overnight," said Annamaria, 67, a pensioner and supporter of the prime minister who also declined to give her last name.

"It takes time, but things are getting better," she added, saying she believed that crime and migrants had become less visible of late.

World.title: US slaps 100% tariffs on drones to counter Chinese dominance
World.content:
New US tariffs of up to 100% took effect on Thursday on drones and certain drone components, as Washington pushes to lower its import reliance in an industry that China dominates.

 

US President Donald Trump signed an order setting out the duties in August, as the White House flagged "the national security threat posed by imports of drones and their components".

The order also aims to boost domestic supply chains.

Drones have become a cornerstone of modern warfare and surveillance, as the war in Ukraine has starkly demonstrated, and US officials argue that dependence on Chinese-made drones and components — chiefly produced by market leader DJI — leaves the country's military and critical infrastructure exposed to disruption, espionage and battlefield disadvantage.

Drones with a takeoff weight exceeding 25 kilograms, as well as those with thermal imaging capabilities and docking stations, face a 100% tariff.

Smaller drones face a 25% duty.

Some components of drones that are "not particularly sensitive" will also face duties, but those only come into effect on 9 February next year.

China expressed opposition to the planned tariffs shortly after they were unveiled by Trump, with Beijing urging Washington to withdraw the duties.

A commerce ministry spokesman said the tariffs would "disrupt the global drone supply chain and further undermine a fair and competitive market environment".

He said China firmly opposed the move.

Chinese company DJI, founded in 2006, has captured more than two-thirds of the global drone market in recent years, according to several studies.

Since 2022, however, DJI has been on a US list of Chinese firms linked to the country's military and subject to restrictions on access to US technology.

DJI has fought its inclusion on the list.

World.title: Outrage as Maltese tycoon acquitted of reporter Daphne Caruana Galizia's murder
World.content:
A Maltese court acquitted tycoon Yorgen Fenech of orchestrating the car-bomb killing of investigative reporter Daphne Caruana Galizia on Wednesday, sparking outrage from her family and media freedom advocates.

 

The wealthy businessman had stood accused of masterminding the 2017 assassination of 53-year-old Caruana Galizia, which sparked unprecedented protests and brought down a government.

Caruana Galizia's family said in a statement that Fenech's acquittal was "denying her the justice she deserves."

Her son Matthew Caruana Galizia said jurors had made a "terrible decision...that our country may never recover from."

The European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF) said the verdict sent "a disturbing message to those who attack and kill journalists."

Dubbed a "one-woman WikiLeaks", Caruana Galizia had exposed corruption at the highest level in the country, shining a spotlight on murky links between Malta's business and political elites.

Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech exits the courthouse after being acquitted of ordering the killing of Daphne Caruana Galizia in Valletta, 2 September, 2026 AP Photo

Her murder shocked the world and put Malta, the European Union's smallest member state, in the spotlight over its apparent rule-of-law failings.

The killing also led to a political crisis and the resignation of then-premier Joseph Muscat in January 2020 after widespread anger and mass protests over his perceived efforts to protect friends and allies from the investigation.

A two-year public inquiry published in July 2021 concluded that the state should "shoulder responsibility" for the murder due to the "atmosphere of impunity" the government had created.

Fenech, a tycoon whose business interests spanned the energy and tourism sectors, was arrested on his yacht in 2019 as he tried to sail out of Malta after a middleman in the murder was offered a pardon to identify those involved.

Prosecutors had accused Fenech of ordering the journalist to be killed because she was on the brink of publishing a compromising article about his uncle.

Protesters hold photos during a protest outside the office of the Prime Minster of Malta by civil groups Occupy Justice and Republica, 29 November, 2019 Image Rene Rossignaud/AP

'Beyond outraged'

Five people have been convicted so far in relation to the murder for supplying the explosives and carrying out the killing.

In June 2025, Robert Agius and Jamie Vella were convicted of supplying the bomb that killed Caruana Galizia and sentenced to life in prison.

The three men who carried out the murder, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio together with Vince Muscat, are serving prison sentences after being found guilty of their role.

A 437-page report written by a panel of three judges in 2021 found that the state had shirked its duty to protect Caruana Galizia and subjected her to personal attacks and verbal abuse from politicians.

The atmosphere created a "favourable climate" for her assassination and there was "convincing evidence" that her killers knew they would be protected by "persons in the highest state positions."

"Accountability is now overdue for all those who enabled, facilitated, or protected her murderers," the family said in their statement on Tuesday.

"Nine years after Daphne's brutal assassination, the institutional failures that enabled her murder remain unaddressed and unreformed."

Media watchdog Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said it was "beyond outraged."

"The verdict means that almost nine years since the assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia, the Maltese authorities have failed to identify and convict the mastermind.

"Full justice must be served and Maltese authorities must implement the long overdue measures protecting journalists and media freedom," it added.

World.title: 'Social jet lag': Why mismatched sleep schedules could be fuelling anxiety in teenagers
World.content:
As school starts and routines return to "normal," many adolescents will struggle with early mornings after a summer of sleeping in and irregular holiday schedules. Throughout the school year, pupils count down to the weekend, hoping to recover the hours of sleep lost during the week — a pattern researchers call 'social jet lag'.

 

It is precisely the ‘social jet lag’ that might be negatively affecting young people’s mental health, a new study by the University of Southampton in the United Kingdom found. And with biological sleep changes occurring in adolescence, addressing youths’ sleep needs and even reconsidering school start times might be a way forward, researchers say.

The review included 12 studies, involving over 230,000 participants, and found that teens experiencing greater levels of ‘social jet lag’ are more likely to report higher levels of anxiety. It seems to be a vicious circle, as higher anxiety levels also predict greater ‘social jet lag ’, but the authors noted this is an association rather than a proven cause-and-effect relationship.

These findings highlight the importance of behavioural strategies that target healthy, regular sleep as a tool to improve mental health in adolescence, the authors wrote.

Anxiety is already the most common mental health problem among adolescents. The World Health Organization estimates that, globally, 4.4% of 10–14-year-olds and 5.5% of 15–19-year-olds experience an anxiety disorder – intense, persistent fear or nervousness that is hard to control.

Worryingly, mental health struggles in adolescence can have impacts later in life, highlighting the need for early identification and intervention.

Why teenagers' body clocks shift

People have a specific chronotype — whether someone is a morning or an evening person. While it is normally stable throughout life, the authors noted a significant shift towards eveningness in adolescence.

“During puberty, the body’s internal clock usually shifts back by a few hours, meaning teenagers naturally don’t start feeling sleepy until later and would ideally wake up later too,” said Sarah Chellappa, a co-author on the paper from the University of Southampton.

“Teenagers also face demands on their time, from early school starts to socialising online, which can rob them of sleep, especially during the week.”

The clash between this preference and early school start times creates a "perfect storm" for circadian misalignment, when the internal body clock is mismatched with the outside time.

“It’s important to look beyond what individuals can do alone and recognise how broader societal systems can influence sleep,” said Hannah Ravenhall, lead author of the paper.

“This starts with acknowledging the biological sleep changes that occur in adolescence, advocating for their sleep needs, and reconsidering secondary school start times to support young people’s wellbeing.”

The authors wrote that it is important that public health recommendations promote sleep health amongst adolescents and emphasise the importance of consistent sleep timing.

In practice, that could mean schools reconsidering start times and parents rethinking evening screen rules — small structural changes that, researchers argue, may do more for teenagers' mental health than simply telling them to "go to bed earlier."

World.title: Is coach travel underrated? Here are five journeys in Europe to take
World.content:
Think of coach trips, and you may conjure up an image of a rather naff way to see the world, favoured by people of retirement age.

 

Now, though, coach trips are having something of a renaissance – and they’re actually a great way to explore countries with ease and in comfort.

The Geneva-headquartered International Road Transport Union (IRU) is backing this trend and singing its praises.

“Coaches bring visitors from airports, ports and railway stations to historic cities, coastal destinations, mountain villages and cultural landmarks,” an IRU statement said.

“They make school trips possible, support business events and conferences, enable group travel and provide affordable holidays for families, young people and seniors alike.”

The body also points out coaches have the flexibility to reach smaller towns, rural regions and emerging destinations, something that’s not always possible with other forms of transport.

It says they’re relatively excellent for the environment, as high passenger capacity combined with greenhouse gas emissions per passenger means they’re comparable to long-distance rail, and coach trips are often more affordable than other holiday options.

If you’re keen to experience a coach trip for yourself, these are some of the best options currently running across Europe.

The Road to Rome - Insight Vacations

The quality and comfort of coaches can vary significantly, but Insight Vacations offers luxury coaches with double legroom and a decent Wi-Fi connection.

Its “Road to Rome” package is a great way to take the plunge into the world of coach trips. Starting in Paris, this 12-day tour will take passengers through France, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Austria, Italy, and the Vatican City.

Guests will stay at a variety of four-star hotels and experience the destinations with expert guides and skip-the-line access at top attractions.

Coaches are a great way to see many of Europe's treasures Michele Bitetto/Unsplash

Best of Italy - Trafalgar Coach Tours

Starting and ending in Rome, Trafalgar’s tour of Italy is a great option if you’d rather get to know one place in particular.

This tour, the operator’s most popular, takes passengers from the Eternal City to the likes of Tuscany, Venice, Florence and Pompeii over 13 days.

Guests will also get the chance to visit beautiful Capri by boat, and see underrated Lake Maggiore, a rival to hugely popular Lake Como, which is also a stop on this trip.

The benefit of exploring just one country is that you can get to know a lot of the culture and learn more of the language and customs, without the need to learn to say “hello” and “thank you” in multiple vernaculars.

Balkan Kaleidoscope - Penguin Travel

If the Balkans are on your travel bucket list, you may want to consider a coach trip around the region.

Penguin Travel’s Balkan Kaleidoscope kicks off in Sofia, before heading to Belgrade in Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina’s capital of Sarajevo.

The air-conditioned coach also rolls through Croatia, Montenegro, Kosovo, Albania and North Macedonia, and takes in UNESCO sites including Dubrovnik's Old Town and Kotor Bay.

Guests, who will have stayed in comfortable three-star hotels, will end the trip where they started in Sofia, where they can head home or continue exploring the fascinating Balkans.

The Best of Eastern Europe - Globus

Beginning and ending in Berlin, this Globus tour takes 14 days and offers a comprehensive overview of what it calls Eastern Europe (although some may argue the countries explored are technically Central Europe).

From the German capital, a luxury coach will ferry passengers through Germany, Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Austria, and Czechia.

Guests can see Berlin's Brandenburg Gate, Warsaw's Gothic Cathedral of St. John, and Prague's iconic Astronomical Clock.

The route, which covers some 2,048km, also features stops at Auschwitz, Jasna Góra Monastery in Częstochowa, Poland, and Dresden's Zwinger Palace – all accompanied by expert commentary.

Berlin-Prague-Vienna-Budapest - FlixBus

If you’re not a fan of organised holidays, it’s actually entirely possible to go it alone and plan your own European coach trip.

Enter FlixBus, which recently revealed its favourite options for “trip-maxxing” using its buses.

As Euronews Travel reported at the time, FlixBus named several four-stop routes with journeys under five hours apiece, and a trip from Berlin to Prague and onto Vienna and Budapest came out on top.

That particular route offers great nightlife, particularly in Berlin, and solid history and culture in all four cities.

Going it alone also means you can choose where you stay each night, and budget accordingly. There are also slightly fewer opportunities to make friendships on the coach due to the short journeys, but that might be something which appeals to a certain type of traveller…

World.title: 'We have to contribute to nature': Meet the communities 'marrying glaciers' to bring new water to life
World.content:
The world's highest peaks are located in the Himalaya and Karakoram mountain ranges, part of a vast mountain belt stretching across Asia. But beneath their grandeur lie some of the planet's most fragile ecosystems.

 

As temperatures continue to rise, glaciers are melting faster, increasing the risk of glacial lake outburst floods and disrupting the natural flow of meltwater. As glaciers shrink, less water is released in spring and summer, when communities need it the most.

In the Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan - an autonomous territory in the wider disputed Kashmir region - communities are turning to the Indigenous practice of glacier grafting, known locally as Gang Khswa, to combat water scarcity and adapt in the face of climate change.

What is glacier grafting?

Glacier grafting is a traditional method in which local communities create new, artificial glaciers in high-altitude regions to create a reliable source of water for irrigation, livestock and daily life.

The technique is often referred to as a glacier marriage, when ice is collected from so-called male and female glaciers and transported to a new grafting site, chosen by the community, to create a new glacier.

The male glacier is typically grey in colour and contains debris such as soil, sand and pebbles. The female glacier, by contrast, is lighter, almost transparent, clear from debris and impurities and produces more water.

Dozens of porters collect pieces of ice from both male and female glaciers. They then transport the ice to the newly-selected grafting site in wooden baskets on their backs, travelling by car as far as the terrain allows and then continuing on foot.

The ideal grafting site to create a new glacier needs to be at an altitude of at least 4,000 metres, have a high permafrost level, have maximum wind explosure and minimum explosure to sunlight, and ideally should be north-facing, Dr. Zakir Hussain Zakir, Director of Planning and Development at the University of Baltistan, explains to Euronews.

Two clay pots holding water from the river Indus separating "male" and "female" ice pieces at a grafting site. Baltistan Culture & Development Foundation (BCDF)

Once at the site, locals will have either dug a well or located an existing cave to place the ice in. The male and female ice pieces are placed inside, separated by clay pots holding water from the Indus river.

The ice is then covered with layers of sawdust, charcoal and apricot kernels. The process is repeated several times, creating multiple layers to protect and insulate the ice.

"It is a marathon activity," Dr. Zakir continues, explaining that the process can take up to 48 hours from ice collection to planting.

"From the collection of the ice pieces from the source to the destination, the ice has to be kept continuously moving," he adds, explaining that the ice is not allowed to touch the ground at any time during the journey.

While the site is surveyed and preparations are carried out during summer, the actual grafting takes place in October. By then, temperatures at altitudes of at least 4,000 metres will have dropped below zero, but there will be no snowfall yet.

Once the new glacier is exposed to several snow cycles, it will slowly start to expand. If successful, the glacier will start to root and produce water after about ten years. After roughly another decade, the glacier will have grown into a reliable water source.

Dr. Zakir highlighted two other techniques derived from glacier grafting: ice towering and avalanche harvesting.

Ice towers, also called ice stupas as their conical shape resembles a Buddhist sanctuary, act as ice reservoirs designed to melt slower as its surface area is not fully exposed to the sun. Developed in Ladakh, the technique involves passing glacier meltwater through underground pipes and spraying it into the freezing air.

Avalanche harvesting, a recent innovation, involves the installation of a mesh net in a narrow gorge to capture and store snow and ice from avalanches.

An ecological practice rooted in tradition

Although glacier grafting was only revived in the 1990s, the ecological practice goes back centuries and is deeply rooted in local tradition, knowledge and ancestry.

"The history of glacier grafting is largely oral, not written, although some books contain references [to the craft]," Nazir Ahmed, CEO of the Baltistan Culture & Development Foundation, explains to Euronews.

The history of glacier grafting is believed to date back to the 14th century. According to historical accounts, the Persian Sufi saint Mir Syed Ali Hamadani is said to have grafted the first glacier as a defence tactic to help deter invaders.

Porters travelling up to glacier grafting site, carrying ice pieces in wooden baskets on their backs. Baltistan Culture & Development Foundation (BCDF)

The unique craft is deeply intertwined with local traditions, including reciting verses from the Quran, singing a folk lullaby to the 'baby' glacier, and performing spiritual rituals.

"There are three myths," Ahmed explains. "One is that you need to carry the ice at night [...]. It is said that by carrying the ice during the day, God will not be happy, as you are bringing a new object in the territory."

"Secondly, when you're carrying the ice, you cannot talk to each other, otherwise you will become mute."

"And third, when the ice is buried at the top, you cannot see it for at least two years, otherwise, someone will die in your family," Ahmed concludes.

While these beliefs are rooted in mythology, the culture and heritage foundation CEO explains that they also serve a practical purpose.

Carrying the ice at night decreases the chance of disruptions and minimises melting because temperatures are at their lowest, while travelling in silence helps ice porters maintain a steady pace. Once buried, the newly planted ice must be left undisturbed for several years, allowing it to properly root while protecting it from being taken or disturbed by others.

The Baltistan Culture & Development Foundation (BCDF) is a local organisation formed by the people of Baltistan, dedicated to preserving and restoring heritage, promoting local culture and traditions, and protecting the region's environment.

In 2025, the BCDF received funding from the United Kingdom's Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO), allowing the foundation to expand its projects.

"Through the project, we grafted ten glaciers in different villages in Baltistan, six ice towers in different villages and one botanical garden in the University of Baltistan," Ahmed explains.

Prior to the funding, the foundation could only undertake smaller-scale projects, transporting up to 200 kilograms of ice. But it's now able to transport more than 1,000 kilograms of ice at a time.

The foundation has not yet received funding from either the provincial or federal government, although efforts are underway to have glacier grafting recognised by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage.

'How can the life giver itself be lifeless?'

From start to finish, the community plays a key role in the practice. No glacier can be seeded without the community's consent first, and once the grafting is complete, locals take on the responsibility of caring for the 'baby' glacier. They monitor its progress, report on its development and add snow when necessary to help it grow.

The Passu Glacier south of Passu village in Upper Hunza, Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan. 13 June, 2026. Evelyn Ann-Marie Dom

"We have to contribute to nature, to the climate, to the environment," Dr. Zakir says. "Because we are consuming snowmelt water for our entire life, and if we don't contribute something, it would be unjust".

He explained that this responsibility is rooted in the region's ancient civilisation and its spiritual foundation.

"In Bonism, we consider that all forms of water are sentient beings," he said. "Water is a life giver, so how can the life giver itself be lifeless?"

Young people are needed to continue the glacier grafting tradition

With community at the heart of the practice, youth engagement is crucial to keeping the tradition alive, especially as the region faces the growing impacts of climate change.

But Nazir Ahmed points out a growing challenge: many young people leave their communities to move to urban cities.

"If we talk about Skardu district, almost over 90 per cent of people are in school. And then after graduation, they usually go to cities like Karachi, Lahore or Islamabad for further study," the BCDF CEO explains, adding that grafting is also a labour and time intensive practice.

"I don't see this as a decline in environmental concern," Zeeshan Abbas, team leader at the youth-led initiative Siachen Sherpa, points out to Euronews. He says that alongside climate change, young people are increasingly concerned about issues such as education, employment, economic security and migration.

"Many young people understand that glaciers are changing and that climate change is affecting the region, but few have the resources, opportunities or institutional support to participate in field projects".

Abbas also believes the way climate action is presented needs to change.

"If we tell young people that climate change is a crisis, they can become overwhelmed," he said. Instead, he argues, younger generations should be empowered to see themselves as capable of developing solutions.

According to the 19-year-old, his generation holds a powerful and unique position in society.

"We inherit Indigenous knowledge from our communities, but we also have access to modern science, digital tools and technology, and global networks," Abbas says, highlighting how Siachen Sherpa aims to bridge these two forms of knowledge.

"Local communities understand the landscape through generations of experience - where water flows, how the terrain behaves, where freezing occurs and how seasonal conditions change. Technology helps us complement that knowledge through satellite information, GPS, terrain and altitude data and field observations," he added.

"Young people should not be treated as only victims of climate change, they should be given the opportunity to become researchers, innovators, field practitioners and decision-makers," Abbas concluded.

Countries contributing less to global emissions often suffer more

Pakistan's Third Pole glaciers irrigate 90 per cent of agricultural land and sustain more than 220 million people, according to the World Economic Forum.

The Third Pole, or the Hindu Kush, Karakoram and Himalaya mountain range contains the world’s largest volume of frozen freshwater outside the Arctic and Antarctic polar regions.

Experts warn that human-caused global warming is placing unprecedented pressure on these regions, with floods, landslides, avalanches and droughts increasing in frequency and intensity.

"In Northern Pakistan, the melting of the Hindu Kush, Karakoram, and Himalayan glaciers due to rising temperatures have created 3,044 glacial lakes in the federally-administered territory of Gilgit-Baltistan and province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa," the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the leading UN organisation fighting to end the injustice of poverty, inequality and climate change, wrote in a statement.

People walking through the village of Sost, with a vast mountain range as backdrop in Upper Hunza, Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan. 12 June, 2026. Evelyn Ann-Marie Dom

"It is estimated that 33 of these glacial lakes are hazardous and likely to result in glacial lake outburst floods," the statement further read, adding that such flooding can release millions of cubic metres of water and debris in just a few hours.

Last week, a glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering a tsunami-like flood in Nepal and Tibet.

There are several causes of glacier collapses. On the one hand they can be normal, cyclical processes. Increasingly, though, they are being driven by human-induced climate change.

Despite contributing less than 1 per cent of global emissions annually, Pakistan is one of the countries most vulnerable to climate change. Meanwhile, a 2025 study revealed that the world's wealthiest 10 per cent are responsible for two-thirds of global warming since 1990.

World.title: Europe's most charitable countries: Where do people give the most?
World.content:
Nearly six in ten Europeans gave money to good causes in 2025, either by directly helping people in need, donating to charity or giving for religious reasons. This is according to the World Giving Report by the Charities Aid Foundation (CAF).

 

In its latest global report, CAF surveyed 60,443 people in 105 countries between 5 January and 18 February 2026 about giving throughout 2025, with nationally representative country samples generally ranging from 250 to 1,000 adults.

According to the findings, the most generous European countries included Ireland and Romania. Looking specifically at charitable giving, Ireland and the Netherlands had the highest shares of people donating to charity. Romania also ranked among the highest when measured by the proportion of income given, with charitable donations averaging around 0.4% of income in all three countries.

According to CAF’s data, more than two-thirds of people in Ireland were charity donors in 2025, slightly more than in the Netherlands.

Romania presents a radically different picture: only 27% gave to charity, yet charitable donations averaged 0.4% of income.

When examining how much countries give overall, including religious causes and direct donations to people in need, the survey found that Romania climbed to the top of the EU ranking, with donations averaging 0.9% of income. It was followed by Croatia with 0.8% and Ireland with 0.7%.

Total donations as a proportion of income were lowest in Latvia, while those given specifically to charities were lowest in Hungary and Slovakia.

No EU country makes the world's top 10 for generosity

Overall donations in the bloc’s three largest economies — Germany, France and Italy — averaged just 0.4% of income in 2025.

Europe is the least generous continent when giving is measured as a share of income, despite being overwhelmingly made up of high-income economies. Europeans donated an average of 0.6% of their income, compared with a global average of 1%.

Outside the EU, Ukraine stands out, with 61% of people giving money and donations averaging 1.2% of income.

According to the report, there is a strong relationship between how much people donate in a country and how strongly they feel a sense of belonging to their local community.

Countries where more than 80% of the population feel a strong sense of belonging give, on average, three times as much as countries where fewer than half of people feel this way.

Who do Europeans give to and what causes do they support?

In Europe, giving to charities was the most common route, with 38% of people donating this way. Another 26% gave directly to people in need, while 14% gave to religious organisations or for religious reasons.

Globally, direct giving was the most common form, with 36% giving money directly to people in need.

More than one-fifth of donors, 22%, supported charities that work across multiple countries. Europeans also favour international charities, with Norway and Sweden being the only countries where more than half of donors supported organisations working internationally.

For Europeans, the most widely supported cause was children and young people, backed by 29% of people who donated.

Global rankings

The difference between the most and least generous countries is striking.

According to the report, Nigeria pocketed the top spot as the world’s most generous country, with people giving an average of 2.8% of their income to charities, religious causes or directly to people in need.

The contrast with Europe is particularly striking: all of the global top 10 are low-income or lower-middle-income countries, while Europe recorded the lowest average giving as a share of income of any continent.

Eight of the top 10 most generous countries are located in Africa, while two are in Asia. In these countries, 80% of people donated, compared with the global average of 61%, while they gave an average of 2.1% of their income — more than double the global average of 1%.

Donors in these countries gave nearly half, or 45%, of the money they donated directly to people and families in need.

At the other end of the scale is Japan, where people donated an average 0.2% of their income — the lowest proportion among the 105 countries surveyed.

The economic gap between the two countries is striking: Japan's nominal GDP per capita is roughly 28 times Nigeria's.

Japan also recorded the lowest level of trust in charities among the countries surveyed, with an average trust score of five out of 10. Only 15% of people in Japan donated specifically to charity in 2025.

The survey found that two in five people who did not donate said it was because they could not afford it. At 39%, this was by far the leading reason for not giving. The report also found that those living in high-income countries were the most likely to say they could not afford to give, at 44%, compared with 37% in other countries.

The second most common reason for not donating was preferring to offer support in other ways, cited by 17%. Among this group, most said that they had given goods, volunteered or fundraised.

World.title: Russia to close branches of Germany's Goethe-Institut
World.content:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the move was in response to Germany's decision to close the Russian House in Berlin after blaming Moscow for an attemped drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Thursday that Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centers would be closed in Russia.

In remarks carried by Russian news agencies TASS and Interfax, Lavrov said Goethe-Institut branches would be closed in the Russian cities of Moscow, St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg.

The statement came after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted ‌drone ⁠attack at ⁠the Leipzig/Halle Airport. Germany's response to that incident included closing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn.

'End' of German cultural presence in Russia

"Of course they will be closed after our cultural center was expelled from there [from Berlin]," Lavrov said, speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.

"They deliberately took this step — they could not have failed to understand — which means the end of their cultural presence in Russia," Lavrov said, according to state news agency TASS.

He added the centers had remained open "despite all the Ukrainian complications in our relations with the West."

Russia has also threatened to take further measures, possibly including the closure of Germany's consulate general in St. Petersburg.

On Wednesday, Russia's Foreign Ministry summoned the charge d'affaires of the German Embassy in Moscow to protest Berlin's response to the August drone incident. According to the ministry, the official was called in over what it described as anti-Russian actions and statements by the German leadership.

On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence to blame Moscow for the explosives-laden drone.

Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What is the Goethe-Institut?

Russia's first Goethe-Institut opened in Moscow in 1992, shortly after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

The cultural organization operates in around 100 countries worldwide, promoting the study of the German language and providing information about German culture and society.

The Goethe-Institut is one of the last German institutions still operating in Russia.

Moscow has labeled several foreign organizations "undesirable," effectively banning them from operating.

In 2018, Russia ordered the closure of the British Council following a diplomatic dispute with the UK.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

World.title: US: 3 dead including suspect in Minneapolis shooting
World.content:
The motive for the shooting is still unclear. Local authorities and the FBI are responding to the incident.

Two people were killed and the suspect also died after a shooting at a downtown Minneapolis apartment building Wednesday afternoon, police said.

Three Minneapolis police officers were injured, Sgt. Garrett Parten said at a news conference Wednesday evening. Two officers suffered gunshot wounds. All three were in stable condition, according to a hospital spokesperson.

One victim was fatally shot at the scene, while the other died after being taken to Hennepin County Medical Center, Parten said.

Minneapolis police responded shortly after 4:30 p.m. local time (21:30 GMT) and urged the public to stay away from the area. Two police officers were among those wounded, officials said. Seven patients were taken to Hennepin Healthcare Medical Center, according to the hospital.

FBI also involved in response as motive unclear

The FBI is responding to the shooting and "will offer any and all resources necessary to assist local authorities," Director Kash Patel said in a post on the social platform X.

No further information was immediately available about the incident. The motive for the shooting is still unclear and information has not been released yet on the identity of the shooter.

Video posted on social media showed police officers aiming rifles toward an apartment tower near the Minneapolis Convention Center. Officials also warned residents to avoid the densely populated Loring Park neighborhood.

The shooter was confirmed dead at the scene, according to US media reports Image: ABC affiliate KSTP/REUTERS

"Grateful to law enforcement actively working to ensure the safety of our neighbors in Downtown Minneapolis this afternoon,” Minnesota Governor Tim Walz said. “Minnesota is praying for our first responders.”
