World.title: PM Magyar meets Costa, sets conditions for backing EU’s next 7-year budget
World.content:
The Hungarian government will only be able to approve the European Union’s new seven-year budget if it serves the interests of Hungarian people and businesses, Prime Minister Péter Magyar told European Council President António Costa during a meeting in Budapest on Wednesday.

In a Facebook post following the meeting, Magyar said he had also told Costa that Hungary expected an early solution to the issue of the EUR 1 million-a-day fine imposed under the previous Hungarian government to be suspended.

According to Magyar, he also stressed that, particularly in light of events in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in Africa this summer, Hungary would continue to maintain the legal framework and physical border barrier needed to stop illegal migration.

“Hungary will continue to protect the European Union’s external borders. And we expect these efforts to be recognised at European level as well,” Magyar said.

The prime minister added that he had reiterated during the meeting that Hungary does not support an accelerated EU accession process for any candidate country.

Hungary opposes fast-track EU membership

The comments come as the EU prepares its next seven-year budget, with member states facing negotiations over how the bloc’s financial priorities and funding will be structured for the coming period.

Magyar’s remarks also show the Hungarian government’s position on migration and EU enlargement, signalling that Budapest intends to maintain its existing border protection measures while opposing what it considers accelerated accession procedures.

World.title: Michelin-starred chef brings a new taste of Hungary to Time Out Market Budapest
World.content:
Ákos Sárközi is bringing together the culinary worlds of Borkonyha and Textúra in a new, more relaxed concept at Budapest’s Time Out Market. Fúzió by Textúra & Borkonyha will open on 11 September, offering Hungarian-inspired bistro dishes with a creative twist.

A new restaurant concept is coming to Time Out Market Budapest this September, as Michelin-starred chef Ákos Sárközi brings his latest culinary venture to the capital’s popular food hall.

Fúzió by Textúra & Borkonyha will open on 11 September at the Corvin Palace on Blaha Lujza Square, combining the distinctive culinary identities of two well-known Budapest restaurants in a more relaxed and accessible format.

The concept is designed to introduce a wider audience to Sárközi’s approach to Hungarian cuisine, with playful, modern takes on familiar bistro dishes.

Two restaurants, one culinary vision

Fúzió has grown out of the professional collaboration between Borkonyha and Textúra, two Budapest restaurants led by Sárközi Ákos alongside co-owners Tamás Horváth and Zoltán Kalocsai.

Borkonyha has been one of the most consistent names in Hungarian gastronomy. It received its Michelin star in 2014 and has retained the distinction ever since. Its cuisine combines traditional and contemporary Hungarian flavours with influences from Transylvanian culinary traditions and international gastronomy.

Textúra, which joined Borkonyha as its sister restaurant in 2018, is now entering a new chapter of its own, moving closer to the approachable world of bistro dining in both its food and atmosphere while retaining the creativity and experimentation that define its kitchen.

Although the two restaurants have distinct personalities, they complement one another closely. Fúzió aims to capture precisely this balance, adapting it to the informal, communal setting of Time Out Market.

The new concept is also intended to reach diners who may not regularly visit traditional restaurants but are interested in high-quality food served in a quicker, more relaxed setting.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Hungarian bistro classics with a creative twist

At the heart of Fúzió will be Hungarian-style bistro cuisine, interpreted through Sárközi’s playful and inventive approach.

Several dishes will be available exclusively at Time Out Market Budapest, including duck liver with Tokaji Aszú, pear and breadstick, juicy roast pork brioche with a thyme sauce, and “Barack virág” (“Peach blossom”) Rákóczi túrós, a creative take on the beloved Hungarian cottage-cheese dessert.

The duck liver dish brings together traditional Hungarian ingredients and contemporary presentation, while the roast pork brioche takes inspiration from szalontüdő, a classic Hungarian dish traditionally made with offal.

“There is beauty in simplicity, but when it is combined with creativity, it can become something memorable. We should be proud of the diversity of Hungarian cuisine,” said Ákos Sárközi, executive chef.

For Sárközi, one of the key aims of Fúzió is to make high-end gastronomy feel less distant and intimidating.

“People often put Michelin-starred chefs in a bubble and think that I only make dishes that are difficult for everyone to understand. At Time Out Market, I have the opportunity to show that I am the same ordinary person I have always been and always will be: I love cooking and I love eating,” he said.

The experience goes beyond the plate

Márton Tibor, the manager and coordinator of Borkonyha and Textúra, will play a central role in Fúzió’s day-to-day operation. He will oversee the team, help maintain the restaurant’s professional standards and coordinate the new concept.

Preparations for the 11 September opening are already underway, with test cooking sessions taking place and the team taking shape. The aim is to create an experience that goes beyond simply having a meal.

“It is a huge source of pride for me to represent Fúzió at Time Out Market. It is another professional journey and challenge, where we are stepping outside the traditional walls of a restaurant and entering a marketplace where gastronomy and culture meet directly and create a shared experience,” Márton Tibor said.

The team will also help guests navigate the menu, offering explanations and personal recommendations so that diners can comfortably explore a new take on Hungarian bistro cuisine.

If you missed it: Gordon Ramsay chooses Budapest for first Central European restaurant – opening date revealed

A new addition to Time Out Market’s autumn line-up

Fúzió will join Time Out Market Budapest’s existing selection of restaurants and three bars, adding another culinary direction to the venue’s offering.

Located inside the Corvin Palace at Blaha Lujza Square, Time Out Market Budapest brings together chefs, restaurants, drinks and cultural experiences under one roof. Constant curation and renewal are central to the international Time Out Market concept, with new culinary partners regularly joining its venues.

Balogh Olivér, owner of Time Out Market Budapest, said Fúzió represents exactly the kind of new addition the Market is looking for: a distinctive concept offering high-quality gastronomy in a more accessible format.

The arrival of Fúzió will also coincide with a busy autumn at the Market. The venue will celebrate its first anniversary in September with special programmes and offers, while the autumn season will feature seasonal harvest-inspired dishes, wine events and cultural programmes.

Time Out Market Budapest

Address: 1 Blaha Lujza Square, Corvin Palace, 1085 Budapest

Opening hours: Daily, 11:30–23:30. Kitchens close at 22:00, while the last call at the bars is at 23:00.

Fúzió by Textúra & Borkonyha opens: 11 September

Reservations and further information are available through Time Out Market Budapest’s official channels.

World.title: Hungary could publish up to 80,000 names in Communist-era secret service files
World.content:
Hungary could soon see tens of thousands of names revealed from the country’s Communist-era secret service files, with government estimates suggesting that as many as 60,000–80,000 people could be identified.

Bálint Ruff, head of the Prime Minister’s Office, told Telex that the figure was based on professional estimates concerning the potential disclosure of names contained in the files.

“I have an idea of the number,” Ruff said, while stressing that he did not know whether the documents would include people who later became important political or economic figures after the fall of Communism in 1990.

“The agent files are a very important part of our shared past, and there will be many things in them that will cause sadness for many families,” he said.

Who could appear in the files?

The possible publication of tens of thousands of names could make the Communist-era secret service files one of the most politically and socially sensitive historical disclosures in modern Hungary.

Ruff did not say that all of the people whose names could appear were necessarily secret agents or informants. The files may contain the names of people who had various connections to the state security apparatus, meaning that the precise nature of an individual’s involvement would need to be established from the documents.

He also said he did not know whether people who went on to become prominent political or economic figures after 1990 would be among those named.

If you missed it: Hungary submits landmark bill to open Communist-era secret service files

Around 100 documents could be declassified this week

Ruff said he hoped that approximately 100 documents known as “No. 3,000 resolutions” would be declassified and published later this week. He said questions of potential criminal responsibility would have to be decided by investigating authorities.

According to Ruff, the documents concern decisions and contracts that were signed by identifiable officials. He noted that the relevant “3,000” documents were signed by the prime minister in office at the time.

The government has also indicated that it intends to make public information concerning the travels of János Lázár, who served in senior government positions under Viktor Orbán. Ruff claimed that he knew where Lázár had travelled, what he had done and why the information had previously been kept secret. He said these details would also be made public.

Government says complaints involve HUF 2 trillion

The disclosure of the historical documents comes alongside a broader government investigation into the use of public money under previous administrations.

Ruff said the government had so far filed complaints in cases involving a total value of HUF 2 trillion (EUR 5.4 billion).

One of the ongoing investigations concerns Századvég, a Hungarian think tank that Ruff said had received between HUF 20 billion and HUF 30 billion in public money over the past decade for research and studies. He said a criminal complaint would also be filed in connection with that case.

The government has already filed a complaint concerning Observer, a media-monitoring company, over what Ruff described as “exorbitant” sums paid for its services.

He also referred to the Kommentár Foundation, claiming that properties worth “twenty billion” forints had been purchased for the organisation. Ruff added that colleagues were currently calculating the sums paid to the Nézőpont Institute.

The allegations and complaints mentioned by Ruff do not in themselves establish criminal wrongdoing; any potential criminal liability will ultimately be determined by the competent authorities.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

A long-running question in Hungary

The fate of Hungary’s Communist-era secret service files has been a contentious issue for decades. Successive governments have faced pressure to make the records more accessible and clarify the activities of the former state security services. The issue is particularly sensitive because some people who were connected to the Communist-era system later became influential figures in post-1990 Hungary.

If the government proceeds with the planned disclosures, the publication of tens of thousands of names could reignite long-running debates about political responsibility, collaboration with the former regime and the extent to which the past has been fully confronted. For many Hungarian families, however, the revelations could have consequences far beyond politics, potentially exposing secrets that have remained hidden for generations.

World.title: Orbán government secretly allocated more than EUR 1.35 billion public funds just before April’s election
World.content:
The Orbán government secretly allocated at least HUF 500 billion (EUR 1.36 billion) in public funds in the months before the April election, according to an investigation by Hungarian news outlet 24.hu based on previously non-public government decisions obtained through a public-interest data request.

The money was allocated to companies, foundations, associations, cultural organisations, dioceses and various areas of the state budget. Funding was also provided for sporting events, other programmes and property purchases.

55 secret Orbán government decisions released

According to 24.hu, the documents consist of 55 so-called “2000” government decisions obtained from the Prime Minister’s Office. They had not previously been publicly available. The Prime Minister’s Office reportedly determined that these 55 documents could be disclosed because their publication did not conflict with national security, defence or law-enforcement interests.

Based on their numbering, however, 24.hu estimates that another 28 decisions could remain confidential. The disclosed documents reveal hundreds of billions of forints in government allocations and commitments.

Billions allocated to companies

Sixteen companies received a combined HUF 47 billion (more than EUR 127.67 million), with individual allocations ranging from HUF 190 million to HUF 14 billion (from around EUR 516,000 to more than EUR 38 million). One of the largest packages, worth around HUF 14 billion, was conditionally offered to Rosenberger Magyarország Elektronikai Kft. and Rosenberger Automotive Cabling Kft. for manufacturing capacity expansions at three sites outside Budapest.

Vajda-Papír Kft. was awarded more than HUF 11.5 billion (more than EUR 31.2 million) for an investment in Dunaföldvár, with a substantial part of the funding reportedly due to be paid in 2027.

HUF 6.2 billion for heritage foundation

The Orbán government also awarded HUF 6.2 billion (more than EUR 16.8 million) to the Central European Foundation for the Preservation of Built Heritage, which has been associated with Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó.

Companies established by the foundation have acquired properties in neighbouring countries, including derelict historic buildings, with plans to convert some into hotels. The reason for the HUF 6.2 billion allocation was reportedly not clear from the Orbán government’ decision.

Other spending included HUF 706 million (around EUR 1.9 million) for the state company responsible for managing state-owned castles and HUF 76 billion (almost EUR 206.5) for the construction of the Danube bridge at Mohács.

HUF 8.6 billion for motorcycle racing

The Orbán government also allocated HUF 8.6 billion (more than EUR 23.35 million) to support the year’s MotoGP and Superbike motorcycle racing events. Meanwhile, HUF 1.043 billion (around EUR 2.83 million) was set aside for the establishment of two infant homes in Esztergom and Zalaegerszeg.

One of the final confidential decisions reportedly came after the government’s election defeat. Signed by Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, it instructed ministers to take steps to ensure previously undertaken financial commitments were fulfilled before the government handover, where their lawful fulfilment could be established.

In case you missed it: Internal documents show Orbán-linked politician and businessman had unlimited power over Hungary’s public media

Legal questions over secret decisions

Miklós Ligeti, legal director of Transparency International Hungary, told 24.hu that using “2000” decisions to allocate budgetary funds was unlawful in formal terms. According to Ligeti, Hungarian law requires budget reallocations and financial allocations to be published in the Official Gazette, meaning they cannot be made through unpublished decisions of the Orbán government.

This is a legal assessment rather than a court ruling, and the legality of individual decisions remains a matter for the relevant authorities or courts. The disclosures have nevertheless raised fresh questions over the transparency and timing of the Orbán government’s use of public funds in the period surrounding the election.

World.title: Hungary condemns Russia’s ‘serious threat’ after alleged drone plot in Germany
World.content:
Hungary has condemned what it describes as an increasingly dangerous pattern of Russian hybrid activity in Europe, offering its “full solidarity” to Germany after Berlin accused Moscow of involvement in an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said Hungary was “deeply concerned” by the growing number and intensity of Russian hybrid operations on European soil.

“Recent incidents in Germany demonstrate an increasingly dangerous and reckless pattern of behaviour that poses a serious threat to European security and resilience,” she wrote on X.

The foreign minister added that Hungary was ready to support Germany in tackling hybrid threats.

Hungary is deeply concerned by the growing number and intensity of Russian hybrid activities on European soil. Recent incidents in Germany demonstrate an increasingly dangerous and reckless pattern of behaviour that poses a serious threat to European security and resilience.… — Anita Orban (@_OrbanAnita) September 1, 2026

Germany blames Russia for attempted airport attack

The statement came after Germany formally accused Russia on 1 September of being behind an attempted explosive drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

German authorities reportedly discovered a drone carrying explosives at the airport in August, close to several Ukrainian cargo aircraft. Evidence gathered at the scene was said to point towards Russian involvement.

Berlin responded by summoning Russia’s ambassador and ordering the closure of Russia’s Consulate General in Bonn, among other measures. Moscow has denied any involvement in the incident.

The alleged attack is being investigated as part of a larger pattern of suspected Russian hybrid operations in Europe, which have included alleged sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns and other forms of covert activity.

Budapest calls for stronger EU and NATO cooperation

Orbán said these developments demonstrated the need for Europe to strengthen its ability to withstand hybrid threats.

“In the face of these challenges, strengthening the resilience, unity and collective preparedness of the European Union and NATO is more important than ever,” she said.

Hungary also expressed its willingness to help Germany respond to the threats, saying it stood in “full solidarity” with its European partner. The position is notable given Hungary’s traditionally more accommodating relationship with Moscow compared with many other EU and NATO members.

Under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, Budapest frequently criticised EU sanctions against Russia and maintained diplomatic and economic links with Moscow even as relations between Russia and the West deteriorated following the invasion of Ukraine.

World.title: BREAKING: Hungary blocks Ukraine’s EU accession again – Here’s what Budapest wants
World.content:
Hungary has blocked Ukraine’s EU accession process for a third time, with the government saying it will only lift its objection if Kyiv makes progress on the rights of the country’s Hungarian minority.

The latest dispute emerged at the European Council’s Working Party on Enlargement and Countries Negotiating Accession (COELA), which held its first meeting after the summer recess on Tuesday, 1 September.

According to Ukrainska Pravda citing European Pravda’s sources in Brussels, Hungary refused to approve the screening results for Ukraine’s second and third negotiating clusters. Without unanimous support from all 27 EU member states, the Council cannot move forward with formally opening the clusters.

Budapest links its position to minority rights

The Hungarian government has said that it will not support further progress in Ukraine’s accession talks until Kyiv takes what Budapest considers necessary steps to fulfil its commitments concerning national minority rights.

The issue is particularly sensitive because Ukraine is home to a sizeable ethnic Hungarian community in the Transcarpathia region, near Hungary’s eastern border.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has previously taken a somewhat different approach to Ukraine from his predecessor, Viktor Orbán. In June, Magyar and Ukraine reached what the Hungarian leader described as a “historic agreement” aimed at guaranteeing the educational, cultural, linguistic and political rights of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia.

Despite that agreement, Budapest has maintained objections to several stages of Ukraine’s EU accession process.

What are the two clusters Hungary is blocking?

The latest Hungarian objection concerns Cluster 2, covering the EU internal market, and Cluster 3, which deals with competitiveness and inclusive growth. Hungary had previously blocked technical preparations for Ukraine’s Clusters 2–6. It subsequently lifted its objection to Cluster 6, which covers foreign and security policy, trade policy and relations with third countries.

In July, Hungary also supported advancing Cluster 3 for Moldova. However, most EU member states, led by Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, opposed separating Moldova’s and Ukraine’s accession tracks. As a result, neither country made progress on the matter at the time.

The next COELA meeting is scheduled for Wednesday, 2 September, although Ukraine and Moldova are reportedly not on the agenda, Kyiv Post writes.

Ukraine’s accession talks remain complicated

Ukraine formally began its EU accession negotiations in 2024, but opening individual negotiating clusters requires the unanimous agreement of the bloc’s member states. That gives Hungary significant leverage over the process.

The latest blockage comes after EU governments formally opened the first negotiating cluster — “Fundamentals” — for Ukraine and Moldova on 15 June.

Under the previous government, Viktor Orbán repeatedly opposed Ukraine’s EU membership and used concerns over the rights of the Hungarian minority as one of the reasons for his position. His government had also held up the opening of the first cluster for years.

The change in Budapest’s approach under Magyar has therefore been notable, although it has not removed Hungary’s objections to Ukraine’s accession process.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Budapest says it does not want all clusters opened at once

Magyar has previously argued that Ukraine’s accession negotiations should proceed gradually rather than seeing all six clusters opened simultaneously.

“There are six clusters in total, and we don’t think opening them all at once is a good idea,” he said in June, arguing that the process should also take into account the Western Balkan countries that have spent years working towards EU membership.

For Kyiv, however, every delay is significant as it seeks to advance through the lengthy accession process and bring the country closer to EU membership.

World.title: Contemporary art breathes new life into small railway station in northern Romania
World.content:
The building of the railway station in Săcel, in Maramureș County, will host contemporary art and community programs as part of a project developed by the Romanian Association for Contemporary Art (ARAC)/ Anca Poterașu Gallery.

The station in Săcel (Halta Săcel) is located on an active railway line, with four trains stopping there daily.

This summer, the building was repaired and adapted for cultural activities in a project “preserving the building’s identity and complying with the specific requirements of railway infrastructure.”

Romania’s national railway company CFR has made the building of the train station available to ARAC for the project Linia Izei Art Center. As part of the project, the building has been turned into a permanent space dedicated to contemporary art, artist residencies and community programs, while railway operations in the area continue, CFR announced.

Linia Izei Art Center is inaugurated on Thursday, September 3, with the exhibition Rhythms of Continuity, gathering works by the artists Matei Bejenaru, Iosif Király, Aurora Király, Ioana Cîrlig, Megan Dominescu, Iulian Bisericaru, Mihaela Moldovan, Dan Vezentan, Radu Marțin, Anton Király, Ilie Mihali and Anetta Mona Chișa. The projects were developed in relation to the heritage, landscape and communities of the Iza Valley.

World.title: Paul Lynch, David Foenkinos and Aleksandar Hemon among guests of this year’s literature festival in Iași
World.content:
The Iași International Literature and Translation Festival (FILIT) returns this October, when the public will have the opportunity to meet leading names from the Romanian and international literary and cultural scene.

Among the authors who will be present in Iași are Paul Lynch, the winner of the 2023 Booker Prize for the novel Prophet Song, which has received numerous other international awards and has been translated into more than 35 languages, and French novelist and playwright David Foenkinos, known for his best-selling novels, which have been translated into around 40 languages.

The festival will also welcome Parinoush Saniee, the author of The Book of Fate, which was banned twice in Iran before becoming an international bestseller translated into more than 26 languages and receiving numerous awards. Also attending will be Aleksandar Hemon, the Bosnian-American writer whose numerous accolades include major international literary prizes. He is the author of the novels The Lazarus Project and The Nowhere Man, and co-wrote The Matrix Resurrections, the fourth film in the sci-fi franchise.

Other authors announced by the Iași festival include: Elena Alexieva (Bulgaria), Éric Chacour (Canada), Yavuz Ekinci (Turkey), Milena Michiko Flašar (Austria), Ramon Gener (Spain), Dinçer Güçyeter (Germany), Hallgrímur Helgason (Iceland), Roskva Koritzinsky (Norway), Alexandre Lenot (France), Andriy Lyubka (Ukraine), Laura Pariani (Italy), Anna Sólyom (Hungary), Marek Torčík (Czech Republic), Hattie Williams (United Kingdom), and Gabriella Zalapì (Switzerland).

The Romanian writers taking part in this year’s edition include Gabriela Adameșteanu, Simona Antonescu, Andreea Berechet, Iulian Bocai, Lavinia Braniște, Geanina Cărbunariu, Gilbert Costache, Gelu Duminică, Filip Florian, Delia Grigore, Florin Irimia, Ilinca Mănescu, Mircea Mihăieș, Alex Moldovan, Ana-Maria Negrilă, Ioana Pârvulescu, Florin Pitea, Radu Paraschivescu, Andreea Sterea, Adriana Ștefan, Daniel Timariu, Ioana Unk, Cristian Vicol, and Vlad Zografi.

Poets Andrei Dósa, Silvia Goteanschii, Emanuel Guralivu, Emanuela Ignăţoiu-Sora, Vasile Leac, Ciprian Măceșaru, Andrei Novac, Sorina Rîndașu, Codruța Simina, and Moni Stănilă will also meet audiences at events throughout October.

FILIT 2026 will also bring together translators who make it possible for Romanian authors to reach bookstores and publishing markets abroad. They include Iulia Badea-Guéritée (France), Alexandru Bulucz (Germany), Jan Cornelius (Germany), Anna Kaźmierczak (Poland), Eva Kenderessy (Slovakia), Joanna Kornaś-Warwas (Poland), Borja Mozo Martín (Spain), Marian Ochoa de Eribe (Spain), Charlotte van Rooden (the Netherlands), Andreea Scridon (Romania/US), and Imre Szőcs (Romania).

This year’s FILIT takes place from October 21 to October 25. The full list of guests, which will include other writers, cultural managers, publishers, journalists, and artists, will be announced at a later date.

World.title: Social Democrat PSD and far-right AUR reportedly sign parliamentary agreement
World.content:
Lawmakers from the Liberal (PNL) and Save Romania Union (USR) parties protested on September 2 against the Social Democrats' breach of the agreement governing the former ruling coalition, after PSD supported the allocation of several administrative positions to representatives of the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) and SOS Romania.

PSD parliamentarians signed an agreement with representatives of AUR, the SOS Romania party and the national minorities group on the allocation of positions in the Permanent Bureau of the Chamber of Deputies, Csoma Botond, the leader of the Hungarian party UDMR's deputies, said, as reported by Bursa.ro.

“PSD formed a new majority, and we learned about this agreement in the plenary session. We did not sign it. It was signed only by PSD, AUR, SOS and the national minorities group. (...) We have only one quaestor position in the Permanent Bureau, UDMR, in all parliamentary sessions, in all eight parliamentary sessions during the mandate. And there was talk that maybe, maybe we should not have a quaestor position in all parliamentary sessions,” said Csoma Botond, the leader of UDMR's deputies, told Agerpres.

PSD deputy Mihai Ghigiu explained that the new appointments to leading positions in the Chamber of Deputies were made legally, under an agreement between the leaders of the parliamentary groups, including PSD and AUR, denying that PSD had formed an alliance with AUR and SOS Romania, according to G4media.ro. He argued that voting for the appointment of an AUR representative as secretary of the Permanent Bureau of the Chamber of Deputies “does not represent an understanding between PSD and AUR.”

“Yesterday, exactly that happened: a different rotation was operated compared to what was decided a year or so ago. The group leaders, the majority of whom represent the majority of deputies, decided on this new rotation. So no one was deprived of a position, no one was deprived of any right, but effectively a different form of rotation was established for those who exercise the function of secretary of the Chamber,” Mihai Ghigiu said in Parliament.

The reaction came after USR and PNL said they would challenge before the Constitutional Court of Romania (CCR) the decision adopted by the Chamber of Deputies to replace their representatives with deputies from AUR and SOS Romania.

World.title: EC reportedly requires Romania to provide clarifications on Integrity Agency Law
World.content:
The European Commission has required Romania to provide clarifications regarding the so-called "Fritz amendment" in the new Integrity Agency Law, which leaves the mayor of Timișoara without a mandate. Specifically, the Commission seeks to understand how the law can be applied retroactively without being retroactive in itself, according to G4media.ro and Digi24.

According to information from Digi24, European Commission officials want to know whether these changes continue to preserve legal certainty, comply with European law and respect the principle of proportionality, as well as whether the law is being applied retroactively.

In recent weeks, there have been heated debates in Romanian society between the government and the opposition, as well as between those who amended the law and those who oppose the amendments.

USR representatives said that the law applies retroactively to those found to have been in a conflict of interest, meaning that the punishment takes effect as soon as the law is promulgated by the president of Romania, for an act for which the respective mayor was found guilty in the past.

This situation does not concern only the mayor of Timișoara, Dominic Fritz, the leader of USR. There are several other mayors across the country who could be affected.

Brussels also wants to assess whether the principle of proportionality is being applied, according to Digi24, given that the punishment must also be assessed according to the seriousness of the offence. The automatic termination of a mandate obtained through an election can represent a particularly serious consequence.

The Integrity Law is being assessed under the sixth and final PNRR payment request, which has not yet been submitted by the Romanian authorities.

World.title: Asirom launches anti-drone insurance coverage in Romania
World.content:
Asirom announced a first for the Romanian insurance market: compensation for damage to buildings and property resulting from armed conflicts - a type of coverage that the insurance industry typically excludes from standard policies due to its unpredictable nature, according to a press release.

Specifically, if an insured home suffers material damage caused by a drone or its fragments, regardless of their origin, owners covered by the Căminul Meu policy will now receive compensation for the damage caused.

Recent years have brought a change in perspective for Romanians, as incidents related to regional conflicts have turned a risk that was until recently considered theoretical into a real concern for many homeowners.

“People don't have to be insurance specialists to understand whether they are protected or not. If a drone or its fragments reach the territory of Romania and damage a home, the question that every person asks is simple: am I compensated? From September 2, for Asirom clients who have Căminul Meu home insurance, the answer is yes,” explained Mădălin Roșu, President of the Board of Directors of Asirom Vienna Insurance Group.

The coverage extension to the Căminul Meu home insurance policy applies to direct material damage to the insured home and property caused by: war and civil war; acts of terrorism; sabotage; military revolt and coup d’état; insurrection, revolution and rebellion; politically motivated intentional acts of destruction; and the expenses necessary to remove debris resulting from such an event are also included, within the limits established by the policy.

World.title: Market incentives and rising installed RES-E capacity encourage more BESS investment in Romania
World.content:
During August, the power output capacity of Romania’s BESS installations increased by 100 MW, while their storage capacity rose by 335 MWh, indicating significant expansion and a shift towards equipment with longer discharge durations.

At the end of the month, Romania reached 1,094 MW of installed BESS power capacity and 2,310 MWh of storage capacity, Economica.net reported.

The largest storage facility to enter commercial operation last month was the 160 MWh Glodeni 3 battery, operated by Energyglod, owned by businessman Claudiu Șugar.

The largest battery in Romania is the 400 MWh facility in Florești, Cluj County, operated by Nova Power and Gas, part of the Romanian group E-Infra, which is currently the market leader in terms of installed storage capacity. It is followed by the 300 MWh battery operated by Belgian company Aukera in Gura Ialomiței and the 206 MWh facility in Iaz, operated by Energy Capital Group, part of Turkey’s GÜRİŞ group.

Romania already has significant solar capacity installed, with more than 4,000 MW of dispatchable capacity, which can charge batteries at midday and then discharge electricity during the evening peak, when demand is highest.

At peak times, producers are sometimes forced to disconnect their facilities, where possible, or pay consumers to take surplus electricity, resulting in negative prices. In the first half of the year, the number of hours with negative prices increased by 33% in Germany and by 237% in Spain compared with the first half of 2024, according to Digi24. European network operators plan to spend hundreds of billions of euros on grid modernisation over the next decade.

World.title: Spot electricity price in Romania up 25% m/m, doubles y/y in August
World.content:
The average price on Romania’s day-ahead market (DAM) reached RON 793 (some EUR 150) per MWh in August, up around 25% from July and more than double the RON 396 per MWh recorded in August 2025, according to Economica.net and Profit.ro, which compiled data from the local market system operator OPCOM and the European association ENTSO-E.

The Cernavodă nuclear power plant operated with only one of its two units for 13 days and was completely shut down for the rest of the month due to the low flow of the Danube, which dropped to historic levels and no longer allowed the reactors to be adequately cooled. In parallel, also due to the lack of water, hydropower production was massively reduced.

Even though batteries have been installed on a rolling basis in Romania in recent months, the storage capacity, now at 2,300 MWh, is nowhere near sufficient to cover peak evening consumption with electricity released from batteries charged with solar energy during the day.

Therefore, during the evening and night hours, consumption relied on significant and expensive imports, putting additional pressure on prices. The increased use of gas-fired power plants and coal-fired units also contributed to higher average prices.

This evolution will put pressure on suppliers’ offers to households, which should increase the commodity component of electricity prices by a few percentage points. The cost of electricity accounts for only approximately 50% of the total end-user price, with the remainder consisting of fees charged by transmission and distribution companies, as well as taxes.

Despite all the price increases prompted by the harsh natural conditions that caused the shutdown of the Cernavodă nuclear power plant, Romania had only the sixth-highest spot price among the EU’s most expensive markets, according to Profit. Higher prices than in Romania were recorded in Ireland, Hungary, Slovenia and Croatia, while prices were marginally lower in Slovakia and Austria. This points to a supply deficit across the Central European area, probably also influenced by the low level of the Danube.

For the year-to-date period, Romania had the fourth-highest spot electricity price in the EU, with an average daily price of EUR 120 per MWh, surpassed only by Italy, Ireland and Hungary. Immediately behind Romania in the ranking are the same Central European countries, confirming the generation and transmission constraints affecting the region.

Romania ended 2025 in fourth place among the EU’s most expensive spot electricity markets, with an average daily price throughout the year of EUR 108.17/MWh, surpassed only by Ireland (EUR 116.55/MWh), Italy (EUR 115/MWh) and Hungary (EUR 108.5/MWh).

Although Romania dropped one place compared with the previous year, when it ranked third, having been overtaken by Hungary, its average day-ahead electricity price in 2025 was nevertheless almost EUR 5, or 4.5%, higher than in 2024, when it stood at EUR 103.5/MWh.

World.title: Romania’s government drafts contingency plan to keep Cernavoda nuclear power plant safe
World.content:
After detonating a large rock and sinking several barges, the government of Romania has drafted a new plan to raise the level of the Danube near the Cernavodă nuclear power plant (NPP) in order to maintain the safety of the nuclear installations, which require a minimum amount of water even when not generating power.

The intervention is necessary as the flow of the Danube is forecast to decline further starting on September 10, the government announced.

At the current Danube level near the Cernavodă NPP (1.86 metres), both reactors are shut down, and all efforts to raise the water level have failed so far. The maximum flow of the Danube at the entrance to the country is expected to remain below multiannual averages in September, October and November, according to the three-month forecast published by the National Institute of Hydrology and Water Management (INHGA). Resuming power generation at least over the coming weeks therefore remains uncertain.

The National Emergency Committee, under the government’s supervision, has adopted a new decision establishing “a phased plan of measures to ensure the water flow necessary for the safe operation of the Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant (CNE).” The term “operation” used in the official release refers, however, to the maintenance of the nuclear facility rather than to electricity generation.

The intervention plan will be triggered if the water level drops to 1.58 metres in the Cernavodă NPP water intake basin and provides for several stages, depending on how the situation evolves.

The government does not indicate the current water level in the Cernavodă NPP water intake basin. Public data indicate a level of 1.86 metres at the Cernavodă Canal, near the NPP. When the water level reached this value, the NPP shut down its second reactor.

Thus, in the first stage, several loaded ships and/or barges will be positioned along an alignment approximately 600 metres long, so that the flow in the Old Danube branch will direct a larger volume of water towards the entrance to the Danube-Black Sea Canal and, implicitly, towards the power plant’s water intake, the government said.

In the second stage, a modular closure using pontoons and dams will be installed along a section of approximately 170 metres in the area of the power plant’s connection canal. As a backup option, this system can be replaced with a temporary stone dam.

''If the intervention actions in the first two stages do not ensure the necessary effect, the National Administration 'Apele Române' and Nuclearelectrica will put into operation high-capacity pumps, which will ensure the pumping of additional water towards the water intake for cooling the power plant,'' the quoted source announced.

World.title: Russian Drone Attacks Unite Romania, Moldova and Ukraine to Counter Threat
World.content:
On Moldova’s National Day on August 27, when President Maia Sandu attended a military parade in Chisinau alongside Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky and their Romanian counterpart Nicusor Dan, at least five Russian drones entered the country’s airspace.

Sandu called Russia’s action an attempt to intimidate – and vowed to invest more in cooperation and defence.

“The sky above us shows us most clearly how important our cooperation is. Russia’s brutal war against Ukraine is being felt beyond its borders: the airspace of Moldova and Romania has been violated dozens of times,” she said.

“Even today, on the eve of our celebration, Russian drones entered our airspace in a clear attempt to intimidate us. I say clearly and firmly, in the presence of our friends: we will not be intimidated!” Sandu declared.

Russian drone incursions have increased in recent months.

World.title: ‘Not Mere Incidents’: Kosovo Questions Femicide Approach after New Killings
World.content:
The first victim was 25 years old and pregnant, the second aged 80. The first was shot, the second beaten to death. They both died in late August, both - allegedly - at the hands of their husbands.

Kosovo’s acting president, Albulena Haxhiu, took to Facebook to vent her anger and call for "the harshest punishment".

"Enough is enough with the killing and violence against women," Haxhiu wrote. "Just two days ago, another woman was killed, these cases cannot be treated as isolated incidents. The life and dignity of every woman must be protected by every possible means."

World.title: As Montenegro Eyes EU Accession, Croatia Wants ‘Issues’ Resolved
World.content:
From missing people to boat ownership, borders to memorial plaques, neighbours Croatia and Montenegro have their differences, but the question of whether or not these might block the latter’s accession to the European Union is a moot one.

Podgorica is the frontrunner to become the next member of the bloc, possibly by 2028, but fellow former Yugoslav republic Croatia fired a shot across its bows a month ago with a letter stating that Brussels “cannot and does not want to import bilateral disputes and therefore open issues must be resolved urgently, so that they do not burden bilateral relations or the accession process”.

The EU works on the basis of unanimity between its 27 members, so like Bulgaria in the case of North Macedonia, Croatia effectively holds a veto over Montenegro’s accession.

World.title: Croatia Sentences Bosnian Citizen for Glorifying Mladic
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Mural of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade. Photo: EPA/ANDREJ CUKIC

A Croatian court has handed a suspended prison sentence to a Bosnian national found guilty of glorifying the late convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.

Police from the Korenica Border Police Station announced on Tuesday that they had filed a misdemeanour charge against a 43-year-old over social media posts in which he glorified Mladic. According to police, the man posted photos, symbols, songs and texts on social media that “publicly honoured and expressed gratitude to a person convicted of war crimes”.

Mladic was convicted by the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. He died aged 84 in a UN jail in The Hague on August 26.

In the posts, among other things, the man thanked Mladic for “freedom” and said “he will never be forgotten”. The police stated that such content caused agitation and distress among citizens and so constituted an offence under the Law on Misdemeanours Against Public Order and Peace.

Following an investigation, the 43-year-old was brought before a court, which sentenced him to 15 days in prison but suspended the sentence.

The man had been living in Korenica as a foreign worker with a temporary residence permit.

Such cases are not uncommon in Croatia.

On August 28, police arrested 31-year-old Serbian influencer, Marko Stojkovic, in Split after he displayed tattoos depicting Draza Mihailovic, a Serbian World War II collaborator with the Nazis who is considered a war criminal in Croatia. He was charged with disturbing public order and peace as well as violating the Anti-Discrimination Act.

“By publicly displaying several inappropriate images tattooed on his body, he disturbed public order and peace and, with the aim of causing fear and creating a hostile and humiliating environment, violated human dignity and caused public unrest,” Split police announced, adding that his behaviour also violated the Anti-Discrimination Act.

The court sentenced Stojković to 15 days in prison. Following the conclusion of the proceedings, he will be expelled from Croatia and banned from re-entering the country for the next five years.

World.title: Serbia’s Grief Over Mladic’s Death is Neither Honourable Nor Dignified
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

On August 27, I received a push notification on my phone saying that Ratko Mladic had died.

In Serbia, where denial of war crimes has become part of official policy, and where everyone is now waiting for elections to be announced, I knew we would likely miss this opportunity to deal with the past in a dignified and responsible manner.

If it is true that the past is the story we tell ourselves about ourselves, then our story perfectly explains what is keeping us trapped.

World.title: Serbia NGOs Condemn Push to Allow Construction on Fire-Damaged Land
World.content:
Two non-governmental organisations, Transparency Serbia and the Renewables and Environmental Regulatory Institute, RERI, on Wednesday criticised newly adopted law amendments that may allow construction on sites where forest has been destroyed by wildfires.

The amendments to the Law on Planning and Construction, adopted by parliament on August 31, allow for the construction of public infrastructure facilities, or facilities for which a public interest has been established.

“All of this took place during the horrific and unprecedented wildfires that engulfed Deliblatska Pescara (Debilato Sands), the largest sandy area in Europe, an invaluable reservoir of biodiversity that is a protected area of exceptional (Category I) and national importance, as well as a Special Nature Reserve,” the organisations said in a press release.

The amendments stipulate that “forest land where the forest has been damaged or destroyed by fire” retains the designation assigned to it by the planning document in force prior to the fire.

But they also state that an exception to this rule allows a change of land use where it is necessary to implement a project for which a public interest has been established, or for the construction of public infrastructure facilities.

Transparency Serbia and RERI also noted that the provisions concerning construction on forest land damaged by fire were not included in the original draft law submitted by the government to parliament but were introduced through amendments adopted at a session of the parliamentary committee.

This further reduced the transparency of the legislative process, they said.

“The lack of transparency in the authorities’ handling of these legislative amendments, rather than reassuring an alarmed and concerned public, has instead opened the door to further suspicions regarding the future fate of the land affected by the fires,” their press release added.

More than 3,500 hectares of Deliblato Sands Special Nature Reserve in northern Serbia were impacted by severe wildfires in August. There have been active wildfires in other parts of Serbia. The wildfires affecting the Deliblato Sands and other areas have burned around 13,920 hectares, according to Copernicus data as of 26 August.

World.title: Kosovo President’s Election Jeopardised by Party’s Inner Divisions
World.content:
LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku at a press conference on Tuesday, September 1, 2026. Photo: BIRN

Six MPs from the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, will not follow the decision of the party’s leadership on a joint presidential candidate with the ruling Vetevendosje Movement, potentially jeopardising a possible end to Kosovo’s political crisis and prompting yet another election.

The six have been named as Avdullah Hoti, Hykmete Bajrami, Arben Gashi, Armend Zemaj, Kujtim Shala and Janina Ymeri.

“They are causing irreparable harm to the entire process and – inevitably and unnecessarily – driving the country toward snap elections,” LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku told the media on Tuesday.

“This position is detrimental to Kosovo and to the LDK. Any future elections triggered by this refusal – given that the candidate was excellent – will have electoral consequences that consolidate absolute power and will impact the LDK itself,” he added.

On Monday, following a meeting between Vetevendosje and LDK leaders Albin Kurti and Abdixhiku, the latter announced Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and former diplomat, as their joint pick for the presidential post.

But soon after, former PM and LDK MP Avdullah Hoti went on Facebook to warn that he does “not support this candidacy for President of the Republic of Kosovo – not for personal reasons but based on a political and institutional principle”, hinting at the divisions within the LDK.

Acting PM Kurti told the media on Tuesday evening, after Abdixhiku’s announcement, that a fresh election now looked more likely.

“After three rounds of elections [since February 2025], it appears there is a desire, will and an interest to head into a fourth election in less than two years,” he said. He added that a new meeting with Abdixhiku was needed.

In the last elections, in June, Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, well ahead of the next-placed Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, which won 22 seats. The LDK came third with 18 seats – but only 12 of these would now vote for the chosen president.

Vetevendosje has claimed it can call on 62 votes to form a new government, again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

But in the presidential election, Sejdiu must win at least 80 MPs’ votes in the first two rounds. In a potential third round, he would need a simple majority of only 61 votes.

The announcement of the joint presidential candidate was a move to end the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since the parliamentary elections in June. Parliament has yet to be inaugurated, as the parties have not agreed on the next president. Without an agreement, new elections seem inevitable.

Amid the institutional logjam, the provisional speaker, Avni Dehari, from Vetevendosje, refused to resume the inaugural session that started on August 6.

Vetevendosje also refused to submit a name for the new speaker, first demanding an agreement with the other parties on the new president.

World.title: ‘This Is How We Lived Here’: Documenting 16 Years in Hungary Under Orban
World.content:
Those who stayed

The vast majority, of course, stayed in Hungary and adopted different survival strategies.

A journalist working for Hungary’s public service broadcaster confessed to Varadi that now he feels he was a coward. He was “only” responsible for cultural content, did not have to do political reporting, but he was one of the hundreds who helped operate what many now refer to as “a factory of lies and propaganda” on state channels.

“I never crossed a professional red line myself,” he justifies in the interview, but goes on to admit that he earned a good salary that afforded him and his family a comfortable life.

While many talk about intimidation, self-censorship and adaption to the system, some stories prove that courage did sometimes pay off. A man who worked on development projects in a provincial town described the mounting pressure he felt from local authorities to award projects – and the public money that came with them – to Fidesz-aligned companies. Yet he did not bow, and decided to maintain strict application criteria. He was prepared to be fired, but to his surprise nothing happened. There were no reprisals.

The conversations often take a turn and raise questions about individual or joint responsibility. “Many people ask the question how could this all happen to us? And above all: why did we let it happen?” Varadi says.

Did Hungarian society simply follow the century-old patterns of making compromises, adapting and succumbing to pressure in order to survive, as was done under the rule of the Turks, the Habsburgs and the Soviets?

“One thing is for sure: there were no guns pointed at people’s heads,” Peter Kreko, director of the Budapest-based Political Capital, tells BIRN.

Kreko, a social psychologist, finds it perhaps most surprising that Orban managed to keep his grip on power for 16 years without resorting to violence, primarily through the manipulation of information. “This was a perfect ‘information autocracy’,” he says.

Kreko believes people always had a choice, and this was especially true for those working for the state media or the public administration. But many followed what historian Timothy Snyder has described as ‘anticipatory obedience’: trying to figure out what is expected of them and behave accordingly.

When it comes to conformism or adaptation, Kreko says, Hungary is not very different from its regional peers, but it is certainly true that Hungarian society has a historical tendency to bow to authoritarian leaders.

“What we see is that many people were afraid, felt intimidated,” is how Varadi explains it. Many feared negative consequences if they spoke up. Many sacrificed their right to free speech for their comfortable lives. And by doing so, many became accomplices of the system.

Stefano Bottoni, an Italian-Hungarian historian researching Central European modern history, points to the general lack of solidarity and mistrust in Hungarian society. “There were no institutions people would have trusted. The most common channel to rebel against the system was to write angry Facebook posts,” Bottoni tells BIRN.

He believes stronger trade unions, something like Solidarity in Poland in the 1980s, would have helped build critical communities, but they are virtually non-existent in Hungary. “We helped weaken the resilience of the system, believing that we don’t need those institutions, we will figure out a survival method all by ourselves,” he says.

Varadi shares this analysis: “Many people felt powerless and left alone. When the teachers went on to strike there was virtually no solidarity from the society.”

World.title: This Map Shows Just How Hot Croatia Has Been This Summer
World.content:
September the 3rd, 2026 – This map shows just how hot Croatia has been this summer, with drought and unstable rainfall causing serious agriculture issues.

The State Hydrometeorological Institute (DHMZ) has published an analysis of temperature and precipitation amounts for summer 2026. Index reports that the data shows that almost the whole of Croatia had an extremely warm summer, while parts of the country, especially the east and part of central Croatia, were markedly dry. The mean seasonal air temperature during the summer was noticeably higher than the average for the reference period 1991–2020. According to DHMZ data, deviations of the mean temperature ranged from 1.8 °C in Daruvar and Makarska to as much as 3.3 °C at Puntijarka and Zavižan.

an extremely hot summer for croatia

According to the percentile distribution, summer 2026 has so far been extremely warm across almost the entire territory of Croatia. The only exceptions were Varaždin and Daruvar, where the summer was classified in the very warm category. The DHMZ map shows that very large temperature deviations were recorded throughout the country. In addition to Puntijarka and Zavižan, where the temperature was 3.3 degrees above normal, in Parg, Senj and Gospić the deviation amounted to 2.9 °C. In Osijek the mean summer temperature was 2.8 °C above normal, in Dubrovnik 2.7 °C, and in Zagreb, Bjelovar and Pazin 2.4 °C above the average. Percentiles at numerous stations were very close to the maximum values. In Osijek, at Puntijarka, Zavižan and in Dubrovnik they amounted to 99.9, which shows how unusually warm the summer was in relation to the climatological normal.

droughts caused serious issues for eastern and central croatia

DHMZ also published data on precipitation amounts. Deviations relative to the 1991–2020 normal ranged from only 24.7 percent in Gradište, where 51.2 millimetres of rain fell, to 119.2 percent on Rab, where 193.5 millimetres were measured. The most pronounced precipitation deficit was recorded in the east of the country. Gradište and Slavonski Brod had an extremely dry summer. The map shows that in Gradište only about a quarter of the usual summer precipitation amount fell, while in Slavonski Brod around 37 percent of the normal was recorded.

Very dry conditions were recorded in Osijek, Daruvar and Parg, as well as in the western part of central Croatia, i.e. in the area of Zagreb, Puntijarka, Sisak and Karlovac. In Zagreb and Karlovac around 51 percent of the usual precipitation amount was recorded.

rainfall along most of the coast was relatively normal

It was also dry in the vicinity of Križevci, Ogulin and Gospić, at Zavižan and on Lastovo and Vis, i.e. at the Komiža station. In the rest of Croatia the precipitation amount was within normal limits. This also applies to a large part of the Adriatic, including Rijeka, Senj, Zadar, Šibenik, Split, Makarska and Dubrovnik. Thus, summer 2026 has been one of exceptional temperature terms across all of Croatia, while the distribution of precipitation was considerably more uneven, with a particularly pronounced drought in the east and in part of central Croatia.

World.title: Kaljski dialect Officially Declared Protected Cultural Asset of Croatia
World.content:
September the 3rd, 2026 – The Kaljski dialect from Kali has officially been declared a protected cultural asset of the Republic of Croatia.

The Kaljski dialect, spoken in Kali on the island of Ugljan, has officially become part of Croatia’s protected intangible heritage. By decision of the Ministry of Culture and Media dated the 26th of August, this specific island speech has been entered into the Register of Cultural Assets of the Republic of Croatia under the designation Z-8010. Morski reports that the Kaljski dialect is a distinctive speech that belongs to the Central Chakavian dialect of the Chakavian dialect group. In its explanation, the competent ministry particularly emphasised its unique linguistic structure, as well as the invaluable role it plays in preserving the local identity, rich history, customs and everyday life of the residents of Kali.

This prestigious recognition is the result of many years of effort and dedication by the entire local community. Side by side in the preservation and promotion of the indigenous expression are the “Srdelica” Kindergarten, the Kali Branch School and the parent “Valentin Klarin” Primary School, with strong support from the Kali Public Library, numerous local associations, the Tourist Board and the Municipality of Kali itself.

The particular value of this linguistic story lies in contemporary projects aimed at documenting and transmitting the speech. As part of the Kalipedia project, an extensive online dictionary has been created that today numbers around three and a half thousand words enriched with authentic audio recordings. At the same time, through the Kalamra project, free speech recordings of residents of all generations have been recorded and digitised, while the “Kualjska besida” initiative systematically encourages children and young people to creative and literary expression in their native Chakavian. With the official acquisition of the status of a cultural asset, concrete protection measures have also been secured. In the coming period, detailed documentation, scientific research and the lasting transmission of the Kaljski dialect to new generations will be carried out, with the continued active engagement of the entire local community.

World.title: Around 78,000 People Were Registered as Unemployed in Croatia in July
World.content:
September the 3rd, 2026 – Approximately 78,000 people were formally registered as being unemployed in Croatia back in July, which is a figure that is 0.1% less than in June.

Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that Eurostat estimates that 13.5 million people were unemployed across the EU back in July, of whom 11.3 million were in the Eurozone. According to a report by the European statistical office Eurostat, the unemployment rate in the Eurozone and the European Union remained more or less entirely unchanged in July compared with June, while it slightly decreased in Croatia. Specifically, it stood at 6.4 percent across the Eurozone and 6.1 percent at EU level. Compared with the same month last year, the unemployment rate rose by 0.1 percentage points.

Furthermore, Eurostat estimates that 13.5 million people were unemployed across the EU in July, of whom 11.3 million were in the Eurozone. Looking at the situation on a monthly basis, the number of unemployed people fell by 41,000 across the EU, while it remained unchanged in the Eurozone. As for Croatia specifically, the unemployment rate back in July stood at 4.3 percent, which is 0.1 percentage points lower than it was in June and half a percentage point lower than in the same month in 2025. Around 78,000 people were registered as formally unemployed in July, which is 1,000 fewer than the previous month and 8,000 fewer than back in July 2025.

Countries with a lower unemployment rate than Croatia were the Czech Republic (3.3 percent), Poland (3.4 percent), Malta and neighbouring Slovenia (both 3.5 percent), Bulgaria (3.6 percent), Cyprus (3.9 percent), and Germany and the Netherlands (both 4 percent). The highest rates were recorded in Finland (10.5 percent), Spain (10 percent) and Sweden (8.7 percent). For Croatia, Eurostat also publishes quarterly data on youth unemployment. In the second quarter of 2026, that particular rate stood at 16.4 percent, with around 19,000 young people registered as formally unemployed.

World.title: Jadrolinija Extends Sailing Season for High Speed Zadar-Ancona Line
World.content:
September the 3rd, 2026 – Jadrolinija has decided to extend its sailing season for the high speed Zadar-Ancona line until September the 6th.

Jadrolinija has stated that for its very first season of operation, the high speed Zadar-Ancona line has achieved positive results and great interest from passengers on both sides of the Adriatic. Poslovni reports that Croatia’s largest ferry company, Jadrolinija, will extend the first season of the high speed Zadar–Ancona line until the 6th of September due to excellent passenger interest.

“Jadrolinija has extended the sailing season for this line until the 6th of September, with additional trips on Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays, as well as promotional ticket prices. For adults the ticket costs 80 euros while children aged 3 to 12 travel for 40 euros,” Jadrolinija stated. They recalled that they introduced the high-speed Zadar–Ancona line this year as a new international connection that brings the Croatian and Italian sides of the Adriatic coast closer and enables travel between the two cities in approximately four hours on the vessel Jelena, which has a capacity of 400 passengers.

The strong interest from passengers on both sides of the Adriatic and the good response confirms the importance of fast, simple and direct connections between Croatia and Italy outside of air travel. It also confirms the Zadar-Ancona line’s potential for the further development of tourist and transport links between the two coastlines.

Back in 2025, Jadrolinija carried 12.6 million passengers, which is on a par with the previous record year and confirms stable demand, as well as 3.8 million vehicles, which is two percent more vehicles than the previous year. The growth and trend of these operational indicators are also accompanied by positive financial results. Jadrolinija’s fleet now comprises 58 vessels with an average age of 27.8 years, which is below the European average of around 33 years. Fleet renewal remains the company’s most important strategic project.

World.title: Has the Much Anticipated Croatian Robotaxi Failed?
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – Has the Croatian robotaxi story ended? It has been revealed that Mate Rimac’s Verne may need to return 89.7 million euros if it is determined that the project has indeed failed.

The company Verne, which has been engaged in developing the much anticipated robotaxi project, is prepared to return 89.7 million euros in advance payments drawn from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan if the evaluation of what has been achieved so far in the project shows that the contracted obligations have not been fully met. “The company is prepared to return all funds,” Verne said in its announcement.

an ongoing procedure

The Verne project, partially financed from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NPOO), officially ended on the 31st of August, but the key part of the procedure is still to come, the final evaluation that will show whether all contracted obligations have been fulfilled. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the company has stated, as touched on above, that it is prepared to return all funds if the competent authorities determine that the objectives have not been fully achieved, according to the announcement. The company has so far drawn 89.7 million euros in advance payments from the NPOO project, while it has raised more than 140 million euros from various private investors.

The Verne robotaxi project has therefore formally ended, but the procedure is not finished. Within one month, Verne must submit a report on all activities carried out, costs incurred and final results achieved. On the basis of that documentation, the competent authorities will carry out the final evaluation and determine what of the contracted obligations has actually been fulfilled.

what we know so far

The delivery of all prototypes of fully autonomous electric vehicles envisaged by the project has been verified, testing has been carried out, and regulations have been adopted. “The project ended on the 31st of August. The company is now submitting, within one month, a report on all activities carried out, costs incurred and final results achieved. On the basis of that report, the competent authorities will make the final evaluation of the project, i.e. an assessment of what has been successfully fulfilled in the project,” Verne stated.

According to the company’s claims, some of the objectives have already passed the verification of the competent institutions. The delivery of all prototypes of fully autonomous electric vehicles envisaged by the project has been verified, appropriate testing has been carried out, and regulations governing autonomous driving have been adopted. However, three remaining objectives still need to receive a final assessment, and the outcome of the project will largely depend on them. These are: the issuance of 50,000 free vouchers for rides in fully autonomous vehicles to persons with disabilities, the production of fully autonomous electric vehicles adapted to the needs of passengers with disabilities, and the establishment and operational readiness of specialised infrastructure.

multiple amendments have already been made

“In the implementation of the project so far, the competent institutions have verified that all verification prototypes of fully autonomous and electric vehicles have been successfully delivered, that appropriate testing has been carried out, and that regulations on autonomous driving have been adopted,” the company stated. They add that the public will be informed after the competent authorities complete the procedure of assessing the success of the project.

The main result of the project, for which Project 3 Mobility was approved 179.5 million euros from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, was supposed to be a fully autonomous electric vehicle of the fifth level of autonomy. That objective did not change even after multiple amendments to the contract and extensions of deadlines. The Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure particularly emphasised this back in April, when the last annex to the contract was signed.

The fifth level represents the highest level of autonomy. Such a vehicle does not need a driver and is not limited to predefined areas or driving conditions. Neither Verne nor any other company in the world has a vehicle of that level of autonomy today.

there are still many unknowns in the story

As Mate Rimac revealed recently, the fact is that Verne has, in addition to EU funds, also attracted more than 140 million euros in private funds. The robotaxi is already driving the streets of Zagreb. Uber is a strategic partner, and Pony.ai is the technology partner. Verne will be the owner of the fleet and the operator of the service, Pony.ai will provide the autonomous driving solution, while Uber will integrate the service into its global ride-hailing network, which will be an additional option alongside the Verne application. Together, the companies are building a commercial robotaxi service in Zagreb, and over time also in additional European and international markets, with plans to expand to a fleet of thousands of autonomous vehicles in the coming years.

“It’s difficult even to determine precise deadlines for when this will become a profitable business. It’s a kind of adventure, but all partners see potential in it. It will be a great story, but realistically it will take quite a lot of time. It wouldn’t be particularly serious to forecast now when this will be a sustainable business model,” was Rimac’s answer to the question about the profitability of the robotaxi business itself.

World.title: Petition Launched After Removal of Lokrum Nudist Beach
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – A petition has been launched by dissatisfied local people following the removal of a favourite Lokrum nudist beach.

The decision to remove the signs marking out the way to a favourite Lokrum nudist beach has sparked a wave of reactions among residents of Dubrovnik. Morski reports that after the signs were taken down, a group of people decided to take concrete steps and launched a petition calling for a solution that would allow the long-standing practice to continue.

“With this petition, we wish to encourage those responsible to find a legal framework for the lawful continuation of the tradition of naturism on the island of Lokrum. Back during the mid-1960s, with the establishment of the Lokrum Reserve, signs designating a swimming area for nudists were put up by the institution above the cliffs on the eastern side of the island of Lokrum.”

As a reminder, the public first learned about the removal of the signs from a reaction by Professor Igor Legaz, who confirmed on the 26th of August that the signs pointing to the Lokrum nudist beach had been removed, noting that the nudist beach in that area had operated contrary to the applicable regulations.

“This concerns a stretch of coastline about 300 metres long, characterised by a series of large natural stone slabs, which has been under general use since yesterday. For that reason, I thank the Management of the Lokrum Reserve and the director for the step they have taken, because that ‘special-purpose beach’ on the island of Lokrum had in any case been established contrary to the provision of Article 80, paragraph 2, point 2 of the Maritime Domain and Seaports Act,” Legaz said.

While part of the public welcomes the alignment of the situation on the ground with the Maritime Domain Act, the initiators of the petition emphasise the historical and cultural significance of that section of the coast and appeal to the competent institutions to find an appropriate model that would allow the lawful retention of the naturist tradition on the beautiful island of Lokrum.

World.title: September Sea Temperature Records Broken in Split and Komiža
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – The September sea temperature records have been broken in both Split and Komiža, with strong warmth still beating down on the Croatian coast.

The sea was unusually warm along a large part of the Croatian coast on the first day of September. According to DHMZ data, at 14:00 yesterday, the temperature measured in Split was 28.0 degrees, in Komiža 28.2 degrees, and near Dubrovnik it also stood at 28.2 degrees. Index reports that the sea is even warmer on Mljet. In Malo jezero at 2 p.m. as much as 30.2 degrees was measured, in Veliko jezero 29.9 degrees, while on the open sea near Mljet the temperature was 28.8 degrees.

september records have been broken in split and Komiža

Data from both Split and Komiža is particularly interesting. According to the DHMZ bulletin for September 2025, the previous absolute September maximum in Split was measured at 27.3 degrees, measured on the 2nd of September 2015. In Komiža, the record was also 27.3 degrees, set on the 2nd of September 2024. Yesterday afternoon’s 28.0 degrees in Split is therefore 0.7 degrees higher than the previous September record, while Komiža with 28.2 degrees exceeded the old record by as much as 0.9 degrees. These are operational DHMZ data, so the final values will be confirmed after data processing. For comparison, during the whole of September last year the highest measured value in Split was 25.0 degrees, and in Komiža 24.6 degrees. Even in the very warm September of 2024, the maximum recorded in Split was 27.0 degrees. The average sea temperature in Split that September was 24.0 degrees, a full 1.7 degrees above the climatic average for the period 1991–2020.

a mere 1.4 degrees lower than the absolute record for that particular station

Yesterday afternoon’s 28 degrees in Split is only 1.4 degrees lower than the absolute record for that specific station. In Split back on the 15th of July 2024 a temperature of 29.4 degrees was measured. Values from Mljet should not be directly compared with the long-term series from Split and Komiža. Malo and Veliko jezero are measured by automatic sensors and aren’t part of the same long-term series of the four stations – Rab, Split, Hvar and Komiža – that DHMZ uses in monthly analyses of September sea temperatures. Surface sea temperature at the classic stations is measured approximately 30 centimetres below the surface.

World.title: Croatia Records Modest Tourism Growth in First Half of 2026 as EU Nights Rise 1.7%
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – Eurostat reports that Croatia has recorded modest tourism growth throughout the entire first half of 2026, as EU overnight stays rise.

Over the first six months of 2026, tourist accommodation establishments across the European Union recorded 1,321 million overnight stays, a 1.7% increase compared with the same period in 2025 (1,299 million nights), according to official data released by Eurostat on 1 September 2026. Eurostat reports that while the EU as a whole continued its recovery and expansion, growth was highly uneven across member states. The strongest increases were recorded in Ireland (+14.6%), Malta (+9.9%) and Slovakia (+5.9%). Nine countries registered declines, with the sharpest falls in Cyprus (–7.7%) and Romania (–6.7%).

Croatia, long one of Europe’s leading tourism destinations, registered only a mild increase of approximately 0.5% in overnight stays during the same period. This placed the country near the bottom of the group of member states that still achieved positive growth, just ahead of Finland and the nine countries that recorded outright declines.

international visitors drive the numbers up

Foreign (non-resident) tourists accounted for 48.9% of all overnight stays in the EU in the first half of 2026. Nights spent by international visitors grew by 2.5%, nearly three times the increase recorded by domestic guests (+0.9%). Dependence on foreign visitors varies dramatically across the bloc. Malta (95.2%), Cyprus (92.6%) and Luxembourg (87.7%) recorded the highest shares of foreign overnight stays, while Germany (18.5%), Poland (19.8%) and Romania (23.0%) remained heavily reliant on domestic tourism.

Croatia’s modest 0.5% growth comes against a backdrop of strong overall EU performance and particularly rapid expansion in several smaller markets. The figures cover the traditionally quieter first half of the year, before the peak summer season. Full-year results will depend heavily on performance in July, August and the shoulder months of September and October. Eurostat’s data underlines that while tourism demand in Europe remains resilient, competition for visitors is intensifying and growth is no longer automatic even for established destinations.
