NEW DELHI: With two PILs heaping allegations against functioning of advocates regulatory body Bar Council of India and questioning legality of its Apr 2025 resolution giving a five-year term to chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra, Supreme Court Wednesday said no resolution can override the statutorily prescribed two-year term.A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said even if a BCI resolution generously gives a five-year term to the chairperson, his tenure ex-facie cannot exceed beyond 2027 notwithstanding the legality of the resolution.No resolution can alter the statutorily provided two-year tenure for the chairperson,â the bench said.The petitioners questioned the lavish spending of crores on felicitation functions, organising seminars and alleged misuse of Bar Council of India trust funds to open law colleges in states and demanded a high-level inquiry into the councilâs affairs.The bench said the elections to state bar councils had been completed and directed the completion of co-option of women members by the high court chief justices concerned in consultation with newly elected members within two weeks.The entire composition of state bar councils, including co-opted women members, would be notified within a week thereafter.It said the newly formed state bar councils would elect their representative to BCI a week later to enable the latter to conduct fresh election of the chairperson and the vice-chairperson.Till then, the BCI governing body would act in a pro tem manner and not take any policy decision.On the benchâs suggestion, the council volunteered to invite the attorney general and the solicitor general to its meetings.Mishra has been chairperson of BCI since Nov 9, 2014.The petitioners asked whether a statutory authority entrusted with âregulating more than 20 lakh advocates, administering legal education, conducting the All India Bar Examination, exercising disciplinary jurisdiction, and safeguarding independence of the legal profession, can lawfully permit prolonged concentration of regulatory authority in the same hands through successive and substantially uncontested termsâ.

World.title: FSSAI licence of iconic Hyderabad hotel Shadab  suspended over food safety violations
World.content:
The Telangana Standards Authority for Food and Essential Drugs (TG SAFE) has shut down two cafes and suspended the FSSAI licence of Hotel Shadab, Madina Circle branch following inspections on Wednesday, that found multiple violations of food safety and hygiene norms.

A total of nine enforcement teams comprising Food Safety Officers and police personnel conducted a special drive at 19 cafes and snack points across Hyderabad on Wednesday.

During the inspections, officials found several violations, including establishments operating without valid FSSAI licences or registrations, poor hygiene in food preparation areas, improper handling and storage of food, expired and spoiled food articles, and infestations of houseflies and cockroaches. Some food handlers were also found without headgear.

Dreamz Cafeteria in Bagh Lingampally and Asiatic Cafe in Panjagutta were closed after officials found that they were operating without valid FSSAI licences or registrations.

The FSSAI licence of Hotel Shadab in Madina was suspended and the management was directed to stop operations following multiple violations related to hygiene, sanitation and the storage of meat and other food articles. However, when The Hindu enquired with the restaurant, they were open for business on Wednesday night.

Officials also discarded perishable food items that had been exposed to dust and flies. Tea powder, ginger-garlic paste, biscuits and other food articles suspected to be adulterated were seized and sent for analysis. A total of 15 food samples were collected on suspicion of adulteration.

TG SAFE said improvement notices would be issued to 12 establishments, including Cafe Persia, Bahar Biryani Cafe, Cafe Deccan, Honeymoon Cafe, Rio Restaurant, Friends and Cafe, Diamond Point Hotel, Hotel Imroz, Blue Sea Tea and Snacks, Nimrah Cafe and Bakery and Gulzar Foods. The establishments will be re-inspected to check compliance with food safety norms, officials said.

TG SAFE further added that show-cause notices will also be issued to Golden Cafe, Dreams Cafeteria, Mirosa Cafe and Kitchen, Asiatic Cafe and Hotel Shadab, with further action proposed for imposing penalties.

World.title: Supreme Court asks Prashant Bhushan to approach Delhi High Court in case of lawyers beaten at BCI premises
World.content:
The Supreme Court granted liberty to advocate Prashant Bhushan on Thursday (September 3, 2026) to approach the Delhi High Court seeking relief for young lawyers who were beaten up while protesting at the Bar Council of India (BCI) premises on August 21.

A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant was informed by advocate Prashant Bhushan that he had come directly to the apex court as several petitions connected to the BCI is being heard by the court.

Mr. Bhushan, in an oral mentioning, alleged BCI chairperson, senior advocate Manan Kumar Mishra, had later on referred to the protesting lawyers as “legal cockroaches” who were dealt with by “our lawyers”.

Mr. Bhushan sought a CBI probe into the affair.

Justice Joymalya Bagchi said though lawyers have a right to protest, the legal fraternity was still a disciplined community, which had multiple fora to present their grievances.

Mr. Bhushan said nobody however had a right to beat up anyone. The protesting lawyers were mostly in their twenties, he said.

The senior lawyer said he would comply with whatever the apex court thought best.

Chief Justice Kant observed that it would be more opportune if the petition was filed in the High Court first.

World.title: I’ve watched Chennai grow and change through the years
World.content:
I was born in Chennai and have spent almost my entire life here. My earliest memories are of a very different Madras — quiet roads, broad pavements, tree-lined streets, and spacious homes. Early mornings brought milk and newspaper deliveries, temple music during Margazhi, and MGR songs from loudspeakers.

The Marina Beach was another favourite. It was quieter and cleaner then, and later became part of my routine through morning walks with my dogs and familiar faces along the shore.

December meant the music season. As a busy doctor, concerts offered a much-needed break, while sabha canteens, filter coffee, and conversations became part of the experience.

Chennai has also been deeply welcoming to me as a doctor. I have always valued the trust patients and families place in doctors as well as the city’s interest in healthcare.

I have watched the city become busier and more crowded, with traffic, pollution, heat and changing ways of life. Yet, its warmth and goodness remain.

I have travelled widely, but Chennai has always been where I belong. Its streets hold memories of growing up, friendships, medicine, and every stage of my life.

(As told to Athira Elssa Johnson)

World.title: Trinamool Congress leader Abhishek Banerjee’s office ransacked in Kolkata
World.content:
An office of Trinamool Congress leader Abhishek Banerjee located at Camac Street was ransacked on Thursday morning (September 3, 2026).

Mr. Banerjee alleged that Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) supporters were behind the attack. Videos shared by the Trinamool Congress leaders showed three to four masked men removing equipment from the office, with shattered glass and other materials scattered around, indicating vandalism.

“If this is how the Opposition is to be treated in West Bengal, through violence, vandalism and intimidation, then the Chief Minister has no moral authority to remain in office. He must resign. This is not democracy. This is political thuggery,” Mr. Banerjee posted on social media, sharing videos captured from close-circuit television cameras inside the premises.

The vandalism is reported to have occurred around 4:30 a.m. Trinamool Congress leader Upasana Chowdhury reached the office and said that the police did not respond despite multiple calls reporting the incident.

Also Read: Trinamool worker tortured in custody over signboard dispute, says Abhishek Banerjee

The Diamond Harbour MP urged the judiciary, particularly the Calcutta High Court, to take “serious note of what is happening and acts to uphold the rule of law in West Bengal”.

The premises at 9 Camac Street in Kolkata has been used by Abhishek Banerjee over the past several years. Personnel and Kolkata Police and senior Trinamool Congress leaders on August 27 were embroiled in a scuffle over removing a party hoarding on the building.

The police have registered FIRs and questioned Trinamool leaders in connection with the incident. Abhishek Banerjee and Rajya Sabha MP Derek O’ Brien were also summoned by Kolkata Police in connection with the incident. The premises was inspected by personnel of West Bengal Fire Services, who alleged unauthorised construction.

The Trinamool Congress general secretary is facing more than 16 FIRs after the BJP government came to power in May 2026. The Calcutta High Court has granted him protection from arrest in some of the police cases.

World.title: River-linking is not the solution
World.content:
The Union Minister for Home Affairs Amit Shah’s speech at the Southern Zonal Council’s meeting last month in Mamallapuram has provided a few takeaways on the contentious issue of water sharing. His emphasis on the need for an early resolution of water-related issues in the southern region appears well meaning but it is easier said than done. He had also talked about linking major rivers from the Brahmaputra to the Godavari and the Cauvery, an option that, according to Mr. Shah, can ensure that India faces no water shortage for 100 years.

However, water issues are not that easy to solve. This is evident from the Centre’s response to Tamil Nadu’s demand for the constitution of a tribunal to adjudicate the Pennaiyar river water dispute. Aggrieved over the “violation” of the 1892 inter-State agreement by Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, in November 2019, requested the Centre to establish a tribunal. It had also moved the Supreme Court with the same demand. Since then, two negotiation committees have been formed and 11 meetings held. Eventually, the top court, this February, directed the Centre to form the tribunal within a month and, later, extended the deadline by six months.

Still, the adjudicatory body is yet to be put in place. Meanwhile, the Centre asked the court whether the Pennaiyar dispute could be referred to the Mahadayi Water Dispute Tribunal instead of constituting a new tribunal. This suggestion defies logic as there is nothing in common between the two disputes. Moreover, the Interstate River Water Disputes Act, 1956 does not permit it. This suggestion in the Pennaiyar case gives the impression that the Centre is not keen on expeditiously implementing a judicial verdict in an inter-State river dispute. To cite one more example, the Central government has not yet replied to Tamil Nadu’s demand, in March this year, to constitute a tribunal on the Mekedatu dam project proposed by Karnataka.

A complex problem

Given this background, one need not delve much into the complications that would entail by the inter-linking of rivers. Proponents of river linking, including Tamil Nadu, have been saying that the idea is not to disturb the natural flow of any river but to divert a portion of the surplus water. Many experts are not convinced about this argument as they are worried that once the linking is allowed, regions that benefit may become vociferous in demanding water even in times of distress, eventually depriving original beneficiaries of their quota. This is apart from the concerns over the possible adverse consequences on ecology. In fact, Keralam has been stoutly opposing the Pamba-Achankovil-Vaippar link proposal, which, if implemented, the State says, will affect the Vembanad wetland system, where the Pamba and Achankovil rivers drain. However, the National Water Development Agency says that it has accounted for improving the flow of rivers in lean periods.

In the last 130-odd years, the country has seen only a handful of inter-basin transfer projects, most of which are in south India. The Mullaperiyar dam, the Parambikulam-Aliyar project, the Krishna Water Supply Project, and the Indira Gandhi Canal Project are regarded as successful examples of inter-basin transfer of river waters.

After the Bharatiya Janata Party’s return to power in 2014, the Union government formed a Special Committee for Interlinking of Rivers, which has held over two dozen meetings since then. Needless to say, there has not been much headway.

However, in 2024, Prime Minister Narendra Modi laid the foundation stone for the ₹44,000 crore Ken-Betwa Link Project. This has now led to agitations by the tribal populations in Chhatarpur.

What the governments, both at the Centre and in States, and civil society should focus on is demand side management, instead of perpetually looking for supply side interventions. With land becoming scarcely available and resistance growing among people when it comes to land acquisition, the days of implementing mega irrigation projects are almost over. The priority has to be towards conserving what is available and using it judiciously. A massive programme of sensitising and incentivising farmers on the optimal use of water has to be launched. Indiscriminate extraction of groundwater, facilitated by schemes of free electricity for agriculture in many States, is paving the way for ecological disaster and has to be curbed immediately. Unless water conservation becomes the mantra of all the stakeholders and is practised genuinely, disputes will be the norm.

World.title: KMWA Vidyanikethan unveils new labs and library in Bengaluru
World.content:
Former deputy chief minister Dr. C. N. Ashwath Narayan inaugurated the newly-established Computer Lab, Science Lab and Library of KMWA Vidyanikethan at Mahalakshmipuram in Bengaluru on September 2.

The newly-inaugurated facilities are expected to enhance the students’ learning experience and provide greater opportunities for practical learning, experimentation and research.

Dr. Ashwath Narayan urged students to complement their academic education by developing technological and scientific skills.

World.title: Delhi Police detains ex-bureaucrat over online activity, releases him later
World.content:
Delhi Police’s Special Cell on Wednesday (August 2, 2026) detained former bureaucrat Ashish Joshi and questioned him for several hours in connection with a case regarding his online activity before allowing him to go home. Taking to social media later in the evening, Mr. Joshi confirmed that officials had dropped him back at his residence.

During morning walk

Mr. Joshi, a 1992-batch Indian Post and Telecommunication Accounts and Finance Service (IP&TAFS) officer who retired as an Additional Secretary-rank official on March 31, was picked up during his morning walk.

Two men in plain clothes approached him at Nehru Park and asked him to accompany them to the Special Cell’s office in New Friends Colony.

The development triggered concern among his acquaintances and drew allegations on social media that he had been taken away by police personnel without his whereabouts being disclosed.

Former Congress MLA Sandeep Dikshit, a friend of Mr. Joshi from college days, said he learnt of the incident from Mr. Joshi’s wife after failing to reach him on phone.

“This morning my good friend and someone assisting me in reaching out to civil society Ashish Joshi … has been taken away by two police constables from Nehru Park,” Mr. Dikshit said in his post on X, urging Delhi Police to clarify where he had been taken.

Congress leader Supriya Shrinate also said Mr. Joshi had been picked up by two plainclothes Delhi Police personnel during his morning walk.

“Is the Modi government so uncomfortable with his social media posts that it has to resort to this?” she wrote on X.

Transparency activist Anjali Bharadwaj urged the police to immediately clarify whether Mr. Joshi had been detained, disclose his whereabouts and state the legal provisions under which he had allegedly been taken into custody.

No details given

Delhi Police did not immediately disclose details of the case in which Mr. Joshi was questioned or the specific online activity under investigation.

The allegations came against the backdrop of Mr. Joshi’s recent social media activity, including X posts on the police action against students protesting at Jantar Mantar, the Q1 GDP figures and “failures” in infrastructure projects.

Mr. Joshi had earlier been suspended by the Union government in February 2019 after he sought action against what he described as “incendiary” social media posts by then Aam Aadmi Party legislator Kapil Mishra, who later joined the Bharatiya Janata Party.

World.title: Former DRDO head opens Raghava Aerospace & Defence’s facility in Kokapet
World.content:
India has transformed from an importer to an exporter of defence equipment on the back of the country’s defence manufacturing ecosystem coming of age, former Chairman of DRDO G.Satheesh Reddy said while inaugurating a facility of Raghava Aerospace & Defence (RADPL) in Kokapet, Hyderabad.

Development-cum-production partners, 40% of them from the private sector, across the country are manufacturing missiles, bombs and guns. The Centre has earmarked ₹1.39 lakh crore of the defence budget for indigenous manufacturing under the Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative, a clear signal of the opportunity, he said.

Pointing out to India’s growing engagement as a defence exporter, he cited Armenia showcasing three Indian weapon systems at its Republic Day parade. He urged RADPL to focus not only on indigenous manufacturing, but also on exports, the company said in a release on Wednesday.

Research and development, electronics system design and manufacturing and composite structures are three verticals of focus for RADPL. Its Hyderabad facilities includes a Class 100,000 clean room for microwave assembly, RF and microwave test infrastructure up to 40 GHz, ESD-controlled assembly and integration labs and a full composite manufacturing line.

The company has grown through five acquisitions — DTS (electronic warfare and wideband RF), HQPPL (missile-borne RF systems and telemetry), Signalinx Techsystems (FPGA-based embedded systems and power electronics), Rainbow Advanced Composites (ablative and FRP missile components) and Aerospace Advanced Composites (large composite structures and thermal protection) — integrated into a single design, qualification and production platform.

It announced a joint venture with Peridot Advanced Materials for MALE-300 programme — a fully indigenous MALE-class ISR unmanned aircraft with a 300 kg modular payload bay, 30-hour endurance,30,000 feet in altitude and complete Indian ownership of design IP.

“Mr. Satish Reddy’s message is our roadmap,” said managing director Likhith Reddy Ponguleti.

World.title: Act for Nutrition conference: Govt official says nutritional challenges cannot be addressed without acknowledging population dynamics
World.content:
Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, says lack of investment in nutrition hurts Pakistan’s GDP.

Listen to article 1x 1.2x 1.5x

The second day of a two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’, is being held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel. The conference aims to address Pakistan’s persistent nutrition and stunting crisis.

On the first day, experts at the conference warned that more than four in 10 children under five were stunted and malnutrition was costing Pakistan close to $17 billion annually.

They also said that malnutrition was produced by a combination of poor diets, inadequate healthcare, weak water and sanitation services, poverty and other factors, making a multisectoral response essential.

The two-day conference is bringing together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action.

View the full agenda here.

11:15am - Seventh session begins

The seventh session titled ‘Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — from policy to plate’ has now begun.

11:00am - Govt official says nutritional challenges cannot be addressed without acknowledging population dynamics

Dr Shabana Haider, member (population) in the Planning Commission of Pakistan, said that nutritional challenges could not be addressed without acknowledging population dynamics and demographic dividends could not be reaped without investing in nutrition.

She said that while Pakistan had done a lot on the policy side, the documents themselves were not enough.

“We are very good at framing policies … sorry, excuse me, this has to change … let’s all recognise that our priority has not been population,” she said, adding that population had been neglected as a subject.

10:50am - KP govt official says malnutrition, family planning interlinked

Dr Fazal Majeed, the director of nutrition at the Directorate General Health Services for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, said that Pakistan had a stunting growth rate of 40pc, adding that it was 48pc in KP’s merged districts.

He also said that almost 40pc of women of reproductive age were also anaemic, calling the figures “alarming”.

“Malnutrition, family planning … are interlinked,” he said. He said some of the barriers in KP were fragmented delivery points, geographical and security-related.

Dr Fazal Majeed, the director of nutrition at the Directorate General Health Services for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference, — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

10:35am - Public health professional says history of Pakistan’s health programmes ‘one of isolation’

Dr Talib Lashari, a public health professional with the Sindh government’s health department, said that the nexus between nutrition and family planning was “well established but poorly practised in Pakistan”.

“The history of Pakistan’s public health programmes and initiatives is one of isolation. All the programmes have been well-designed and, to some extent, properly funded, but they were implemented in isolation,” he said.

10:24am - Govt adviser says nutrition needs to be reclassified as a capital expenditure

Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, said that nutrition needed to be reclassified as a capital expenditure rather than as an expense.

“So this single accounting decision suppresses the investment narrative permanently … these are fundamental flaws we need to correct,” he said.

Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

10:17am - Govt adviser says lack of investment in nutrition hurts Pakistan’s GDP

Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, said that population and resources are a “collective failure of capital investment”.

“We are reflecting everything nutrition-related as a health expenditure … every rupee that is withheld from a pregnant women’s diet is a deduction from the country’s gross domestic product in the future,” he said. He said that in the country, nutrition was divided across several sectors.

Siddiqui said that the annual loss from malnutrition was $17bn. He said that in South Asia, labour productivity was suppressed because of nutrition.

“And it is a structural liability to our sovereign credit profile,” he said.

10:08am - World Bank official says nutrition is viewed through ‘a human capital lens’

Sara Shahzad, the senior health specialist from the World Bank, said that the group had 10-year country partnership framework with the government of Pakistan focused on six priority areas, one of which was stunting reduction.

“So the way the World Bank looks at population stabilisation and nutrition, specifically the stunting agenda, is through a human capital lens,” she said.

Talking about stunting, she said that 30-40pc of it occurred before a child was born.

“So, the first 1,000 days are absolutely critical but also the adolescence period,” she said.

Sara Shahzad, the senior health specialist from the World Bank, speaks at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

9:58am - Expert highlights ‘experimentation’ in Pakistan’s population planning

Dr Ali Mir, the country director for the Population Council, said that there was always a tendency in Pakistan of “making the same mistakes again and again”. Talking about Pakistan’s previous population reforms, he highlighted wavering political commitment and policy inconsistency.

“We never explicitly had a population policy till 2002. It was always couched in development planning,” he said.

He said that due to this, Pakistan was constantly “experimenting”. Dr Mir said that now things were moving in the right direction, with the establishment of the Population Council.

Dr Ali Mir, the country director for the Population Council, speaks at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

9:55am - Doctor says nutrition is ‘not an isolated event’

Dr Saima Hamid, the programme and research lead at the Population Council, said that Pakistan’s population growth rate is at 2.55pc. She said that in 28 years, the country’s population would double, putting a huge burden on resources.

“This clearly is a challenge of not just the quantity but also the quality of diet. We need to ensure that diverse nutrition reaches those most vulnerable,” she said.

She also said that Pakistan’s domestic food security was on the decline, adding that “nutrition is not just an isolated event”.

“One sector isn’t really responsible … there is a clear intersection of nutrition, food security, health, purchasing power,” she said.

9:52am - Sixth session begins

The sixth session on how a nation cannot feed, educate or employ what it cannot count on sustaining.

9:50am - 2nd day of conference begins

The second day of the conference begins with a short film titled Leaky Guts from the Aga Khan University.

World.title: Pakistan raises $3bn through dual-tranche Eurobond sale
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan has raised a record $3 billion — its single largest international capital market transaction — through a dual-tranche Eurobond sale that drew nearly $6bn in orders, the Ministry of Finance said on Thursday.

In a statement, it said: “The transaction attracted nearly $6bn in orders — almost twice the amount issued — from a broad and diversified base of institutional investors across global markets and continents.”

“The successful transaction marks a major milestone in Pakistan’s renewed and increasingly diversified access to international capital markets, demonstrating strong investor confidence and Pakistan’s ability to access global funding markets at significant scale,” the ministry added.

The transaction includes $1.75bn through a 5.5-year bond at a coupon rate of 7.5 per cent and $1.25bn through a 10-year bond at 7.9pc, the ministry said.

Pakistan’s last most expensive Eurobond was raised more than a decade ago at an 8.25pc interest rate during the tenure of the PML-N government. It reached maturity a couple of years ago and has already been repaid.

The finance ministry said on Thursday that the total global demand for Pakistani paper amounted to $6bn.

“The competitive pricing across both maturities, together with strong demand extending to the 10-year tenor, demonstrates Pakistan’s ability to mobilise sizeable longer-term financing as international investors reassess the country’s improving macroeconomic and credit fundamentals,” it said. However, the significance of this transaction goes well beyond the amount raised, it added.

“The transaction also represents an important milestone in Pakistan’s broader road to market strategy,” the ministry said.

It said that after the successful inaugural Panda Bond and improvements in Pakistan’s sovereign credit profile, this was the first issuance under the country’s renewed strategic Global Medium-Term Note (GMTN) Programme — creating a platform for diversified access to international capital markets.

“The objective is not simply to raise additional debt. Pakistan is pursuing a broader strategy of active sovereign liability management — diversifying financing sources, extending maturities, reducing refinancing and rollover risks, and creating opportunities to replace shorter-term and more expensive obligations with longer-duration, competitively priced financing, where economically beneficial,” the ministry said.

“Pakistan has already pursued substantial early retirement of domestic debt ahead of maturity. Extending that discipline to external financing is part of the same objective: Borrow better. Extend maturities. Diversify funding. Reduce refinancing risk. Improve the sovereign debt profile. This is the difference between simply borrowing and actively managing the sovereign balance sheet,” it added.

It said that over the past three years, Pakistan’s improving economic trajectory had increasingly been recognised through successive sovereign credit-rating upgrades and renewed access to international capital markets.

“Now, global investors have reinforced that assessment with billions of dollars of actual capital,” it said.

“The depth of the order book, its geographically diversified institutional investor base, and substantial demand for a 10-year Pakistan sovereign instrument together provide a powerful market-based signal of renewed confidence in Pakistan’s medium and long-term trajectory,” the ministry said.

“Three years of rebuilding credibility; nearly $6bn of global investor demand, and a record $3bn issued in a single transaction — it is a landmark moment in Pakistan’s journey from economic stabilisation towards sustainable growth — and a stronger platform for the road ahead,” it concluded.

In April, the government initially raised $500 million through a three-year Eurobond under its GMTN Programme at a coupon of 6.975pc. The issue was subsequently increased to $750m through a $250m green-shoe option after stronger-than-expected investor demand. The bond matures in April 2029.

Pakistan has also repaid a $1.4 billion Eurobond that matured in April, allowing the government to re-establish a pricing benchmark in international debt markets after several years of relying heavily on multilateral, bilateral and commercial financing.

The latest offering extends the maturity profile beyond the three-year tenor used in April, with the proposed five and 10-year tranches providing a test of investors’ willingness to hold Pakistani sovereign debt for longer periods.

World.title: LHC's Justice Raheel Kamran resigns as judge
World.content:
LAHORE: Lahore High Court’s (LHC) Justice Raheel Kamran Sheikh resigned as a judge on Thursday, saying he wanted to pursue legal scholarship, policy research and comparative judicial practice.

He sent his resignation letter, dated of Sept 3, to President Asif Ali Zardari under Article 206 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973.

In the letter, seen by Dawn, Justice Sheikh said his years on the bench had been the most formative and fulfilling period of his professional life.

He wrote that after “deep and sustained reflection,” he had concluded that his further growth as a jurist — and his ability to contribute to the rule of law and access to justice — would be better served by turning to legal scholarship, policy research and comparative judicial practice.

Justice Sheikh thanked his senior colleagues on the bench for their guidance and his staff for their support, saying he was leaving with an “enduring commitment to the Constitution and the rule of law”.

A copy of the resignation was also sent to the LHC registrar.

Justice Sheikh, a graduate of the London School of Economics and a barrister of the Middle Temple, has been serving as an LHC judge since May 2021.

Before his elevation to the bench, he was an elected member of the Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) for a period of five years (2016-2020) and also chaired its Human Rights Committee. His legal practice covered public law, commercial law, taxation and human rights.

He is the son of senior lawyer Akram Sheikh, a former president of the Supreme Court Bar Association.

He was due to reach his superannuation on Jan 30, 2036.

World.title: No thaw until Kabul acts against terrorists: FO
World.content:
• Acknowledging diplomatic progress, Islamabad stands firm on its demand for concrete and verifiable action against TTP, BLA etc

• Outgoing spox Andrabi insists recent US-Iran escalation ‘not a failure of mediation’

• Urges India to implement Indus treaty, says New Delhi can’t treat international law as ‘matter of convenience’

ISLAMABAD: Despite recent diplomatic developments suggesting a renewed push to ease tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan, the Foreign Office on Wednesday remained firm that meaningful progress in relations would depend on the Taliban taking concrete and verifiable action against the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory.

At his final weekly media briefing before he is succeeded by Sajjad Haider Khan, FO spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said Islamabad welcomed China’s continuing engagement, but that external facilitation could not substitute for action by Kabul against terrorist infrastructure.

“Pakistan appreciates China’s constructive and sustained engagement on the issues of Afghanistan,” he said, adding that Islamabad had “always remained positively engaged for constructive dialogue on the subject of Afghanistan”.

Progress, however, would depend on “the Afghan Taliban regime taking concrete and verifiable action against TTP, BLA, and other terrorist organisations operating from their soil into Pakistan.”

His remarks came amid renewed diplomatic activity, including Chinese Special Envoy Yue Xiaoyong’s visit to Islamabad to revive the Urumqi process aimed at preventing further escalation, and an invitation to Afghan ambassador Sardar Shakeb to speak at the National Defence University.

Islamabad, however, sees little proof that the Taliban have moved beyond containing TTP activities. The latest UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team report noted that the Taliban had relocated around 2,000 TTP fighters and their families away from areas bordering Pakistan, and that Taliban leader Hibatullah Akhundzada had warned the group against attacks on Pakistan — but also that Taliban support for the TTP continued as the group escalated attacks and expanded its organisational structure.

For Islamabad, relocating terrorists does not amount to dismantling the command, training and logistical networks that remain at the centre of its concerns.

Mr Andrabi also downplayed readings of the Afghan envoy’s NDU speech as a sign of improving ties. “Envoys visit academic institutions. This is not unusual,” he said. “Such interaction is no yardstick for measuring bilateral relations between the two sides. As such, we should not read too much into this interaction.”

There had consequently been “no change” in Pakistan’s position. “Fact remains that progress in Pak-Afghan relations hinges on verifiable, written assurances from the Afghan side that their territory will not be used for terrorism against Pakistan,” he said.

Iran-US hostilities

The FO said the resumption of hostilities between the US and Iran should not be seen as a failure of mediation, insisting Islamabad remained engaged and hopeful the parties would return to talks once the “logic of escalation” had run its course. Attacks by the two sides have escalated after weeks of relative military restraint, alongside a growing US economic pressure campaign against Iran. “Whilst we remain concerned, and obviously these escalations are not desirable, however, we are not discouraged, and we remain engaged,” Andrabi said. “This escalation should not be termed as a failure of the mediatory process.”

Pakistan has consistently maintained that the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, brokered in June through Pakistani facilitation, remained the framework for reviving diplomacy between Washington and Tehran after its implementation collapsed within weeks. His latest remarks, however, left room for an alternative.

“Our efforts will continue,” he said. “We hope that, when the logic of escalation will exhaust, and it should eventually exhaust, the parties would return to the negotiating table.”

“Whether the parties agree to resume dialogue, this template of peace (Islamabad MoU), or any similar framework copying this template, will be adopted. We remain positive that the parties will eventually return to the dialogue table,” he added.

That marked a subtle broadening of Pakistan’s position, which until now had projected the June MoU as the template for restarting the political process rather than requiring the parties to begin afresh.

On the latest US measures against Iran, the spokesperson said Islamabad had taken note of the sanctions and was assessing their possible impact on bilateral trade. “As regards the potential impact of these US measures on Pakistan-Iran trade, the matter is being carefully evaluated and monitored in coordination with the Ministry of Commerce,” he added — a shift in emphasis from last week’s briefing, when he stressed international law and existing bilateral agreements.

PCA ruling

The FO also urged India to return to full compliance with the Indus Waters Treaty, cautioning that New Delhi’s rejection of the Aug 31 award by the Court of Arbitration — which reaffirmed that the 1960 treaty remained in force and that India could not unilaterally place it in abeyance — did not absolve it of its obligations.

Mr Andrabi said India’s position raised concerns beyond the immediate dispute. “India cannot treat International Law as a matter of convenience, invoking it when useful and discarding it when inconvenient,” he maintained, adding that New Delhi could not disregard “binding treaty obligations and the legal processes to which it freely subscribed, simply because their outcomes are not to its liking.”

Such an approach, he warned, undermined the sanctity of treaties and confidence in established dispute-settlement mechanisms. “India’s rejection of the award cannot extinguish or otherwise alter India’s obligations under the Indus Water Treaty, or its obligations to fulfil the award of the Court of Arbitration,” he said, cautioning that unilateralism over transboundary waters was “particularly concerning and inimical to sustainable peace and stability” in South Asia.

“India should therefore return to full compliance with the treaty, respect the institutional and dispute settlement mechanisms of the treaty, and engage Pakistan constructively within the framework that both countries solemnly accepted,” Mr Andrabi said.

World.title: Master plan violations lead to worsening of Islamabad flooding
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Besides the natural calamity, the Capital Development Authority’s (CDA) negligence is also a major contributing factor to flash flooding in the capital, as the authority failed to properly implement the city’s landmark master plan.

The planned city has been facing flash flooding for the last many years due to poor planning and weak writ. Islamabad received 150mm of rain, which resulted in flash floods, badly affecting three areas – E-11 sector, Park Road near Comsats and Ghauri Town.

After hectic efforts, the city managers, under the supervision of Chief Commissioner and CDA Chairman Sohail Ashraf, brought the situation under control.

But, investigation carried out by Dawn revealed that CDA’s negligence was a contributing factor behind the flooding particularly in the three areas where the course of nullahs had either been changed or their right of way was squeezed by private parties over the last few years.

Encroaching upon nullahs’ right of way reason behind urban deluge

Sector E-11, where a mother and child died in 2021, once again was in the grip of flash floods on Tuesday. However, this time no loss of life was reported, as the city administration had already sealed the houses which were at risk.

A 2005 satellite image of Gumrah Kas shows the nullah meandering through the Chatta Bakhtawar area before reaching Park Road.

In this un-acquired sector, where five private housing schemes are located, both nullahs had been squeezed to create plots. One nullah, which entered from D-12 back in 2012, had been reduced by a housing society from 40 feet to 18 feet. Surprisingly, CDA itself allowed the society to cover the nullah.

Before entering E-11 sector, the nullah had around 100 feet right of way, but in E-11, it reduces to around 18 feet with a sharp bend, which is a constant source of flooding in the area.

The other nullah, which enters this sector from E-10 side, had also been squeezed and a junction of these two nullahs created a bottleneck, forcing the water to gush out. Several buildings and houses were located, allegedly on the right of way of the nullahs in this sector.

A 2026 satellite image shows the nullah in Chatta Bakhtawar turned into a straight channel, with extensive construction along its former alignment.

It is relevant to note here that E-11 sector is located in the heart of the city, and is dotted with unauthorised highrises and apartment buildings. Five cooperative housing societies, including three that do not even have valid layout plans, are also located here.

One of the affected areas - Park Road near Comsats - has a nullah called Gumrah Kas, which overflowed, causing flash floods that entered basements of some houses and badly disrupted traffic. Satellite image of 2005 and 2026 showed that the course of this nullah had been massively changed in this area.

In 2005, the nullah used to flow from private land, but now passes through CDA’s acquired land, with the remaining land used for construction of houses - a step which raised eyebrows.

On the other hand, Ghauri Town, an unauthorised housing society, also faced floods as two natural nullahs passed through the society. Both nullahs were squeezed for construction purposes.

The architect of Islamabad’s 1960 master plan proposed the construction of Lohi Bher Lake in one of the city’s lowest-lying areas to store water and help prevent flooding. Two housing societies now operate in the area, as the CDA did not acquire the land proposed for the lake.

In the same areas after Ghauri Town, Doxiadis Associates, the Greece-based firm which prepared Islamabad’s master plan in 1960, designed Lohi Bher lake/dam as he knew that the area was low-lying and ideal for a dam.

But, the CDA never took any step to acquire the land for construction of the dam. Resultantly, the proposed site is now part of two private housing societies - Jammu Kashmir Farming Scheme and Gulberg Housing Scheme.

Meanwhile, rainwater accumulated on all major roads and in the I series sector. Sector D-12 had also been badly affected, particularly the sector’s markaz.

Several commercial buildings, including City Centre, Family Mart Plaza, Aim Centre and Swiss Centre Plaza, have had their entire basements flooded, inflicting heavy loss to traders. The traders have demanded proper drainage system in this sector to avoid flooding in future.

Meanwhile, CDA and ICT teams remained in the field to get the roads cleared. The CDA chairman visited E-11 sector, Ghauri Town and some other areas along with the deputy commissioner.

Besides, nullahs squeezing issue, the CDA through an amendment to the master plan in 90s, changed status of Zone 4, converting it from green to residential area with a large number of housing schemes, which may be a factor behind climate change. According to Global Forest Watch (GFW), Islamabad lost 14 hectares of tree cover between 2001 and 2025.

Speaking to Dawn, CDA Chairman Sohail Ashraf said a comprehensive plan had been chalked out to tackle flash flooding in Islamabad.

“Four new check dams will be constructed at the foothills of the Margallas to store rainwater while a new nullah will be built in sector E-11 to ensure smooth flow of water. As far as Ghauri Town and other areas are concerned where construction had taken place in right of ways of nullahs, we will remove these constructions,” he said, adding that it is unfortunate that rainwater is not being stored in a water scarcity-hit city.

“Our dam project will not only reduce chances of floods, but also help us meet our water needs,” he said, adding that the CDA will also look into the issue of Gumra Kas’ alignment.

“I can’t say anything about what happened in the past; I would just say that crisis creates an opportunity and with positive mindset, we will take steps to store rainwater and take action to clear right of way of nullahs. I will also get input about the proposed Lohi Bahir lake issue,” he said, adding that “since we sealed the basements and also some houses in E-11, no loss of life was reported unlike the 2021 flooding in this area”.

World.title: Azhar says lack of vision, instability hurting Pakistan cricket
World.content:
• Former skipper believes hard decisions should not breed insecurity

• PCB chief says criticism ‘personal’ rather than driven by genuine concern

KARACHI: Former captain Azhar Ali has blamed a lack of vision, instability and concerns over job security among decision-makers for the repeated upheavals in Pakistan cricket, emphasising the game’s establishment in the country must first identify its problems before embarking on a long-term reform process.

Azhar’s comments came in the wake of Pakistan Cricket Board’s (PCB) decision to sack red-ball head coach Sarfraz Ahmed — who had taken up the job only months earlier and overseen five defeats in six Tests — and hand charge of the side to white-ball coach Mike Hesson for the third Test in England, send seven players home and replace bowling coach Umar Gul with Australian Ashley Noffke.

Selection committee member Misbah-ul-Haq subsequently resigned after reportedly not being consulted over the changes, while several former players and coaches criticised the timing of the shake-up with the series still in progress.

“The real problem is the lack of vision among the people working at the PCB. It also raises questions about the competence of the people making these decisions,” Azhar said when contacted by Dawn on Wednesday.

“Job security seems to be the biggest concern. When you are trying to save your job, competence goes out of the window. If cricketing decisions are not being taken by cricketers, then it is also the fault of the cricketers themselves.”

Pakistan suffered massive defeats in the first two Tests — by an innings and 103 runs at Headingley and by 194 runs at Lord’s — leaving England with an unassailable 2-0 lead in the series.

The ex-Test batter said constant changes had also created insecurity among the players, who were struggling to cope with uncertainty surrounding the team.

“It creates insecurity among the players. You can see it in their body language. They are under mental stress and are not able to absorb everything that comes with these decisions,” he said.

Azhar, however, said difficult decisions were sometimes necessary but needed to be taken within a stable and clearly defined system.

“There are times when you have to make hard decisions, and I think those decisions should be made but the players need to feel that they have some security and that they can stand their ground.”

The 39-year-old identified instability and inconsistency across several areas of the game as major reasons for Pakistan’s decline over the past five to six years.

“There has been instability and inconsistency all around — political instability, changes in coaching and changes in selectors,” he said. “The people running the cricket board are trying to save their job, while the players in the team are also thinking about their own future. I don’t blame the players for that. If I am in their position, I will also think about myself.”

The former captain said Pakistan needed to resist the temptation of repeatedly changing direction and instead conduct an honest assessment of where its cricket stood.

“First of all, we have to make sure that we know what our problem is. If you don’t know the problem, there can be no introspection and no realisation. Until you realise where you stand, the journey towards improvement cannot begin,” he said.

Azhar proposed involving former and current top cricketers in assessing the state of Pakistan cricket before drawing up a long-term plan.

“I would like to see our top cricketers sit together and talk about what they think is wrong with Pakistan cricket and find the right solutions collectively before laying a proper five-year road map. We [then] have to be patient and consistent with it,” he said.

“You cannot keep taking one step forward and two steps back.”

He was optimistic that a properly structured system could restore Pakistan’s competitiveness even if it did not immediately produce a world-beating side.

“I guarantee that if we do this properly, we will not become world-beaters, but we will at least be able to compete. Fans will enjoy watching Pakistan play. Currently, we are becoming irrelevant,” he added.

Azhar also rejected the idea that technical deficiencies among individual players were the principal reason for Pakistan’s struggles, saying the system responsible for developing them needed more scrutiny.

“The ability is there in everyone. If your system supports players properly, they can perform at international level. Technical issues do not matter as much as people think. If our best players are not ready, then we have to look at the system,” he insisted.

“We have to ask ourselves: why have Babar and Rizwan gone backwards? We have to look at how we have wasted these players and why they have declined.”

PCB chairman Mohsin Naqvi on Wednesday, defended the board’s decisions, saying the changes made during the ongoing England tour were necessary after careful consideration.

Speaking to Geo News from London, Mohsin said he was “deeply upset” and “deeply saddened” by Pakistan’s performances and results. He said performance was not the only issue being examined by the PCB, adding that there were “other matters” under consideration, but it was “not the right time” to discuss issues unrelated to cricket.

The PCB chief also hit back at criticism, amid the present turmoil, from a number of former Pakistan players.

“I have never been afraid of criticism, and I never will be,” he maintained.

He reckoned that several among critics did not know the complete story and that some objections were personal rather than driven by concern for Pakistan.

While acknowledging Pakistan’s poor Test record and its position near the bottom of the WTC table, Mohsin pointed to improvements in the white-ball rankings during his tenure, saying Pakistan were fifth in ODIs and sixth in T20Is.

He also rejected claims that cricket had been “destroyed” since he took over.

“Those who say cricket has been destroyed since I came — look at what the [Pakistan] rankings were before [I took charge],” he said while adding that his confidence in Pakistan’s players remained intact and that he would not tolerate their humiliation.

Also on Wednesday, Pakistan team players and officials met King Charles at Clarence House in London. Mohsin was also present at the meeting, where the monarch spoke with the cricketers and team officials.
