World.title: Opinion: ‘An attempt to make Abkhazia’s residents feel part of single political space with Russia’
World.content:
Abkhazia is actively preparing for Russia’s State Duma elections, which will take place on 20 September 2026. Most Abkhazia residents hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, which gives them the right to vote in the elections.

Russia will open 319 polling stations in 152 countries for citizens voting abroad. 35 of them — more than 10% — will open in Abkhazia.

Many people think this is excessive for a small republic with a population of 250,000.

One of those who objects is Akhra Bzhania, a prominent Abkhaz blogger and public figure. He believes that the “excessive” number of polling stations and the active election campaign aim to create a sense among Abkhazia’s residents that they somehow “belong” to Russia.

Akhra Bzhania: “There is a standard procedure for people with dual citizenship who vote abroad.

Usually, two or three polling stations open, plus a polling station at the consulate or embassy. That’s it.

Abkhazia cannot use its budget to cover the costs of holding a constitutional event of a foreign state. That makes no sense.

If someone argues that the Russian side is paying for the campaign, that is even worse!

Let me explain why. Fifty or 60,000 votes from Abkhazia will have no impact on the overall balance of parties in the State Duma.

This means the election campaign here must serve a different, ideological purpose — to create a sense among Abkhazia’s citizens that they share a single political and administrative space with Russia. And from there, a common state is not far away.”

I have no doubt that some Abkhaz citizens with dual citizenship care deeply about the differences between the programmes of Russian political parties. For them, State Duma elections are therefore not only a civic but also a political act.

But in that case, they can plan ahead and vote in Sochi, Krasnodar or Moscow, as Russians living in Armenia, Kyrgyzstan and elsewhere do.

Yet our entire republic is covered with banners urging people to vote for a government body of another country! We plan to open 35 polling stations, just as we do for our own presidential elections!

It seems strange to me — and not only to me — and out of line with the status of our state and the level of Abkhaz-Russian relations.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Abkhazia prepares for Russia’s State Duma elections

World.title: What Pashinyan and Putin agreed in Bishkek amid peak tensions in relations
World.content:
Pashinyan-Putin meeting in Bishkek

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Russian President Vladimir Putin met in Bishkek, where an SCO+ meeting was held as part of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit. Their talks took place late in the evening.

There was no shortage of issues to discuss as bilateral relations have recently become increasingly strained. The previous meeting between Pashinyan and Putin took place on 1 April. Since then, Armenia held parliamentary elections in June, in which Pashinyan’s party won a majority and formed a government. However, the Russian president has yet to congratulate Pashinyan on his victory.

Judging by statements from Moscow, the main issue concerning the Russian authorities is Armenia’s ambition to join the European Union.

In the opening minutes of the Bishkek meeting, Putin said Armenia’s aspiration to join the EU was the country’s legitimate right. However, he said this “creates difficulties” for Armenia’s membership of the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).

“The sooner Armenia decides on the issue of joining the EU, the better. Moscow needs to understand how to develop relations further. The adoption of a law launching the process of Armenia joining another organisation amounts to a declaration of withdrawal from ours,” Putin said.

Pashinyan responded by reiterating that Armenia had no intention of leaving the EAEU.

The Armenian prime minister also recalled that, under the EAEU’s charter, there was no procedure for expelling a member state unless the country itself decided to leave.

“We greatly value our relations with the Russian Federation. We hope these relations are important to Russia as well. I think that Armenia and Russia, and we personally, should treat these relations with great care. I want to confirm that I personally and our government treat them with great care. I am sure that you also treat these relations with great care, and I want to thank you for that,” Pashinyan said.

He stressed that the issue of EU membership had not yet reached the stage at which a referendum could be held. He explained that Armenia did not currently have the alternative of actual EU membership to put before the public. In other words, the issue would be decided once the Armenian authorities had a concrete alternative to offer voters.

Putin, however, stood his ground: “The people should indeed always have a choice. So give them one, and we will close the matter. That’s all. The simplest thing is to ask people: what do you want — this or that?”

After the meeting, the Armenian prime minister posted a video on social media summarising the outcome of the talks.

Pashinyan described the meeting as “very good” and said he and Putin had agreed to continue their “sincere and constructive dialogue” during his visit to Moscow, which is apparently expected to take place in the near future.

“It should be noted that bilateral relations between Armenia and Russia are extremely important for both countries. […]However, it should also be noted that, in the new environment and under the new circumstances, there is a need to rethink these relations. I am convinced that, as a result of this reassessment, relations will become better, more constructive, more mutually beneficial and warmer,” he said.

Context: other issues on agenda

In Armenia, the meeting had been expected to involve difficult discussions on several critical issues. Armenian analysts had also warned that the meeting was unlikely to produce any positive developments on any of them.

In Armenia, there were expectations that the two leaders would discuss holding a referendum on whether the country should remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership.

Russia and other EAEU member states have recently been pressing for such a referendum. The Armenian authorities have responded that there is little point in holding one at this stage, as the country has not yet formally applied for EU membership.

The EAEU comprises Russia, Belarus, Armenia, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.

Meanwhile, there has already been talk within the EAEU of discussing Armenia’s status in the bloc. However, under the union’s charter, only Armenia itself can decide to withdraw. As Pashinyan has repeatedly pointed out, there is no other procedure for ending its membership.

At the same time, on 24 August, the Armenian prime minister raised the possibility of submitting a formal application for EU membership. This prompted a fresh wave of criticism and an even sharper reaction in Russia. Commentators there said that “EU membership is a marathon lasting decades”, while Yerevan would feel “the costs of breaking with Russia and the EAEU here and now”.

Russian experts even predicted a “fatal outcome” for Armenia. According to them, the country faces a choice between “Turkification” and a “Ukrainian scenario”.

The two leaders had also been expected to discuss Russian restrictions on imports of Armenian food and other goods, which were introduced in May and remain in place.

Russia has traditionally been a key export market for Armenia. However, since the restrictions were introduced — which Russia has attributed to concerns over product quality — Armenian goods have increasingly been exported to EU countries, where higher standards apply.

Armenian analysts had also expected the two leaders to discuss Armenia’s membership of the Russian-led CSTO military alliance.

The Collective Security Treaty Organisation comprises Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Armenia.

Armenia has effectively frozen its participation in the organisation for the past two years in response to what Yerevan sees as inaction by its allies.

When Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s sovereign territory in 2021-22, its CSTO allies neither intervened nor condemned Baku’s actions. They argued that the Armenian-Azerbaijani border had not been delimited. Pashinyan responded:

“To say that there is no border between Armenia and Azerbaijan is to say that the CSTO has no defined area of responsibility. And if there is no area of responsibility, then there is no organisation.”

While Pashinyan had previously said he was not concerned about the possibility of Armenia being expelled from the military bloc, just a week before his meeting with Putin he went further, saying he would welcome such a move:

“At least it would relieve us of the dilemma of whether or not to leave [the CSTO].”

In addition, ahead of the leaders’ meeting, Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said the talks would take place at a time “when opposition leaders are being arrested en masse in Armenia”.

He was referring, among others, to the arrest of former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan. Kocharyan is accused of abuse of office, accepting a particularly large bribe and money laundering. A court ordered him to be held for two months. It is the former president’s fourth arrest.

In Armenia, there was speculation that Putin, who has close ties with Kocharyan, might once again ask for his release.

During his previous meeting with Pashinyan in April, Putin expressed hope that Russia’s “friends” and pro-Russian political forces would be able to take part in Armenia’s elections.

He was believed to have been referring to the party of Russian businessman Samvel Karapetyan, who is currently under house arrest on charges of making calls to seize power, as well as a bloc led by former President Robert Kocharyan. Both contested the elections but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.

Representatives of Armenia’s ruling party believe that these pro-Russian forces are encouraging the Russian authorities to take steps that could fuel public discontent. Pashinyan’s team believes the opposition hopes to use such discontent as a means of coming to power.

World.title: Ex Georgian PM Gharibashvili: Unanswered questions over deaths under current leadership
World.content:
Ex-Georgian PM Gharibashvili accuses authorities

Former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili has published another letter from prison, calling on the authorities to answer questions about the circumstances surrounding the death of Lazare Jorbenadze, a human rights defender who had criticised current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

Gharibashvili writes that Jorbenadze died by suicide shortly after journalist Dito Chubinidze published an article for which Jorbenadze had given an interview.

The newspaper Asaval-Dasavali, which published the interview, questioned the theory that Jorbenadze died by suicide. Gharibashvili stresses that the public should receive an answer about the real cause of Jorbenadze’s death.

The former prime minister says he decided to speak publicly on the issue after comparing the contents of a letter he received from government representatives in February this year with other circumstances surrounding the case.

According to Garibashvili, on February 12, he was sent, on the instructions of Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Deputy Prime Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze, an article published in Asaval-Dasavali on February 2, 2026.

The article featured an interview by journalist Dito Chubinidze with Lazare Jorbenadze. Gharibashvili says the article focused mainly on criticism of Kobakhidze and serious allegations against him.

The former prime minister says the message he received expressed suspicion that he himself was behind the article.

“I was sent a message expressing the suspicion — based on a completely false assumption — that I was behind the article,” Gharibashvili writes.

Gharibashvili says he categorically rejected the allegations and told the government representatives that publishing “commissioned articles” was not something he did.

In his letter, Gharibashvili also mentions journalist Dito Chubinidze and former Alliance of Patriots leader Irma Inashvili, stressing that he had no involvement in their political or journalistic activities.

The former prime minister believes these events shed more light on one of the points in the letter he received, which referred to “supporters” such as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili.

“Now the picture is clear to me, and I have received answers to all my questions: why did the first point of the letter say that ‘such supporters as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili’ raise serious doubts and cause significant damage to the interests of the Kobakhidze-Mdinaradze team” Gharibashvili writes.

In another part of the letter, the former prime minister criticises Mamuka Mdinaradze, saying that his mistakes led not only to his removal from office but also to his departure from politics.

Gharibashvili stresses, however, that in his view, Mdinaradze’s departure from politics will not make up for the damage he believes Mdinaradze and Irakli Kobakhidze caused to the country, its people and the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Gharibashvili also writes that questions remain in society about the deaths of other people during the period when Irakli Kobakhidze and Mamuka Mdinaradze were leading the country.

Context

The first corruption charge against former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili was brought in October 2025. Investigators accused him of legalising illicit income on a particularly large scale. A second charge – accepting a bribe on a particularly large scale – was brought on August 24, 2026.

Gharibashvili made his first statement from prison on August 17. In a Facebook post, he wrote that a letter had been sent to him on the orders of Bidzina Ivanishvili [oligarch, founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party] and that it “left him no choice” but to confront the “evil that insults his dignity”.

Gharibashvili published his second letter from prison on August 19. In it, the former prime minister claimed that the aim of his arrest was his political destruction and said he had initially decided against legal action to avoid confrontation with the authorities.

According to Gharibashvili, he was forced to fight back.

Gharibashvili also said he received a letter from Mamuka Mdinaradze in July. He said that on the same day he explained his position to Mdinaradze and again confirmed that he had no intention of returning to politics.

News from Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan versus Western media: Why were different reports labelled a single ‘information campaign’?
World.content:
Azerbaijan and foreign media

Four separate reports about Azerbaijan have appeared in international media: a TVP World programme by Poland’s public broadcaster on political repression, an Independent report on the conditions in which Ali Karimli is being held, a BBC analysis of political prisoners, and a Guardian review of a documentary about Karabakh.

Baku responded with two official statements. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry summoned Poland’s ambassador over the TVP World programme and handed him a protest note. In a separate statement, the Media Development Agency described the other three publications as possible elements of a single “targeted information campaign”.

However, when examined individually, the reports clearly differ in their subject matter, format and main sources.

TVP: international success and domestic repression

The central question of the TVP World programme “Peace in Azerbaijan comes with repression”, broadcast on 26 August, is why Azerbaijan’s political space continues to shrink despite Baku’s growing international influence.

The programme discusses the arrests of journalists from AbzasMedia, Meydan TV and Toplum TV, as well as criminal cases against opposition figures, activists and researchers. Presenter Benjamin Lee and İPEK Centre deputy director Türkan Bozkurt discuss oil revenues, the transfer of power within one family, the legitimacy Ilham Aliyev gained from victory in Karabakh, relations with the West and the position of national minorities.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry described the programme as biased and the presenter’s conduct as provocative. Since TVP receives state funding from Poland’s budget, the Azerbaijani side linked the programme’s content to the Polish government’s position and described its broadcast as an “unfriendly act”.

The Independent: conditions of Ali Karimli’s detention

The British newspaper’s 30 August report focuses on a narrower issue. The family and lawyers of Ali Karimli, the detained chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, say he has no access to safe drinking water, ventilation, adequate sleep, outdoor exercise or reading materials. A Human Rights Watch representative says the authorities have not presented convincing evidence to the public in his case. The UK Foreign Office confirms that it has raised the issue with Azerbaijani authorities.

The article’s emotive headline highlights the family’s claim that authorities are trying to “break” Karimli. The report also describes the charge against him as “treason”. Officially, however, prosecutors have charged him under an article concerning actions aimed at the violent seizure of power and the forcible alteration of the constitutional order. This is a specific point on which Baku could request a correction.

The newspaper also says it contacted Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry for comment but received no response.

BBC: figures and the case of Igbal Abilov

The Russian Service of the BBC’s article “Why is Ilham Aliyev stepping up repression?”, published on 31 August, focuses not on Ali Karimli but on Talysh researcher Igbal Abilov, who received an 18-year prison sentence.

The BBC analysed lists compiled by the Institute for Peace and Democracy from 2021 to May 2026. It concluded that the number of political prisoners had more than tripled, while the average prison sentence in politically motivated cases reached about 12 years in 2026. The article also examines the cases involving AbzasMedia, Radio Azadliq and Toplum TV, as well as the trials of researchers Bahruz Samadov and Igbal Abilov.

The fact that the calculations rely on lists compiled by a single human rights organisation may be open to debate. However, the BBC explains its methodology in detail, includes Ilham Aliyev’s position that he denies political persecution, and says it contacted the Penitentiary Service for comment but received no response.

Who is restricting access to the official position?

The MEDİA Agency accuses foreign news organisations of failing to seek Azerbaijan’s official position. However, in February 2025, the BBC closed its Baku bureau on the Foreign Ministry’s instructions. The bureau had operated in the country since 1994.

The Foreign Ministry cited the principle of reciprocity and the lack of a legal basis for the bureau’s operation. When authorities restrict the work of local bureaus and government agencies leave journalists’ requests unanswered, foreign news organisations have to rely more heavily on lawyers, relatives and experts based outside the country.

The information landscape that Baku describes as one-sided may therefore partly result from the authorities’ own media policies.

The Guardian: a review of a film about Karabakh

The Guardian article is not a political investigation. It is a short review of The Black Garden, a documentary by director Alexis Pazoumian. The film explores the wartime experience of Karabakh Armenians through the stories of two children and a young soldier who lost a leg.

The review’s introduction says Karabakh Armenians fought against “countless military campaigns” by the Azerbaijani army. However, it does not mention the First Karabakh War, the occupation of Azerbaijani territories, Azerbaijani internally displaced people or other aspects of the conflict. The reviewer also acknowledges that the film lacks a broader political and historical context.

Baku can reasonably criticise this one-sided presentation. However, expecting a film critic to seek comment from the Azerbaijani government would mean applying standards associated with news journalism to a piece about culture.

What do the different reports have in common?

What the four publications have in common is not any proven coordination between them, but the fact that the picture of Azerbaijan they present differs from the government’s official narratives.

TVP and the BBC question the authorities’ arguments about domestic stability and the legitimacy of criminal prosecutions. The Independent raises concerns about the conditions in which a particular detainee is being held. The Guardian, meanwhile, presents the Karabakh war primarily through the experience of the Armenian side.

The reports therefore cover different subjects, but within a single week they touch on three sensitive areas for the Azerbaijani state: domestic political control, relations with international partners and the historical narrative surrounding Karabakh. Baku sees them as part of a single attack not because their content is similar, but because all four diverge from the international image that the Azerbaijani authorities seek to project.

Is the “information campaign” proven?

The MEDİA Agency statement does not specify which facts in the reports are incorrect, nor does it provide evidence that could indicate coordination between the news organisations. At the same time, it claims that the authors did not attempt to establish Azerbaijan’s official position.

However, The Independent says it sent a request for comment to Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry. The BBC quotes the president’s position and says it also sought comment from the Penitentiary Service.

A separate response to each report would have been more convincing. In the case of the Guardian, the authorities could have pointed out factual inaccuracies in its account of the historical context. For The Independent, they could have provided a documented response to the claims about the charges against Karimli and his conditions of detention. The BBC could have received alternative data on the criteria for including people on political prisoner lists and on sentencing statistics. TVP could also have been asked to give the Azerbaijani side a right of reply on air.

Grouping all the reports together in a single statement and presenting them as a politically motivated campaign erases the differences between them. Moreover, the absence of specific rebuttals does not end the debate. Instead, it creates the conditions for further reporting.

The confrontation here is not simply a conflict between “Baku and Western media”. The main problem is that the state places verifiable factual errors, editorial assessments, statements by human rights groups and even a film review in the same political category. This approach does not weaken the criticism. On the contrary, it creates the impression that different news organisations really are acting as a united front.

Although the agency said it intended to take “necessary measures”, it did not specify whether this meant seeking corrections and a right of reply, filing an official complaint or taking other steps.

Azerbaijan and foreign media

World.title: Baker Hughes, OGDCL team up to maximize recovery from mature fields
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. Baker Hughes has signed a multi-year contract with Pakistan’s Oil & Gas Development Company (OGDCL) to enhance production and recovery from mature oil and gas assets, the company said.

Under the agreement, Baker Hughes will work with OGDCL to assess production challenges at the Tando Alam Oil Complex and Pirkoh gas field and develop tailored redevelopment plans covering more than 120 wells.

Tando Alam is a producing conventional oil field located onshore Pakistan. According to GlobalData, the field had recovered 86.63% of its total recoverable reserves, with production reaching a peak in 2004. Based on current economic assumptions, production is expected to continue until the field reaches its economic limit in 2050.

Pirkoh is a producing conventional gas field also located onshore Pakistan. GlobalData says that the field has recovered 99.91% of its total recoverable reserves. Production peaked in 1995 at around 180 million cubic feet per day (MMcfd) of natural gas. The field is estimated to have about 0.08 million barrels of oil equivalent (MMboe) remaining, including 0.45 billion cubic feet (Bcf) of natural gas reserves.

As part of the initial phase, Baker Hughes will identify opportunities aligned with OGDCL’s production targets and economic objectives, while recommending integrated technology and digital solutions to improve well performance and recovery.

The companies will then move to operational execution, with Baker Hughes deploying technologies including AI-enabled chemical injection solutions to improve flow assurance, as well as targeted well workovers and interventions aimed at restoring output from underperforming wells.

“Through our close and collaborative working relationship, we will help OGDC get more value from their existing assets through integrated planning and technology solutions that unlock vital sources of untapped domestic energy supply,” Baker Hughes Executive Vice President of Oilfield Services & Equipment Amerino Gatti said.

World.title: Second day of 4th International Mine Action Conference underway in Baku
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. The 4th International Mine Action Conference, jointly organized by the Azerbaijan National Agency for Mine Action (ANAMA) and the UN Office in Azerbaijan, is continuing its work on the second day, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

The theme of the conference is “Humanitarian Demining for Urban Recovery: Setting Standards of Excellence for Safe Settlements.”

The second day of the conference will feature panel discussions on “Policy Integration in Mine-Affected Urban Recovery,” “Technology & Innovation for Safer and More Effective Humanitarian Demining,” and “Country Case Presentations: National Experiences and Lessons Learned in Humanitarian Mine Action.”

The conference aims to discuss ways to raise global awareness of Azerbaijan’s mine problem, strengthen international cooperation in humanitarian mine action, highlight the role of mine clearance in ensuring safe and sustainable recovery, promote innovative approaches and the exchange of best practices, and mobilize international efforts to address the threat posed by mines.

More than 400 representatives from 60 countries are taking part in the 4th International Humanitarian Mine Action Conference hosted by Baku. Participants include senior officials from a number of countries, representatives of UN agencies, officials from leading international organizations and national mine action centers, as well as representatives of diplomatic missions accredited in Azerbaijan.

Will be updated

World.title: President Tokayev reappoints Kazakhstan’s transport minister
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. Nurlan Sauranbayev has been reappointed Minister of Transport of Kazakhstan.

According to the press service of the Kazakh president, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed the corresponding decree.

On August 28, the Government of Kazakhstan resigned before the newly elected unicameral parliament - the Kurultai.

Sauranbayev was born on May 20, 1967. He graduated from the Kazakh State University named after S.M. Kirov. From 1997 to 2011, he worked at national companies in the railway and oil and gas sectors.

From 2011 through 2014, he served as Vice Minister of Industry and New Technologies of Kazakhstan, and from 2014 to 2016 as Deputy Minister of Defense.

Sauranbayev served as akim (mayor) of Shymkent from 2017 to 2018. From 2019 to 2021, he headed the Department of State Control and Organizational-Territorial Affairs within the Administration of the President of Kazakhstan.

On June 30, 2025, Sauranbayev was appointed Minister of Transport of Kazakhstan by presidential decree.

The following government appointments were also made today:

Serik Zhumangarin was reappointed Deputy Prime Minister - Minister of National Economy of Kazakhstan.

Jaslan Madiyev retained his position as Deputy Prime Minister - Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development of Kazakhstan.

Dauren Kossanov was reappointed Minister of Defense of Kazakhstan.

Erzhan Sadenov was reappointed Minister of Internal Affairs of Kazakhstan.

Ghalymzhan Koishybayev retained his position as Deputy Prime Minister - Head of the Government Office of Kazakhstan.

Nurlybek Nalybayev was reappointed First Deputy Prime Minister of Kazakhstan.

Kanat Bozumbayev was reappointed Deputy Prime Minister of Kazakhstan.

A nationwide referendum on the adoption of Kazakhstan's new Constitution was held on March 15, 2026. The new Constitution officially entered into force on July 1, 2026.

Under the new constitutional model, the position of Vice President was introduced, while the Kazakhstan People's Council was established as the highest constitutional consultative body representing the interests of the people of Kazakhstan. The former bicameral parliament, consisting of the Mazhilis and the Senate, was transformed into a unicameral Kurultai.

World.title: Green Corridor Alliance discusses key parameters of Kazakhstan's power system
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. The Green Corridor Alliance JV discussed key technical parameters of Kazakhstan’s electric power sector with KEGOC and CESI SpA.

This was announced by Tural Aliyev, CEO of the Green Corridor Alliance JV, on his LinkedIn page.

Meanwhile, it is noted that the Green Corridor Alliance JV (GCA) held a technical meeting with the Kazakhstani power grid management company KEGOC JSC, a shareholder of GCA, and the Italian technical team from CESI SpA.

“During the meeting, the parties discussed key data and operational parameters of Kazakhstan’s generating capacity.

In particular, they reviewed schedules for the commissioning and decommissioning of generating facilities, minimum active power, mandatory equipment operation requirements, efficiency, forced outage rates, and maintenance periods,” the post states.

It is emphasized that this data is crucial for the ongoing feasibility study of the “Central Asia–Azerbaijan–Europe” project to create a green energy corridor.

On April 4, 2025, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan, with the support of the Asian Development Bank and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, announced the launch of the first phase of the “Trans-Caspian Green Energy Corridor” initiative. As part of the initiative, the countries signed a cooperation agreement on the preparation of a feasibility study, which provides for the integration of the three countries’ power systems and the creation of a route for supplying renewable energy to Europe.

A joint venture, the Green Corridor Alliance, headquartered in Baku, was established to manage the project. The project’s feasibility study is being conducted with financial support from the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB).

World.title: Shell to acquire stakes in bp’s Tupinambá, Conifer exploration assets
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. bp and Shell have agreed on the terms of a deal under which Shell will acquire a 50% stake in the Tupinambá exploration block in Brazil’s Santos Basin, as well as a 30% stake in five leases covering the Conifer exploration prospect in the deepwater Gulf of America.

The transactions are part of bp’s disciplined capital allocation strategy aimed at becoming a simpler, stronger and more valuable company, bp said.

Following completion of the transactions, bp will retain a 50% interest in Tupinambá and a 70% interest in Conifer and will remain operator of both assets.

“Brazil and the Gulf of America are important regions for bp, and bringing together two experienced operators can help unlock the potential of both opportunities. This collaboration will help strengthen our position in both as we progress exploration activity,” said Gordon Birrell, bp’s EVP Upstream.

Completion of the Tupinambá transaction remains subject to regulatory approvals.

Tupinambá is an offshore exploration block in the Santos Basin, located within Brazil’s pre-salt polygon. The block was awarded to bp in the second cycle of Brazil’s Permanent Offer for Production Sharing (OPP) on December 13, 2023.

As part of the bid, bp offered the Brazilian government a 6.5% share of oil production, representing a 33.2% premium over the minimum required in the tender.

According to Brazilian state-owned Pré-Sal Petróleo S.A. (PPSA), R$7.047 million was paid in signature bonuses, while R$360 million in investments are planned during the first phase of the contract, covering the exploration period.

The Conifer prospect is located in the Keathley Canyon area, approximately 250 miles southwest of New Orleans, Louisiana, near bp’s Kaskida development.

bp was awarded four leases covering the Conifer exploration prospect in August 2023 following Lease Sale 259. The fifth lease was awarded in February 2026 as part of the Big Beautiful Gulf 1 Lease Sale.

The initial Conifer exploration well is expected to be drilled in 2027.

World.title: President Japarov appoints new head of Kyrgyzstan’s SCNS
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov has appointed Maksat Asanaliev as chairman of the State Committee for National Security (SCNS).

This was announced in a statement by the press service of the Kyrgyz President.

According to the decree signed by the head of state, Maksat Asanaliev was appointed to the position in accordance with the Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic.

"President of the Kyrgyz Republic Sadyr Japarov signed a decree, according to which, in accordance with paragraph 2 of Part 1 of Article 70 and Article 71 of the Constitution of the Kyrgyz Republic, Maksat Asanaliev was appointed chairman of the State Committee for National Security of the Kyrgyz Republic," the statement said.

Furthermore, Maksat Asanaliev was relieved of his previously assigned duties.

World.title: Tokayev reappoints ministers of national economy and digital development
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. Serik Zhumangarin has been reappointed as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy of Kazakhstan.

According to the press service of the President of Kazakhstan, the relevant decree was signed by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

On August 28, the Government of Kazakhstan resigned following the election of the country’s newly established unicameral parliament, the Kurultai.

Zhaslan Madiyev has also retained his position as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development of Kazakhstan.

A number of other government appointments were also made today.

By decree of the Head of State, Dauren Kossanov was reappointed as Minister of Defense of Kazakhstan.

Yerzhan Sadenov was reappointed as Minister of Internal Affairs of Kazakhstan.

Ghalymzhan Koishybayev retained his position as Deputy Prime Minister and Head of the Government Office of Kazakhstan.

Nurlybek Nalibayev was reappointed as First Deputy Prime Minister of Kazakhstan.

By decree of President Tokayev, Kanat Bozumbayev was reappointed Deputy Prime Minister of Kazakhstan.

A national referendum on the adoption of the new Constitution of Kazakhstan was held on March 15, 2026. The new Constitution officially entered into force on July 1, 2026.

Under the new constitutional framework, the position of Vice President was introduced, while the Kazakhstan Halyk Kenesi (People’s Council of Kazakhstan) was established as the highest constitutional advisory body representing the interests of the people of Kazakhstan. The country’s bicameral Parliament, consisting of the Mazhilis and the Senate, was transformed into a unicameral Kurultai.

The Kurultai elections were held in Kazakhstan on August 23, 2026. According to the Central Election Commission, the total number of registered voters was 12,623,289. A total of 9,351,539 people, representing 74.08 percent of registered voters, participated in the elections.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s oil price skyrockets above $101
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. The price of Azerbaijan’s Azeri Light crude rose by $4.35, or 4.46%, from the previous level to $101.96 per barrel on a CIF basis at Italy’s Augusta port, a source from the oil market told Trend.

At Türkiye’s Ceyhan port, the price of Azeri Light increased by $4.47, or 4.72%, to $99.21 per barrel on an FOB basis.

The price of Urals crude grew by $4.5, or 6.34%, to $75.48 per barrel.

Meanwhile, the price of Dated Brent crude produced in the North Sea scaled up by $4.53, or 4.82%, to $98.49 per barrel.

Azerbaijan’s 2026 state budget is based on an average oil price of $65 per barrel.

According to Trading Economics, oil prices fell below $91 per barrel on Thursday after three consecutive sessions of gains. Investors are assessing the resumption of military operations in the Middle East and efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the report states.

“U.S. President Donald Trump stated that the latest attacks on Iran would be short-lived. At the same time, he emphasized that the U.S. is prepared for further strikes and reaffirmed his previous statements that Washington controls the Strait of Hormuz.

This week, the U.S. launched new strikes against Iranian targets in the vicinity of this strategically important waterway. The attacks came after about a month of relative calm, and Tehran responded by launching drones and missiles at U.S. bases in the Middle East.

Despite the resumption of military operations, oil tankers continued to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. It is reported that an average of 8 million barrels of oil are transported through the strait daily.

“According to official U.S. data, crude oil inventories fell by 4.5 million barrels last week. This is the first decline in inventories since late July,” the report states.

World.title: Sabalenka fumes over reporter's 'parties' claim after US Open win
World.content:
Double defending champion Aryna Sabalenka has bristled at a reporter's suggestion the events and appearances surrounding the US Open had included "parties and fun" after she cruised past Polina Iatcenko 6-1, 6-1 on Thursday (AEST).

The Belarusian, who had faced a similar line of questioning after her first-round win, fired back that her off-court appearances had not come at the expense of her preparations for the grand slam.

"You guys are, like, a joke. Parties, fun … like, why would you even say that? Why would you even think about that? What kind of question is that?" the world number one said.

"Just because I posted, like, some activities with brands, and you think that I've been partying, not training?" she added, cutting the exchange short.

Turning to her performance against Iatcenko, the four-time grand slam winner said she was pleased with both her level and her focus after another dominant performance at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

"I've been working really hard, but I feel like I'm kind of moving away from trying to be perfect on court," Sabalenka said. "I know that you cannot be perfect, and I'm just trying to work with what I have right now."

Sabalenka will continue her search for a third straight title in New York and avoid ending the year without a major, as she tries to recover her best form after not winning a title since claiming the Miami Open in March.

"I think I struggled a little bit in the middle of the season. Once again, I'm not going to defend myself or explain why, what happened, but I'm happy with my level," the 28-year-old said.

"I can definitely say that mentally I'm way stronger than I was in the middle of the season, and physically I also feel stronger. I feel like I'm on my level of play, and I just want to bring the right focus on the match every time."

Reuters

World.title: Small businesses scan for fake cash as counterfeit seizures soar
World.content:
When Thirroul business owner Calvin Gorsuch's employee was handed a $100 bill by a customer last weekend, they instantly knew it was a fake.

That was because his business, Ohana Home, runs every bill under a blue-light machine.

"So we picked up that it was fake," Mr Gorsuch said.

"They were adamant that it was genuine, but we kept refusing it, and then they left."

Mr Gorsuch said he put the safeguard system in place after the business was stung with a counterfeit $50 note last December.

Calvin Gorsuch says staff turned the customer with the counterfeit note away. (ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt)

Fake notes hit small businesses

Later that same day, neighbouring shop owner Adrian Erdedi's employee was counting the till and noticed something "a little bit odd" about a $100 bill.

"Eventually we identified that it was a fake note taken by one of the other staff members during the day," he said.

The business owners both said more local traders were reporting the same issue.

Mr Erdedi said he posted about the incident on a local Facebook page, where he was overwhelmed by responses from other business owners across the Illawarra.

"There's been a lot of people coming out saying they've had the same notes coming through," he said.

"From what I've heard, there are also $20 notes involved now."

High quality deceptions

In the past financial year, the Australian Border Force (ABF) made 700 detections of counterfeit cash entering the country, intercepting fake notes with a value of $6 million.

That was more than 50 times the number of counterfeit currency imports detected the previous year.

In a statement issued last month, the ABF said there had been "a concerning improvement in the quality of counterfeit notes".

Adrian Erdedi found this fake $100 note in his till at the weekend. (Supplied: Adrian Erdedi)

Mr Erdedi said he could not believe how realistic the fake $100 note was.

"It could have easily been missed if you're not looking for these specific things on the note," he said.

" Once we compared it with another $100 note, you could see the difference, but you had to look really closely to find those little defects. "

Adrian Erdedi's business was hit with a fake note at the weekend. (ABC Illawarra: Rory McDonald)

Mr Gorsuch said in 10 years working in retail, he had seen the quality of fake notes improve substantially.

"In the past when we got fake notes, they were paper-based, and if you scrunched it, it wouldn't pop back," he said.

"The ones now are a polymer, so to the touch they feel more real.

"The colour seems to be the distinguishing factor."

New measures

In Australia, it is against the law to make, possess or knowingly use counterfeit money.

The maximum penalty for producing fake banknotes is 14 years in jail.

On its website, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) advises that suspect banknotes should be reported to police and that counterfeits had no value, meaning scammed businesses would not be reimbursed.

Mr Gorsuch said fake cash also ended up costing local businesses at a time when cost-of-living pressures were already biting.

After the first scam in December, his employees had been trained to verify every note that came through using a blue-light scanner near the till.

Employees now scan every note through the machine. (ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt)

“Every bill we accept we quickly wave it under the light and then that usually shows the invisible UV marks, and then we know it's a genuine note,” he said.

Polymer notes issued by the RBA after 2016 also have a serial number and date of manufacture that light up under blue light.

Mr Erdedi said he had also ordered a blue light and was now training employees to check every note.

World.title: Girl's death after petting zoo visit 'very rare', health authorities say
World.content:
A Victorian girl has died after a weeks-long battle against an infectious disease that her parents say may have been caused by bacteria she contracted at a petting zoo.

The girl's family, who did not wish to be named, confirmed she had been in hospital with a brain injury and kidney failure caused by hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).

An online post from the girl's family said she spent six weeks in an intensive care unit before her death on August 31.

The syndrome is caused by a type of bacteria known as STEC which can be transmitted from animals to humans.

In an online post, the girl's family said she likely contracted the bacteria from a farm "where she held, rode and petted animals".

Occurrence 'very, very rare'

Addressing reporters on Thursday afternoon, Victoria's Deputy Chief Health Officer Clare Looker described cases of the bacterial infection progressing to HUS as "very, very rare".

She said only between one and five cases of HUS were reported in the state each year.

Dr Looker confirmed Victoria had recorded two cases of HUS so far this year, but no common cause had been identified and no facilities had been linked to both cases.

"We know this bacteria exists in many farm animals, so I don't think that shutting a single farm that is taking all the right public health protective measures would stop the risk for children or the community," Dr Looker said.

" At this stage, there's no consideration for that. "

While she would not provide details of the girl's death, Dr Looker said petting zoos had formed part of the health department's investigation.

"We're comfortable that we have fully risk-assessed those settings and taken appropriate control measures," she said.

She urged Victorians to wash their hands after coming into contact with animals.

The Department of Health urged Victorians to wash their hands after coming into contact with animals. (Pexels)

There have been 179 STEC bacteria notifications so far this year in Victoria, compared with 158 detections this time last year.

Dr Looker said this nonetheless represented a "marked increase" in detections since 2023, possibly because of increased testing and improved detection methods.

Premier expresses condolences

The girl has been remembered as courageous and a fighter on a GoFundMe fundraising page set up in late July to support her battle with the illness.

On the page, the girl's parents said their daughter had also tested positive for the illnesses RSV and parainfluenza after being admitted to hospital.

In a post following her death, the family described the emotional toll of her decline as "torture".

"The torture as a parent of not being able to console your own child, not through lack of trying anything and everything you possibly can but because they are truly inconsolable," the family's post said.

" The not knowing if your child will ever talk, smile, walk, run, play, or recognise you again. "

Premier Ben Carroll said his thoughts were with the family.

"This is horrific, that a young person had lost their life," he said.

"I want to extend my heartfelt condolences to the family. I can't imagine what they're going through."

Health officials say the bacteria is commonly found in farm animals. (Unsplash: Jessica Wagner)

HUS is caused by the presence of certain E. coli bacteria known as STEC, which can be transmitted from animals to people and produces the life-threatening Shiga toxin.

The Department of Health said young children, pregnant women, older people and people with weakened immune systems are at greater risk of the syndrome.

HUS is considered an urgent notifiable condition in Victoria, with medical professionals required by law to notify government authorities upon diagnosis.

The department investigates all reported cases of HUS to identify potential sources of infection and prevent further spread.

"The loss of a child is an unimaginable tragedy, and our thoughts are with the family and loved ones grieving at this incredibly difficult time," a Victorian government spokesperson said.

World.title: Warning issued for 'dangerous, fast-moving' fire burning near Gladstone
World.content:
The Queensland Fire Department has issued a Watch and Act warning for a "dangerous, fast moving" vegetation fire burning in the Gladstone region.

Twelve crews are working to control the blaze burning near Kirkwood Road, and aerial support has been requested.

Residents are being warned the situation could get worse quickly and they should prepare to leave.

The department said the fire started about 11:50am on the side of the road alongside the Gladstone Tondoon Botanic Gardens.

The rural fire service was also back-burning along the Gladstone trail this afternoon to try and get the fire within containment lines.

The Queensland Fire Department has issued a Watch and Act warning for a fire burning in the Gladstone area. (Supplied: QFD)

The department said the fire is likely to impact the community in the coming hours.

In a social media post this afternoon, Queensland Police said multiple roads had been closed around the suburbs of Glen Eden, Burura, Toolooa and Telina.

The road closures include Kirkwood Road, Dixon Drive, Bukkan Road and Haddock Drive.

"Ongoing diversions and road closures are in place … motorists are encouraged to avoid unnecessary travel," the social media post said.

Resident Jean Williams has lived in the area for five years.

She had been driving home on Kirkwood Road after a trip to the grocery store when she noticed the large plume of smoke.

"It just got bigger and bigger, and then we heard a call at the door; one of our neighbours had rushed up to see … they didn't know how close it was," Ms Williams said.

"Our neighbours are short on water, and they have nothing to fight with; however, they are not in any danger at the moment."

World.title: Morley Market business owners still struggling one year after devastating fire
World.content:
One year on from a devastating fire which destroyed a shopping centre in Perth's north-east, the pain for business owners who lost what they had spent years working on is still raw.

"Seven years I worked hard for my business, and in one night I lost everything," said Mojgan Fakhar, who owned Frida Tattoo Studio at the Morley Market.

"For like two or three weeks … I couldn't even think … it was really hard."

Ms Fakhar's business was one of many ruined in the fire, which last September gutted the shopping centre that had stood in the heart of Morley for decades.

Mojgan Fakhar says she found the weeks after the fire extremely difficult. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

The market housed more than 20 stores and restaurants, most of which were family-run.

While some have managed to re-establish their businesses at other sites, others are still on the hunt for somewhere to start again.

Mohammad Frahim, who ran Monte Carlo Hairstylists, a barber shop within the complex, said despite his best efforts, finding a new site had so far proven impossible.

"It's very hard to re-establish; some people they get a chance, they can do it, some people … are not getting that chance," Mr Frahim said.

Mohammad Frahim and his wife Salma Bano lost their entire business in the Morley Market blaze. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"I'm trying to get back to my business, but it's very hard, because you need a lot of money as well.

"Every day I'm looking in the marketplace, and for any barber shop for sale, but it's hard to find."

Morley Market businesses call for financial aid Business owners affected by a fire which gutted a shopping centre in Perth's north-east are calling for state government support as they begin the recovery process.

Ms Fakhar has moved into a smaller site nearby, but it's an ongoing battle.

"Emotionally I've tried to get back to normal, but still it's not normal or the same as before.

"I rebuilt it, not as big as before, not as equipped as before, but I tried my best to have a nice place for my clients again."

Cause still unknown

In a bitter blow to business owners, authorities could not determine the cause of the fire because of the severe level of damage.

A Department of Fire and Emergency Services debrief document written after the blaze, seen by the ABC, details problems identified during its investigation, including that a "local alarm" was not operational.

The fire quickly took hold of the building in September 2025. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

The debrief said "early detection of the fire would have occurred" if the local alarm had been working and it might have resulted in early containment.

For business owners, that was a tough pill to swallow.

Mina Eshan, who lost more than $200,000 worth of assets when Bella Skin Clinic was gutted in the fire, said there were still too many unanswered questions.

Mina Eshan still does not have all the answers she needs. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"It's not just about money or compensation, it's about something like this not happening again, and not putting other people's lives in danger," she said.

Insurance proving tricky

A number of business owners say they have run into problems getting any of what they lost back through insurance, with some left to regret not having taken out contents protection.

"That was my biggest mistake," Mr Frahim said.

"I had public liability insurance for the shop, but not the contents.

"Three or four times I called [the insurance company], and the receptionist [said] he will call me, but I never got a call back."

The market was demolished after fire gutted the building. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

Mr Frahim said the owners of the destroyed businesses were in desperate need of government support.

"The government should take some decision for the shopkeepers as well, who don't have insurance, who lost the business, lost everything, so somewhere we need help as well."

The City of Bayswater said it had done what it could to support the affected businesses.

"The city quickly established a recovery hub at Morley Library, partnering with a number of agencies and arranging for translators to be onsite across community drop-in sessions, aimed at providing support and advice to affected business owners, employees, tenants and customers," Bayswater Mayor Filomena Piffaretti said in a statement.

The Morley Market is now a vacant site, as pictured from an aerial photo in June. (Supplied: Nearmap)

"Space was also made available at Morley Library for appointments between service providers and impacted business owners."

Ms Piffaretti said the city had not yet received any applications to redevelop the site, which remained vacant and fenced off.

Meanwhile, a multi-million-dollar upgrade of the Morley Galleria shopping centre is well and truly underway across the road.

World.title: Teen granted bail in Brisbane alleged carjacking murder
World.content:
One of several teenagers accused of killing a Brisbane man who was the subject of a "prolonged and brutal assault" before being run over by his own car has been granted bail.

In July, police arrested the 15-year-old boy and six other children aged between 14 and 17, in relation to an alleged attack of a 27-year-old man in Kelvin Grove.

The group allegedly dragged the man from his car, before beating him then stealing his ute.

While trying to stop them from fleeing in his vehicle, he was allegedly run over.

The teen was initially charged with a range of offences including robbery in company and grievous bodily harm, but this was upgraded to murder after the man died in August.

On Thursday, he appeared in the Childrens Court of Queensland in Brisbane where his lawyers successfully argued he should be released ahead of a trial.

The court heard the entire incident was captured on video. (ABC News)

During his bail hearing the court heard the group had allegedly hatched a plan to assault and rob the man.

The court heard the entire incident was captured on video, which had been played during an earlier bail hearing.

Judge Anthony Rafter told the court this was "fairly compelling evidence" as it clearly showed him kicking and punching the man, which his lawyer accepted.

However, Ria Ku told the court her client denied taking part in "any planning in the situation" to specifically target the man and was in the rear passenger seat when he was struck.

She told the court the issue at trial would be the teenager's level of involvement.

"The recordings do show he had taken part in the assault, but that's not to say that he had driven the car," she said.

"My instructions are my client had come in a place of genuine assistance but then as things panned out the matter escalated."

'Violent attack' captured on video

Deputy Director of Public Prosecutions Greg Cummings told the court in the lead up, there was a "throwaway" line from one person about "going to bash a paedophile" but the video and other statements disputed this.

He told the court the teens set upon him immediately for "no apparent reason".

"The recording from the actual events … demonstrates right from the beginning it was a violent attack in order to steal, nothing to do with altruistic purposes whatsoever", he said.

The court heard an autopsy report was still outstanding.

Mr Cummings said because of this it could not be alleged yet whether his death was the result of the earlier assault or from being "flung" from the ute.

"We're just not in a position to say whether the injuries inflicted in the initial assault of which [the teenager] was definitely involved, are those which caused his death," he said.

The court heard the teenager, who was a New Zealand citizen, had no criminal history.

A 27-year-old man died in August after allegedly being beaten and run over in Kelvin Grove in July. (ABC News: Melissa Maddison)

His mother also offered to pay a $40,000 surety for his release.

Judge Rafter told the court the evidence indicates the teen played an active role in a "prolonged and brutal assault" of the man.

"The crown case of the defendant's involvement in the violent assault appears to be very strong if not overwhelming," he said.

However, Judge Rafter told the court the case for murder or manslaughter against the teen appeared to only have "some substance" without an autopsy.

Judge Rafter determined the teenager could be released on strict conditions including that he wears an ankle tracking monitor and abides by a 24-hour curfew.

He cannot leave his home without being accompanied his parents or a representative from the Department of Youth Justice and must not contact any of his co-accused or witnesses in the case.

World.title: Nepal's peak trekking season is approaching but its guides are in mourning
World.content:
At this time of year, trekking guide Eka Devi Mainali would normally be going about her usual preparations for Nepal's peak season.

But instead she's waiting to hear if her friends' bodies have been found, 19 of them.

"I have lost many friends and people I personally knew in this devastating disaster," Ms Mainali told the ABC.

Nepal's peak hiking season runs from September to November.

But for many guides like Ms Mainali, who lead foreigners through the Himalayas each year, they must now carry something heavier into the mountains, their grief.

"It feels very difficult to talk about tourism or business without first thinking about the human tragedy," she said.

"This is not simply a natural disaster. It is a deeply painful time for families who have lost loved ones, homes and livelihoods."

Eka Devi Mainali dedicates 10 per cent of her company's profits towards supporting and empowering women and children. (Supplied: Eka Devi Mainali)

Ms Mainali founded her own trekking company, SheGuide Treks, and has guided tourists along Nepal's most popular routes, including Everest Base Camp, for more than a decade.

Each year, she dedicates 10 per cent of her company's profits towards supporting and empowering women and children.

"My intention is bigger than myself. I want to build something that creates opportunities for women and allows me to give back to children and communities as well," she said.

Speaking from her office in Kathmandu, Ms Mainali sorts through piles of children's clothing she has collected to donate to those in areas affected by the floods.

She described the process as "incredibly painful".

Eka Devi Mainali has collected children's clothing from family and friends to donate to those affected by the floods. (Supplied: Eka Devi Mainali )

She has taken responsibility for coordinating with the families of her 19 friends who are still missing.

"I am standing with their wives and children, doing my best to support and represent their families during this difficult time," she said.

Nepal said 1,118 bodies had so far been recovered, while more than 3,900 people remained missing. At least 38 Australians are among those unaccounted-for.

Conflicted between pain and livelihood

For guides like Shishir Sapkota, the flood spared his own family and friends.

But in a trekking community as tight-knit as Nepal's, this type of loss is felt beyond bloodlines.

"As guides, we are connected to many people in the trekking and local communities, so when something like this happens, it affects us all emotionally, even if our own families are safe," he told the ABC.

Shishir Shishir says when events like the deadly floods occur, the entire trekking community is affected. (Supplied: Shishir Sapkota)

Mr Sapkota has been running his tour business, Mato Manchey Ra Himal, for three years.

He said he enjoyed working as a guide because trekking was "not only about reaching a destination".

"It is also about experiencing the local culture, meeting people and sharing the beauty of Nepal with visitors," he said.

Thinking of the people who have lost their lives, homes and livelihoods, Mr Sapkota said he was toeing the line between sadness and worry about the upcoming trekking season.

"Tourism is the livelihood of many guides, porters, hotel owners, transport workers and local communities," he said.

The aftermath of flash flooding along the Trishuli River. (AP: Rajesh Kumar Singh)

Mr Sapkota said he had tours booked for this season, but the current situation had made his plans uncertain.

He said he hoped for the best for the affected areas and also hoped the trekking season could continue safely.

"Nepal and the people working in tourism need the support of visitors now more than ever."

Trip to Nepal 'not only a holiday'

Tourism operators are keeping tours running while assessing damage to roads and communities.

Intrepid Travel, which operates 26 tours in Nepal, said its customers and staff were safe and it was supporting affected local partners and host families.

"We are closely monitoring developments and continuing to assess the impact on current trips, transportation and accommodation," said Yalamber Rai, Intrepid's general manager for Nepal.

Two of its itineraries pass through the affected region, including the Tamang Heritage and Langtang Valley Trek.

Both normally include an overnight stay in Syabrubesi, a village that suffered significant damage.

"These floods will have lasting impacts on livelihoods, trade, tourism and local businesses," Mr Rai told the ABC.

Most of Nepal's well-known treks continue to operate normally. (Unsplash: Laurentiu Morariu)

Tourism is a vital part of the country's economy, with data showing it made up close to 7 per cent of GDP pre-pandemic.

Nepal's tourism minister, Khadak Raj Paudel, this week urged travellers not to cancel their trips.

"Your coming to Nepal this time does not mean only a holiday. It's a big support to the country fighting this catastrophic tragedy," he said.

Operators also had a clear message: Nepal's industry has not stopped, but routes must be carefully monitored.

"We believe it is important that travel continues responsibly in the regions that are stable and therefore operational," said Bly Carpenter of World Expeditions, a tour company operating for more than 50 years in Nepal.

'Strength and solidarity' on display

Kathmandu's airport remains fully functional, and Nepal's major trekking regions including Annapurna, Everest and Kanchenjunga are operating as normal.

"For people feeling anxious, our message is that Nepal is a large and geographically diverse country," Mr Carpenter said.

"The devastation in the affected communities is immense, but it does not mean the whole country or all trekking regions have been impacted.

"One of the best ways to support Nepal right now is by continuing with planned treks."

Operators stress that supporting communities is incredibly important in the aftermath of the flood. (Supplied: World Expeditions)

He stressed the resilient nature of Nepalis who depend on tourism.

"They live alongside the mountains and know their power, and they are, sadly, no strangers to natural disaster. That doesn't make a loss like this any easier," Mr Carpenter said.

"They are deeply saddened by the events of last Wednesday, as anyone would be, but there is a strength and a solidarity in these communities that continues to move us.

"We are humbled by the quiet courage they continue to show."

For travellers already in the region, the challenge is more immediate.

Utsav Aryal, director of the Nepalese Australian Welfare Society, said those stranded at places like Gosaikunda Lake were being urged to use different paths.

"While an easterly route is an option, it is much longer and far more treacherous for older people to hike compared to the usual western route," he said.

The floods affected many pilgrims visiting Mount Kailash in south-western Tibet. (Reuters: Jacky Chen)

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade's Smartraveller website has advised those going to Nepal to "reconsider" travelling to the flood-affected areas of the Bhote-Koshi and Trishuli rivers due to the risk of landslides and further flooding.

"There remains a high risk of further flooding, landslides and debris flows in affected areas," it said.

World.title: Pipeline companies' major plans to supply east coast with Beetaloo gas
World.content:
Two companies are moving ahead with plans to build new gas pipelines, which they say will significantly increase supply from the Northern Territory's Beetaloo Basin to Australia's east coast.

First gas from the Beetaloo Basin flowed into the NT power grid earlier this week, at a ceremony where NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said the resource could provide "more gas than this country will ever know what to do with".

Infrastructure company Jemena has unveiled plans to build a 400-kilometre connection from the basin to the Northern Gas Pipeline (NGP), which runs from Tennant Creek to Mount Isa, and is the only line connecting NT gas resources to the east coast.

Meanwhile, environmental assessment has started on plans lodged by another company, APA Group, to build a new 1,500-kilometre line directly from the Beetaloo, about 500 kilometres south-east of Darwin, to south-west Queensland.

David Gillespie speaking about Jemena's plans at the NT Resources Week conference. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Jemena managing director David Gillespie said if the proposal was built and the general network was improved, the full potential of the Beetaloo could be realised.

"I do think there is a great opportunity to see the NT or the Beetaloo … [not] being infrastructure constrained," he said.

"The resource is expected to be very material, and so the sort of infrastructure that's being built to support it is typically 20 to 30 years at a minimum."

Mr Gillespie could not say how much it would cost, but said the 622-kilometre NGP cost $700 million to build before it was opened in 2018.

He said Jemena would submit a pipeline permit application with the NT government before the end of the year.

APA chief executive Adam Watson in a statement said his company's proposal was "critical, nation-building infrastructure".

"The North to East Australia Pipeline (NEAP) has the potential to be transformational for Australia's energy market," he said.

" Unlocking the Beetaloo Basin [will] support energy security and transition for households, businesses and our key manufacturing sectors. "

The NEAP requires environmental approval by the Queensland, NT and federal governments.

The NT Government and gas industry have touted the vast shale gas basin as one answer to potential east coast gas shortages. (ABC News)

Gas export goals

Mr Gillespie said both Jemena and APA Group's projects could be financially viable, and his company would not seek public subsidies.

"We're more in concert than we are in competition … a lot of our emphasis is on how we bring gas to market and commercialise that resource as production increases," he said.

"The plans that APA might have, I think, ultimately go to some of the longer-term opportunities for the Beetaloo to be a key export producer."

Mr Gillespie said Beetaloo gas would primarily be used to power the domestic market in its early years, before transitioning to export markets as infrastructure improved.

"The first gas is probably more likely to support those domestic requirements," he said.

"Then as you see the scale of the production ramp up, the infrastructure that's built associated with that will be largely pointing towards an export market.

"Whether that's going east to Queensland, whether that's going north to Middle Arm within the Territory, that's for the market to determine."

World.title: TMK Energy gas rates surge as Mongolian drilling push looms
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears TMK Energy gas rates surge as Mongolian drilling push looms Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright September 3, 2026 — 4:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

TMK Energy has delivered a solid four per cent monthly increase in gas production at its wholly-owned Gurvantes XXXV coal seam gas pilot project in Mongolia, with instantaneous flow rates recently spiking to more than 50,000 standard cubic feet per day (scfd). The company says average daily gas production for August hit 810 cubic metres per day, or around 28,600scfd, up from July’s average of 778 cubic metres per day. The result comes as TMK prepares to kick off a new drilling and well workover program after signing a contract with Major Drilling. TMK Energy gas flare at its LF-07 well in the company’s Gurvantes XXXV project in Mongolia. The progress at Gurvantes XXXV is timely and feeds into a broader national energy strategy. Mongolia’s coal-bed methane sector, while still in its early days, is already being viewed as a domestic power supply solution rather than just an exploration story, with the government in Ulaanbaatar pushing ahead on new gas-fired power generation to ease its current grid constraints. Those constraints stem from ageing Soviet-era coal-fired plants operating with zero reserve capacity, causing severe winter supply deficits and frequent blackouts. Outdated transmission networks waste roughly 25 per cent of generated electricity, forcing the country to import over 20 per cent of its power from Russia and China at high cost.



‘We are tantalisingly close to another breakthrough gas rate being achieved in the near term.’ TMK Energy chief executive officer Dougal Ferguson Furthermore, the rigid coal fleet cannot rapidly ramp up output to balance peak-demand periods or integrate intermittent renewables. Eating outFood Fish Lane unveils a glamorous, old-world cocktail boozer A hidden bar finally disappears entirely at the far end of Fish Lane, replaced by a slick bolthole defined by timber and leather surfaces, vintage framed photos and casino chip-inspired coasters. Matt Shea September 3, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Robbie Lofaro reckons real estate agents have a reputation problem. He should know. He’s a real estate agent. “It’s not the most well-liked profession. There’s a bit of a stigma,” says Lofaro candidly, who is chief executive of Place Purpose Group. Lane’s End opened mid-August at the far end of Fish Lane. Markus Ravik To say that’s why Lofaro has opened a cocktail bar, Lane’s End, at the end of Fish Lane would be a simplification, but it would also largely be the truth. “It’s how appreciative everyone is in hospitality,” Lofaro says when asked what he enjoys about the industry. “Somebody comes into a cocktail bar and they’re just happy to be there. That’s a very different contrast to real estate.”



Lofaro should know. Because he also has a background in hospitality. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Related Article Exclusive Sydney dining heavy hitter takes over iconic Gerard’s site Back when he was a teenager it was a fish-and-chip shop and a cafe. These days it’s Sunny’s, a rooftop bar in Margate. “I still love real estate,” Lofaro says. “I love being able to have an impact on so many people’s lives in real estate, but I think being able to do it in a very different way is exciting.” Lofaro says he wasn’t planning on opening Lane’s End, a second bar right in the thick of the inner city – but perhaps his love for the industry makes him open to such opportunities. Lofaro unveiled it last month in the premises previously occupied by Next Episode, a “secret” hip-hop bar.



The bar has a thoroughly different feel to Next Episode, which came before it. Markus Ravik “I was at Next Episode and one of the bartenders told me the owner was looking to sell. Lane’s End is instead defined by its timber surfaces, plenty of greenery and vintage framed photos, cross-backed timber chairs, casino chip-inspired coasters, and warm lighting. The old hidden frontage has been ditched in favour of something much more welcoming. Markus Ravik



The bar itself is more or less in the same spot, but has been heightened to make it a more comfortable spot to perch. In charge of the design was Amelia Stevenson. Stevenson works social media in Lofaro’s real estate businesses but has a background in hospitality. “She came to me and said, ‘I really want the opportunity to take charge of that.’ I said, ‘Here’s your budget, do what you think is right.’ She’s just 22 and she’s gone and organised the whole fit-out. It’s incredible – much better than I could’ve done myself.” Lane’s End keeps it simple, with a tight list of signatures and twists, but the bartenders will happily make you all the classics. Markus Ravik Stevenson and bartender Hope Kempster have collaborated on a short, sharp cocktail menu of seven signatures and twists – expect drinks such as a fig and vanilla Old Fashioned, and an Aperol Spritz sour – but Lofaro says the barkeeps will happily shake or stir any classic to your tastes.



Beyond cocktails (and a clutch of mocktails), the team is pouring just a couple of white wines and a couple of reds on a rotational basis, the drops drawn from the Sunny’s cellar. Open Thu 4pm-10pm, Fri-Sat 4pm-12am, Sun 4pm-10pm Fish Lane, 5/27 Cordelia Street, South Brisbane instagram.com/lanes.end.bar
