World.title: This sharehouse comedy was given a second chance. Thankfully, it’s better than ever
World.content:
★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview This sharehouse comedy was given a second chance. Thankfully, it’s better than ever Jared Richards September 3, 2026 — 4:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Adults ★★★★ Sitcoms take time to find their comedic groove – even all-timers Seinfeld, Sex and the City and Parks and Recreation had shaky first seasons, with major characters and narrative devices abandoned as the writers homed in on the magic of their show. As streamers order shorter seasons and are ready to cancel a show that’s not an immediate hit, we see fewer shows reach their potential – thankfully, Disney+ and FX gave Adults a chance, returning with a much-improved second season. The Adults crew are back (from left): Owen Thiele as Anton, Lucy Freyer as Billie, Malik Elassal as Samir, Amita Rao as Issa and Jack Innanen as Paul Baker. Billed as Gen Z’s answer to Friends, Adults debuted last year alongside two other hyped comedies also attempting to reach younger audiences, HBO’s influencer-skewering I Love LA and Amazon Prime Video’s campus comedy Overcompensating.



Enjoyable but uneven, all three didn’t quite capture the zeitgeist as hoped – each trying too hard with nonsensical scenes, cameos and references all desperate to be clipped for TikTok. But Adults, to me, kept getting the most in its own way, more focused on gaining attention than making jokes. Related Article Streaming Binge banks on its new Colin From Accounts replacement, as it unveils 2027 line-up Take the pilot’s opening scene on the subway, where the hyper-confident Issa (Amita Rao) confronts a man masturbating on the subway by shoving her own hand down her pants. “Is this the world you want?” she screams. No, not really. And, seemingly, Adults’ creators Rebecca Shaw and Ben Kronengold (former writers on Jimmy Fallon’s The Tonight Show) agree, releasing a prequel special a few months before season two that now retroactively sits on Disney+ as season one’s first episode. Focusing on how Adults’ ensemble of five 20-somethings came to live together rent-free in a Queens sharehouse, the new pilot re-centres the show on friendship, realising that’s the draw a Gen Z Friends needs. Largely unknown prior to Adults, the show’s core cast – comedians Amita Rao and Malik Elassal, Australian Lucy Freyer, TikTok heartthrob Jack Innanen and podcaster-actor Owen Thiele – are excellent comedic actors.



Amita Rao as Issa, Jack Innanen as Paul Baker, Owen Thiele as Anton, Lucy Freyer as Billie, Malik Elassal as Samir. Season two gets out of the way to let each one shine, dialling back big stunts for heightened-but-relatable moments, such as Billie (Freyer) treating the club like a competition during a quarter-life crisis (“I’m unemployed. I’m not cool. If I’m not young any more, then what am I even?”). Meanwhile, the gang catch the sweet, sensitive Paul Baker (Innanen) code-switching into frat bro with other friends, and the bubbly Anton (Thiele) can’t help but revert to a demon whenever near his sister (Raven Symone, one of many well-utilised guest stars). No longer trying to prove how relevant, cool and unique it is, Adults is a much more assured, funny and charming comedy – a lesson we all learn at some point in our 20s. Adults (season two) is now streaming on Disney+.

World.title: A fireball, then screams of agony: Suspected arsonist engulfed in flames, abandoned on pavement
World.content:
A suspected arsonist is fighting for his life in hospital and a second has been left badly burnt after the firebombing of a tobacco shop in Melbourne’s west. The two men were engulfed in flames at the Boss Tobacco shop in Melton about 2.50am on Thursday. CCTV footage shows the premises erupting in flames after apparently being doused in petrol and set alight. A man in a blue hoodie is shown on fire running away from the shop. A man flees as flames erupt at the Melton store. Victoria Police A 23-year-old man was found lying on the ground nearby and flown to The Alfred hospital in a critical condition.



Police are hunting for the other man, who they say left the badly injured man behind and is believed to have significant burns to his hands and feet. Related Article Courts He infamously left jail in a Rolls-Royce. Now a key player in Melbourne’s tobacco wars is back behind bars The pair’s white ute was found alight on the Western Highway in Hopetoun Park shortly after the incident, having been abandoned by the second man. Police said that man was then picked up on the side of the road nearby by a Good Samaritan who dropped him off near the Bacchus Marsh Avenue of Honour memorial about 3.30am. Police said the Good Samaritan had been interviewed and was co-operative.



A witness told 3AW she heard a loud bang and saw a young man on the ground pulling off his pants and screaming in agony. “Over 50 per cent, I’d say, of his body is burnt,” the woman said. “No skin left on his legs, on his hands.” Another witness said: “His skin was hanging off and I feel like he had garbage bags – like burnt garbage bags – hanging off him.” Detective Inspector Chris Murray said the man in hospital could die from his injuries. “Fire is uncontrollable and unpredictable and we can only be thankful it’s not an innocent member of the public who has been injured,” he said.



Police released footage of the alleged firebombing attack. Victoria Police If the critically injured man were to die from his injuries, police said, the second man would be held criminally responsible. Police said they were searching for a second vehicle, a silver single-cab ute, which was seen in the vicinity. While the second ute might not have been involved with the firebombing, “it was certainly seen in the vicinity and/or in convoy with the white ute that rammed the tobacco store,” Murray said. Investigators are treating the case as a targeted attack.



Murray said he was confident the firebombing was linked to organised crime, but did not identify any group or motive. Related Article Updated

Tragedy Katie’s world was full of sparkle. Now her light has gone out in a ‘despicable’ arson attack “We talk about the crime task business model, where [young males] they’re tasked to carry out a job on behalf of someone they wouldn’t know,” he said. “These youths, who’ve got no idea about what they’re doing, they’re not criminal masterminds, and they need to stop.” Police urged anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.



The attack is the latest in a string of firebombings of tobacco shops and licensed venues across Melbourne. In March, a 52-year-old man died after he sustained significant burns following an arson attack in a Chapel Street dessert bar. Burlesque performer Katie Tangey, 27 – described by police as completely innocent – died in February 2025 after she became trapped in a burning home that was mistakenly firebombed by arsonists. World.title: Sorry, Jane Austen, but these Australian novels had us at hello
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsLiterature Sorry, Jane Austen, but these Australian novels had us at hello Sophie Quick September 3, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thanks to Netflix, yet another Pride and Prejudice adaptation is coming our way. Bonnets and Bennets will again infect the zeitgeist, not that we had a real break. We live in a wretched state of perma-Austen. Breaks are hallucinations – and always short-lived. But news of the upcoming series has got me thinking about Jane Austen’s famous opening sentence: “It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.” I cringe whenever it’s quoted or parodied. To be fair, this is more about my distaste for the Jane Austen Industrial Complex than for the sentence itself. It’s fine, I guess. But – in the spirit of sweeping statements – it is a fact that many Australian novelists have written better openers than Austen. I’m here to prove it. Photo: Robin Cowcher “Unemployed at last!” from Such is Life by Joseph Furphy is short, snappy, roguish and an undeniable banger. But I might be biased towards unnerving exclamations because I also love Brian Castro’s opener to Chinese Postman, “How time-honoured custom reverts to ruin!” and Luke Davies’ opener to Candy, “Everything’s f---ing beautiful!” In each case, the reader is plunged straight into a highly questionable perspective. That’s the kind of thing I love in fiction.



The first sentence of Miles Franklin’s My Brilliant Career is also an exclamation: “Boo, hoo!” It’s short and snappy but also annoying. However, since I’m being strict on grammar (counting only one-sentence openers), but loose on what counts as the first sentence (accepting both prologues and first chapters), Franklin’s masterpiece still qualifies for an honourable mention. The prologue begins with bluster: “MY DEAR FELLOW AUSTRALIANS, Just a few lines to tell you that this is a story all about myself – for no other purpose do I write it.” Related Article Literature Podcasters and YouTubers talk too much. Here’s my secret to silencing them Bluff, bluster and bravado are big in Australian novels. The opening to Peter Carey’s Bliss goes much further. “Harry Joy was to die three times, but it was his first death which was to have the greatest effect on him, and it is this first death which we shall now witness.” (The opening to Olivia De Zilva’s 2025 novel, Plastic Budgie, continues this tradition: “People accuse you of lying when you say you remember your birth.”) I love novels that kick off with startling or cryptic images. “The boy is curled up in his bed like a skinny black question mark” from Bitin’ Back by Vivienne Cleven is a great one. And I love “The front door of Thea’s flat was ajar so Lilian gave it a push and went in, her eyes on swivels.” That’s from Elizabeth Harrower’s The Long Prospect. Ellen van Neerven flings the reader into a world of roadhouse pies and lineal confusion with Heat and Light: “It was a slight, old woman in a pie shop off the highway that told me who my grandmother was.” Michelle de Kretser hints at sordid continental glamour with Scary Monsters: “That was the year we went to Sardinia to meet John Berger’s mistress.”



In terms of instant gut-punch, Kim Scott’s Taboo is in a category all of its own: “Our hometown was a massacre place.” The first sentence of Kenneths Cook’s classic, Wake in Fright, is disturbingly riveting: “He sat at his desk, wearily watching the children file out of the room, reflecting that, this term at least, it was reasonable to assume that none of the girls was pregnant.” There have been some knock-out openers in books published in recent years. I’m thinking of Signs of Damage by Diana Reid (“The coroner is difficult to take seriously”) and Nock Loose by Patrick Marlborough (“They blast Cold Chisel and kick off hell”). The first line of Ella Baxter’s Woo Woo is excellent: “Sabine had traumatised only a few people in her life, and one of them was her husband.” Right off the bat, I have a lot of questions. If Sabine has traumatised only a few, what is the expected number of people a vigorous modern woman should traumatise in her lifetime? How am I tracking? The opening line of Diana Reid’s Signs of Damage is a knockout. Of course, there are many great Australian writers who reel readers in slowly, casting their spell over paragraphs. And the one-liners I’ve listed here are only scratching the surface. I don’t have room for all my favourites! But this is an open-and-shut case. Do I need to go on? MY DEAR FELLOW AUSTRALIANS, as we steel ourselves for another ritual force-feeding of a-truth-universally-acknowledged, it is clear that we are not in want of our own great literary opening gambits. I rest my case. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

Focusing on how Adults’ ensemble of five 20-somethings came to live together rent-free in a Queens sharehouse, the new pilot re-centres the show on friendship, realising that’s the draw a Gen Z Friends needs. Largely unknown prior to Adults, the show’s core cast – comedians Amita Rao and Malik Elassal, Australian Lucy Freyer, TikTok heartthrob Jack Innanen and podcaster-actor Owen Thiele – are excellent comedic actors.



Amita Rao as Issa, Jack Innanen as Paul Baker, Owen Thiele as Anton, Lucy Freyer as Billie, Malik Elassal as Samir. Season two gets out of the way to let each one shine, dialling back big stunts for heightened-but-relatable moments, such as Billie (Freyer) treating the club like a competition during a quarter-life crisis (“I’m unemployed. I’m not cool. If I’m not young any more, then what am I even?”). Meanwhile, the gang catch the sweet, sensitive Paul Baker (Innanen) code-switching into frat bro with other friends, and the bubbly Anton (Thiele) can’t help but revert to a demon whenever near his sister (Raven Symone, one of many well-utilised guest stars). No longer trying to prove how relevant, cool and unique it is, Adults is a much more assured, funny and charming comedy – a lesson we all learn at some point in our 20s. Adults (season two) is now streaming on Disney+.

World.title: A fireball, then screams of agony: Suspected arsonist engulfed in flames, abandoned on pavement
World.content:
A suspected arsonist is fighting for his life in hospital and a second has been left badly burnt after the firebombing of a tobacco shop in Melbourne’s west. The two men were engulfed in flames at the Boss Tobacco shop in Melton about 2.50am on Thursday. CCTV footage shows the premises erupting in flames after apparently being doused in petrol and set alight. A man in a blue hoodie is shown on fire running away from the shop. A man flees as flames erupt at the Melton store. Victoria Police A 23-year-old man was found lying on the ground nearby and flown to The Alfred hospital in a critical condition.



Police are hunting for the other man, who they say left the badly injured man behind and is believed to have significant burns to his hands and feet. Related Article Courts He infamously left jail in a Rolls-Royce. Now a key player in Melbourne’s tobacco wars is back behind bars The pair’s white ute was found alight on the Western Highway in Hopetoun Park shortly after the incident, having been abandoned by the second man. Police said that man was then picked up on the side of the road nearby by a Good Samaritan who dropped him off near the Bacchus Marsh Avenue of Honour memorial about 3.30am. Police said the Good Samaritan had been interviewed and was co-operative.



A witness told 3AW she heard a loud bang and saw a young man on the ground pulling off his pants and screaming in agony. “Over 50 per cent, I’d say, of his body is burnt,” the woman said. “No skin left on his legs, on his hands.” Another witness said: “His skin was hanging off and I feel like he had garbage bags – like burnt garbage bags – hanging off him.” Detective Inspector Chris Murray said the man in hospital could die from his injuries. “Fire is uncontrollable and unpredictable and we can only be thankful it’s not an innocent member of the public who has been injured,” he said.



Police released footage of the alleged firebombing attack. Victoria Police If the critically injured man were to die from his injuries, police said, the second man would be held criminally responsible. Police said they were searching for a second vehicle, a silver single-cab ute, which was seen in the vicinity. While the second ute might not have been involved with the firebombing, “it was certainly seen in the vicinity and/or in convoy with the white ute that rammed the tobacco store,” Murray said. Investigators are treating the case as a targeted attack.



Murray said he was confident the firebombing was linked to organised crime, but did not identify any group or motive. Related Article Updated

Tragedy Katie’s world was full of sparkle. Now her light has gone out in a ‘despicable’ arson attack “We talk about the crime task business model, where [young males] they’re tasked to carry out a job on behalf of someone they wouldn’t know,” he said. “These youths, who’ve got no idea about what they’re doing, they’re not criminal masterminds, and they need to stop.” Police urged anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.



The attack is the latest in a string of firebombings of tobacco shops and licensed venues across Melbourne. In March, a 52-year-old man died after he sustained significant burns following an arson attack in a Chapel Street dessert bar. Burlesque performer Katie Tangey, 27 – described by police as completely innocent – died in February 2025 after she became trapped in a burning home that was mistakenly firebombed by arsonists. World.title: Sorry, Jane Austen, but these Australian novels had us at hello
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsLiterature Sorry, Jane Austen, but these Australian novels had us at hello Sophie Quick September 3, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thanks to Netflix, yet another Pride and Prejudice adaptation is coming our way. Bonnets and Bennets will again infect the zeitgeist, not that we had a real break. We live in a wretched state of perma-Austen. Breaks are hallucinations – and always short-lived. But news of the upcoming series has got me thinking about Jane Austen’s famous opening sentence: “It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.” I cringe whenever it’s quoted or parodied. To be fair, this is more about my distaste for the Jane Austen Industrial Complex than for the sentence itself. It’s fine, I guess. But – in the spirit of sweeping statements – it is a fact that many Australian novelists have written better openers than Austen. I’m here to prove it. Photo: Robin Cowcher “Unemployed at last!” from Such is Life by Joseph Furphy is short, snappy, roguish and an undeniable banger. But I might be biased towards unnerving exclamations because I also love Brian Castro’s opener to Chinese Postman, “How time-honoured custom reverts to ruin!” and Luke Davies’ opener to Candy, “Everything’s f---ing beautiful!” In each case, the reader is plunged straight into a highly questionable perspective. That’s the kind of thing I love in fiction.



The first sentence of Miles Franklin’s My Brilliant Career is also an exclamation: “Boo, hoo!” It’s short and snappy but also annoying. However, since I’m being strict on grammar (counting only one-sentence openers), but loose on what counts as the first sentence (accepting both prologues and first chapters), Franklin’s masterpiece still qualifies for an honourable mention. The prologue begins with bluster: “MY DEAR FELLOW AUSTRALIANS, Just a few lines to tell you that this is a story all about myself – for no other purpose do I write it.” Related Article Literature Podcasters and YouTubers talk too much. Here’s my secret to silencing them Bluff, bluster and bravado are big in Australian novels. The opening to Peter Carey’s Bliss goes much further. “Harry Joy was to die three times, but it was his first death which was to have the greatest effect on him, and it is this first death which we shall now witness.” (The opening to Olivia De Zilva’s 2025 novel, Plastic Budgie, continues this tradition: “People accuse you of lying when you say you remember your birth.”) I love novels that kick off with startling or cryptic images. “The boy is curled up in his bed like a skinny black question mark” from Bitin’ Back by Vivienne Cleven is a great one. And I love “The front door of Thea’s flat was ajar so Lilian gave it a push and went in, her eyes on swivels.” That’s from Elizabeth Harrower’s The Long Prospect. Ellen van Neerven flings the reader into a world of roadhouse pies and lineal confusion with Heat and Light: “It was a slight, old woman in a pie shop off the highway that told me who my grandmother was.” Michelle de Kretser hints at sordid continental glamour with Scary Monsters: “That was the year we went to Sardinia to meet John Berger’s mistress.”



In terms of instant gut-punch, Kim Scott’s Taboo is in a category all of its own: “Our hometown was a massacre place.” The first sentence of Kenneths Cook’s classic, Wake in Fright, is disturbingly riveting: “He sat at his desk, wearily watching the children file out of the room, reflecting that, this term at least, it was reasonable to assume that none of the girls was pregnant.” There have been some knock-out openers in books published in recent years. I’m thinking of Signs of Damage by Diana Reid (“The coroner is difficult to take seriously”) and Nock Loose by Patrick Marlborough (“They blast Cold Chisel and kick off hell”). The first line of Ella Baxter’s Woo Woo is excellent: “Sabine had traumatised only a few people in her life, and one of them was her husband.” Right off the bat, I have a lot of questions. If Sabine has traumatised only a few, what is the expected number of people a vigorous modern woman should traumatise in her lifetime? How am I tracking? The opening line of Diana Reid’s Signs of Damage is a knockout. Of course, there are many great Australian writers who reel readers in slowly, casting their spell over paragraphs. And the one-liners I’ve listed here are only scratching the surface. I don’t have room for all my favourites! But this is an open-and-shut case. Do I need to go on? MY DEAR FELLOW AUSTRALIANS, as we steel ourselves for another ritual force-feeding of a-truth-universally-acknowledged, it is clear that we are not in want of our own great literary opening gambits. I rest my case. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.
