World.title: Gloriavale Christian School registration cancelled following special ERO review
World.content:
Gloriavale Christian School's registration cancelled Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

The secretary for education has confirmed Gloriavale Christian School's registration as a private school will be cancelled, after considering the findings of a special Education Review Office review.

Secretary Ellen MacGregor-Reid told the school's leaders in December that she was cancelling its registration because of serious concerns the school was not a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

The school remains open as a result of a High Court challenge by the board, with a judicial review hearing set down for three days in October.

On Thursday, Education Services deputy secretary Geoff Short said the ministry had applied to the court to lift orders preventing the school's closure.

"The secretary for education has decided to cancel Gloriavale Christian School's registration as a private school after considering findings from a special review by the Education Review Office," he said.

"The school currently has around 80 students enrolled and the ministry will work with the school community to determine the most practical timing for the school's closure, with students' best interests guiding those discussions.

"The ministry has applied to the court to lift interim orders relating to the secretary for education's December 2025 decision to cancel the school's registration as a private school to enable this latest decision to be implemented.

"Further information is being provided directly to affected families."

Education Minister Erica Stanford said she trusted that the secretary's decision-making process was robust.

"The secretary for education clearly has concerns, as do the Education Review Office, into the quality of the education that's being provided and the situation those children are in.

Erica Stanford. RNZ / Nick Monro

"I have absolute and utter confidence in Ellen MacGregor-Reid as the secretary for education to have made the right decision."

The special review considered whether Gloriavale met the private school registration criteria and the extent to which it had addressed previous Education Review Office (ERO) concerns identified in a November 2024 visit and July 2025 special review.

ERO's special review report published on Thursday said the school was not meeting one of eight registration criteria, to provide a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

"Inconsistencies between the school and community child protection policies limit assurance that governance oversight is effective and that the school is consistently a physically and emotionally safe place for students," the report said.

"Information was withheld from ERO in relation to provision, monitoring and reporting requirements for health and safety to and by the premises owners.

"ERO is not confident that systems are operating effectively to identify, manage and monitor risk over time or that reasonable steps have been taken."

The report noted that the Teaching Council was investigating two allegations of staff misconduct. The school had provided ERO with the letter of suspension for one staff member.

"Staff members subject to role restrictions have continued to operate in restricted areas. Evidence gathered onsite indicates that one staff member continued to participate in board meetings, despite a requirement that they not do so," the report said.

ERO said Gloriavale's school met the criteria relating to suitable premises, provision of tuition, suitable staffing, suitable equipment, curriculum, managers assessed as fit and proper and suitable tuition standards.

"Overall, some improvement is evident. However, these improvements are partial and, in key areas, not yet sustained," ERO said.

"ERO is not yet confident that the school's systems are sufficiently embedded, consistent and reliable to ensure ongoing compliance with the requirements for registration over time."

The report said the school was providing education for students in Years 1 to 8, with a roll of 84 students.

Gloriavale Leavers Support Trust manager Liz Gregory told Checkpoint she believed the school would always struggle to meet safety criteria.

"Just with the history of Gloriavale, just the way it has operated and the coercive controlling nature. Basically I think the past has caught up with their present," she said.

Gregory said student enrolment at a mainstream school would be a "last resort" for Gloriavale.

"They will keep fighting. Every other option would be preferable to them. It does look like a school closure will go ahead, what the final schooling options look like for the students there, that's yet to be seen."

Ministry letters to Gloriavale obtained by RNZ under the Official Information Act in May detailed concerns from community members, specialists and agencies about the private school, as the secretary moved to cancel its registration.

The letters noted concerns about most teenagers being prevented from progressing beyond Year 11, a lack of support for young victims and abusers and students not being able to use school toilets without fear.

Separately, an Education Review Office special review of homeschooling by Gloriavale families concluded that they were not meeting the legal requirements.

The agency said homeschooling families were living and learning in overcrowded hostels that could be unsafe and some of the children were struggling to write.

In June the ministry said two surplus classrooms were relocated to Awahono School in Ahaura to support roll fluctuations and could also cater for Gloriavale students if families choose to enrol their children there in future.

In a statement in December, Gloriavale's school board said it was "deeply disappointed" by the ministry's decision to cancel its registration.

World.title: Sacked Solomon Islands Finance Minister says Cabinet revolt is imminent
World.content:
Recently sacked Solomon Islands Finance Minister Gordon Darcy Lilo says further resignations from Cabinet are imminent, as Prime Minister Matthew Wale gears up to fight a no-confidence motion.

The motion of no confidence is expected to be tabled on Monday, 7 September.

Lilo - who shares a political party with the motion's champion, Manasseh Maelanga - was removed from Cabinet by Wale this afternoon.

Speaking to RNZ Pacific on the day he was fired, Lilo denied any involvement in planning against Wale, but said he now felt obliged to support the motion.

"I'm caught in between," he said.

"I cannot move (away) from a party member because there are only two of us, so we have to be together in this whole proposition."

Solomon Islands Prime Minister Gordon Darcy Lilo. RNZI / Johnny Blades

Mealanga resigned as Wale's Home Affairs Minister on Monday, joined by Justice Minister Clezy Rore and Commerce Minister Harry Kuma. Lilo did not reveal who he knew, or expected, to quit next.

Wale elevated three government backbench MPs to Cabinet within the week to replace them, rather than pulling from the Opposition. Those MPs - Rexson Ramofafia, Nestor Ghiro and Alfred Tuasuila - had joined the coalition in June.

It means the Government's 33-member majority is drawn down to 29. Rore and Kuma, both People First Party (PFP) members, may be able to sway fellow party members to back the motion.

As a result, Lilo predicted that a swing against Wale was highly likely.

"I think there are valid reasons as well."

"It boils down to the way that Cabinet has ... there seems to be an absence of an operation of a Cabinet Government and that raises a lot of concerns."

Lilo noted that Wale's coalition, formed in the rubble of Jeremiah Manele's government in April, had never formalised terms through a signed agreement.

"It could be that the Prime Minister might have decided to run (the Government) himself... in the absence of that coalition agreement.

"Then, maybe he underestimated the fact that this kind of a situation might arise."

The motion forced Wale home from Palau on Sunday, where he was attending the Pacific Islands Forum leaders summit.

The Prime Minister has vowed to fight on, calling the defectors political opportunists with a "disturbing willingness to put petty political interests ahead of national interest."

"The people deserve the opportunity to see whether the GREAT Coalition can deliver." Wale said in a statement.

"The bigger question is whether 'lack of consultation' is being used as a convenient political justification for a move that may have been contemplated well before the current dispute emerged."

World.title: Bird flu 'hoax' claims spread online
World.content:
Bird flu conspiracy theories being spread on social media Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

As biosecurity and conservation groups work to shield the country's wildlife from any spread of bird flu, researchers say some New Zealanders are embracing false narratives about the virus on social media.

Following three detections of the deadly avian influenza, the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) is encouraging people to report any sightings of three or more sick or dead wild birds, but hundreds of people online are claiming the virus is a hoax.

MPI has been monitoring the spread of the highly contagious viral disease overseas for more than 20 years and the H5N1 strain for the past six, with response and surveillance work underway to protect poultry production and wildlife.

The Department of Conservation has been vaccinating critically endangered species to help curtail any further spread, while a wildlife hospital has set up an off-site triage centre to assess wild birds for symptoms.

Within days of the first case being confirmed in July, disinformation researcher Dr Sanjana Hattotuwa said reality was overtaken online by a script incorrectly casting bird flu as a sequel to the Covid-19 pandemic.

He tracked thousands of social media comments on RNZ and NZ Herald articles, finding that most falsely dismissed bird flu as a hoax or "plandemic".

"By 16 July commenters had converted a biosecurity event into a further episode in an established political story about Covid deception, vaccine injury, captured media, corrupt science, globalist control and the destruction of food sovereignty," he said.

Dr Sanjana Hattotuwa. Supplied

"Disinformation researchers, contrary to what is popularly believed, love to be proved wrong and here in this instance, I was really worried that the first confirmed case of bird flu in Aotearoa would result in exactly the kind of discourse that I ended up studying."

Hattotuwa said commenters were creating a "self-sealing account", where any evidence of H5N1 proved orchestration, uncertainty proved incompetence, absence of confirmed spread proved scaremongering and any official response proved that a planned operation had begun.

When MPI reported no further H5 detections on 24 July, commenters misconstrued that as evidence of fakery, he said.

"They called field staff crisis actors, described systematic surveillance as staged theatre, treated the absence of protective equipment as proof that no virus existed and attacked expenditure on monitoring," he said.

Hattotuwa said inaccurate descriptions of bird flu as "Covid 2.0" or "plandemic take 2" placed the new risk inside an already settled story.

"This framing matters because it removes the need to assess the present evidence," he said.

"Stories and storytelling are what the disinformation community and the conspiratorial community are very, very good at. When you have a community that subscribes to conspiracy, there is actually no space within that discourse for science."

Hattotuwa found on social media, users repeatedly "crowded out" constructive or scientific discussions, manufacturing the appearance of an emphatic popular consensus on comment threads.

New Zealanders are embracing false narratives about bird flu on social media. 123RF

'Evil plot'

Conspiracy theory researcher M Dentith said they had also observed unfounded concerns that bird flu was a hoax or at times "some kind of evil plot by people in power".

"There's a slight libertarian streak within our society. There are certain people who just don't like the idea that governments or people in positions of authority are going to tell people what to do," they said.

Dentith, an associate professor of philosophy at Beijing Normal University, said the scale of the disinformation was very hard to know and could appear exaggerated on social media.

The lack of visible consequences from bird flu appeared to be contributing to doubts, they said.

"This a bad analogy here but we're not seeing chickens on buses snuffling and coughing, we're not really seeing birds being sick in public and thus people going, 'Well, I'm not seeing any evidence of a bird flu, so it can't really be real, right?'"

New Zealand had great early success in eliminating Covid-19. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

The country's successful containment of Covid-19 had inadvertently paved the way for future scepticism, Dentith said.

"Because we were able to control and contain the virus within our policy quite successfully, we didn't see the kind of large scale tragedy that actually may have left an imprint on people's minds. If Covid wasn't a big deal because we didn't see those bad outcomes, then surely when the government is making a big deal out of bird flu, there must be something really suspicious going on there as well."

For people dealing with friends or family members who were bird flu sceptics, Dentith suggested finding common ground and appealing to shared values.

"Many people go, 'Well, just report the facts. Just tell them that, you know, bird flu is real' but telling people insistently that what they believe is wrong doesn't really work. What you need to be able to do is find some degree of commonality and then kind of expand on that to try and get them to consider your particular perspective."

Massey University distinguished professor of infectious disease epidemiology and public health Nigel French said disinformation had become an inevitable reality in modern science communication.

"In almost every aspect of work that I've done on infectious diseases there's disinformation. I think we just have to make sure that the correct information is disseminated as effectively and as widely as possible to counter the disinformation," he said.

New Zealand was well-positioned to respond to bird flu and many people were working hard to minimise the impacts, French said.

"We've had more time than any country really to prepare for this because it's been travelling around the world for some time. We know what the impacts have been elsewhere and that gives us an indication of what it could be like here," he said.

Reporting urged

The Poultry Industry Association was monitoring bird flu developments in Australia and helping New Zealand farmers prepare for a possible incursion, while the New Zealand Veterinary Association was distributing information to help people keep their pets safe.

University of Otago professor of virology Jemma Geoghegan said public monitoring was essential for catching early cases.

"It's usually going to be members of the public that stumble across these animals first and it's really important that they know what to do and what not to do," she said.

Geoghegan urged people to report any unusual bird deaths or illnesses to the MPI hotline, recommending that they take photos or videos from a safe distance while avoiding touching or getting too close to the animals.

World.title: Developer defends reviving controversial Arrowtown Ridgeburn housing project
World.content:
Developer defends controversial Arrowtown housing project Morning Report Download MP3 11m

The developer behind a controversial housing project near Arrowtown is defending a revised fast-track application and says more housing is needed in the area.

Ridgeburn Ltd was offering interest-free deposit loans for first-home buyers and an extra $27 million for road upgrades and bus infrastructure near its proposed 1210-house development and commercial precinct.

The project had been criticised by locals, who argued it was the wrong project in the wrong place, with the potential to choke roads, hurt regional tourism and bypass years of careful district council planning.

The developers temporarily withdrew their application in July after councils highlighted "significant information gaps" and Fast-track panel convenor Jane Borthwick concluded it was not ready to be passed to an expert panel.

But plans were in place to submit again this month.

The director of Ridgeburn, Kurt Gibbons, told Morning Report, one of the big issues the first time around was the development's wastewater plant.

The site of a housing project near Arrowtown proposed by Ridgeburn Ltd. Supplied / Ridgeburn

"We had been working with iwi around replanting and recloaking Morven Hill, which is 54 hectares of native planting, when our wastewater plant put out its disposal we thought the best spot for it would be on Morven Hill.

"After listening to our community and the worries they had we decided to move that disposal field to a lower level slat disposal field."

Gibbons claimed the water which would come out of the waterwater plant would be batheable.

"I think it was going to be a challenging part to the consent being on a hill, it would've taken a lot more time to get people comfortable around that. I think consent was plausible but it would've been challenged."

Gibbons said Queenstown as a whole needed housing, with rental prices too high.

"We've got the highest growth in the country, we've got high rent, high prices and we need supply... we're building supply... we need to plan for the future."

Ridgeburn was not just housing, Gibbons said, it would have office spaces, daycare centres and bars.

"We've got $38m to build a wastewater treatment plant and we've asked Queenstown Council if they want to connect into our plant, they're not interested. We're spending $27m on roading upgrades, you've got a really dangerous intersection already there that has accidents..."

In terms of affordability within Ridgeburn, Gibbons originally said 20 percent of it would be affordable. When Morning Report challenged those numbers he conceded 45 of the affordable houses would be for sale and 135 were rent capped for 10 years, which he said was about 16 percent or 180 houses.

An artist's impression of the proposed Ridgeburn housing project near Arrowtown, Otago. Supplied / Ridgeburn

"Look there's a lot of developments out there, I don't know any other developments in the country that is offering this," he said.

"We have out own wastewater treatment plant, we have our own stormwater management system, we're collecting our own portable water for the site, we're building roads that aren't there that are needed already."

With the wastewater treatment plant there would be sludge that would need to be collected, Gibbons said, but he could not say "off the top of my head" where that sludge would go.

"The team that put it together will know where it's going," he said.

Gibbons said he lived in Arrowtown with his family but knew many people who wanted to live there couldn't due to the lack of affordable housing.

"This is providing public good because it's creating housing, giving people the opportunity to get into a home in an area they want to live."

Responding to Gibbons' comments on Morning Report, Queenstown Smart Growth Initiative said the proposed roading upgrades were focused on roads serving the development and would not solve wider congestion issues.

It also argued the affordable housing proposals would not guarantee long-term affordability and criticised the use of the fast-track process for what it described as an unnecessary out-of-zone development.

"The 90 percent of median market rent being offered on these units is likely just a lower quartile market rent, not necessarily below market, nor affordable for many. This isn't a retained affordable housing programme, it's a developer-led scheme in which he profits from both the rental income and the capital gains over that 10-year period," the group said.

"Some of these 'affordable homes' are dual-key units - two self-contained 32m2 spaces under one title, which suit an investor after a double income stream, not a nurse, teacher or essential worker looking for an actual home."

The project could leave the community facing ongoing infrastructure and traffic costs, the group said.

"An out-of-zone development on this scale isn't needed to meet housing demand. Quite the opposite as being outside the plan is exactly what generates the unreasonable congestion and disjointed infrastructure an in-zone development wouldn't."

Queenstown Lakes District Council declined to comment on the Ridgeburn application specifically - citing the ongoing fast-track process.

However, planning and development general manager David Wallace said the council had previously raised concerns about large, out-of-sequence developments outside growth areas identified in its spatial plan.

"The impacts of any significant development that is out of sequence, unanticipated, unplanned and unserviced in rural environments outside well-known and planned-for development centres may impact the community and tourism sector significantly," he said.

"Significant developments within our spatial plan priority areas required by central government that have been planned for would be appropriate in meeting central and local government requirements for housing growth and minimised impact on communities."

There were many reasons why a council might not support connecting to proposed privately developed wastewater systems, he said.

"That would not support government-mandated spatial planning. Unplanned developments outside of spatial plan priority areas may also feed into an already highly-constrained and congested state highway and local road transport network that hasn't been sufficiently invested in to cater for this style of development," he said.

"It's important to note that cumulative impacts of the many fast-track developments will not be considered under the current fast-track legislation and this is naturally of significant concern for our community."

The council already had sufficient zoned land to accommodate long-term growth and supported the Queenstown Lakes Community Housing Trust (QLCHT) models which delivered enduring affordability, he said.

"All developers have the opportunity to contribute to this proven model by providing a portion of their development to QLCHT."

World.title: 'Young people aren't drinking anything like we used to': Alcohol intake at record lows
World.content:
This story has been updated to correct the total available alcohol consumption figure and attribute that this is among the lowest of all OECD countries

Alcohol consumption in NZ drops to record lows Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Hospitality businesses in Christchurch have pointed to changing habits among young people as a factor amid record low levels of alcohol consumption.

Stats NZ reported total available alcohol consumption per capita fell to below 6 litres of pure alcohol for the year ending June for the first time.

New Zealand's per capita consumption now sat among the lowest of all OECD countries, according to the Brewers Association of New Zealand.

It comes at a time when hospitality businesses were struggling although there was confidence further south that the Garden City was potentially bucking national trends.

Over 420 hospitality companies entered liquidation in the past year, a 42 percent jump on the previous 12 months.

There were 2900 hospitality businesses that ceased trading altogether, an increase of almost 40 percent.

Hospitality businesses in Christchurch have pointed to changing habits among young people. 123RF

In central Christchurch, the picture was a bit more rosy.

Dux Central operations manager Ross Herrick said the bar and restaurant had been steady.

The nearby One New Zealand Stadium which opened earlier this year had made a huge difference.

"On game day, it's a game changer," Herrick said. "It's fantastic. Stadium's doing a lot of good for the city in general, I think."

The sale of low and non-alcohol options had been exponential. But Herrick also pointed to the popularity of alcohol, or lack thereof, among younger people.

"I noticed from my own daughter, the young people aren't drinking anything like we used to. Young people are drinking less and less often, I think. I know my daughter's the worst customer you could ever want," he said.

He estimated young people contributed to about 8 percent of the bar's turnover.

Within a stone's throw on High Street was bar and burger joint Smash Palace.

Smash Palace owner Greg May. RNZ/LouisDunham

Owner Greg May felt Christchurch was bucking the trend seen in other centres.

"I am surprised looking at it from a Christchurch-centric point of view. I think nationally there's some hard times up north."

There had been generational shifts among young people which had contributed to a decline in alcohol consumption, May said.

"A lot of young people are more worried about their health. Alcohol isn't one of the healthiest choices they can make," he said.

There were also economic factors that were keeping things in check, May said.

"Times are tighter at the moment. Energy costs have gone up, housing costs have gone up so people have to cut their cloth where they can."

Smash Palace. SUPPLIED

Several people RNZ spoke to had also seen changes among the habits of younger age groups, and felt there was waning enthusiasm for going out.

"I think in general younger generations are far more emotionally intelligent and see things in slightly different ways than my generation and above," one woman said.

Others also pointed to the cost-of-living, health and greater awareness of the negative effects for a dip in alcohol consumption.

Based on the Stats NZ numbers, beer remained the most popular alcohol beverage of choice, accounting for 59.7 percent of all alcohol available for consumption in 2026. Wine's share had fallen in recent years to 19.9 percent with spirits picking up the difference.

The government has been reviewing the hospitality sector.

World.title: Speed bump removal divides Nelson residents
World.content:
Residents in Nelson's Tāhunanui Hills are divided over speed bumps intended to slow traffic and reduce rat-running on the streets above State Highway 6.

The council decided to remove them after surveying public opinion but a group of residents say the feedback did not accurately portray the wishes of those who live on the affected streets.

Nelson City Council first installed the speed cushions on Moana and Bisley avenues as part of a two-year trial in January 2024.

But elected members voted in March to remove them - against staff advice - after a survey of residents showed 63 percent wanted them gone and only 23 percent supported keeping them.

Some residents said the speed cushions had reduced speeding and the number of crashes. Others said they created disruptive noise and vibrations.

The council heard from advocates and opponents on Thursday.

The speed cushions are scheduled to be removed sometime during the next road resealing season, which begins in October.

Brian Nelson, of the Bisley Moana Speed Humps Retention Group, told the council residents were alarmed by the decision to remove them.

Removing them was the right call in light of feedback to the survey but in recent months it had become clear it was the opposite of what residents in affected areas wanted, he said.

The group reviewed the survey data and, when responses from those who did not live on Bisley or Moana Avenues were excluded, it showed residents were equally divided, Nelson said.

Volunteers then surveyed 109 households in the streets and found 80 percent wanted the traffic calming measures to remain, he said.

"Council evidence clearly shows dangerous speeds of 60 to 80km/h on our narrow, windy roads. Council should not encourage this by removing the speed cushions.

"Your roading engineers know how Bisley Moana fits as a collector road into overall city traffic flows and they recommend retaining the speed cushions."

The speed cushions were installed as a trial in January 2024 but the Nelson City Council voted to remove them in March, after residents complained about the noise and disruption. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Resident Nelson McEwan said the two streets were intrinsically dangerous with sharp blind corners and were slippery following rain.

"Council data shows the cushions have lowered traffic volume by 41 percent, lowered mean speed by 24 percent, halved the accident rate and boy racers have evaporated. Removal of cushions will cause the prior conditions and behaviour to return," McEwan said.

The speed bumps vastly improved safety and McEwan implored the council to reverse its decision and retain the cushions until an equally safe alternative was found.

Resident Pauline Puklowski said the roads had high crash rates, blind corners, hidden access ways and S-bends that attracted competitive racing.

"Thankfully the speed cushions have successfully tamed some of the dangerous driving, night-time boy racers and repeated crashes where residents risk their own safety to act as first responders," she said.

Some residents want the council to reverse its decision to remove the speed cushions saying accidents have halved since their trial began in January 2024. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Residents questioned the $70,000 cost to remove safety measures without an evidence-based justification.

"Council is placing hypothetical fears of vibration and noise above genuine safety. Residents accept normal urban noise like buses and heavy trade vehicles but we do not accept being treated as collateral damage for motorist convenience," Puklowski said.

"You cannot feel safe when you are waiting for the next accident, afraid to cycle or use the footpath wondering if a speeding driver is going to navigate the next corner, or worrying if your children are safe sleeping metres away from a previous crash site."

Speaking in support of the speed cushions being removed, Nicholas Lunn called the debate "a circus" and said the only thing that had changed since the decision to remove them was lobbying by those who wanted to see them retained.

Lunn defended the council's survey results.

The survey by the Bisley Moana Speed Humps Retention Group was subjective because it was done on the doorstep, in-person by the advocates themselves, he said.

Lunn accepted traffic counts and accident rates were lower but he said people were upset and there had to be a better way.

Others did not like the speed cushions in their current form, but wanted some type of traffic calming. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Many residents wanted some form of traffic calming, such as chicanes, plantings or a lower speed limit, just not the cushions in their current form, he said.

"It's time we put this behind us and actually worked together to create sensible traffic calming solutions that you can implement across Nelson," Lunn said.

"Sensible solutions mean solutions that don't upset residents from noise, vibration, swerving, bad driving."

Resident Darryl Ware said the noise was noticeable as soon as the speed bumps were installed and he contacted the council to let them know.

He was told by the engineer in charge of the project that they had not considered the noise, he said.

"Every small ute, small business [vehicle], with a trailer or without a trailer, but carrying metal tools, pipes, bits of things, goes ka-ching, ka-ching over it and that really is disturbing," Ware said.

"Every council in this country, including this one, has in their main charter to provide the ratepayers with quiet enjoyment of their properties - this is directly counter to that."

Mayor Nick Smith acknowledged both sides and said changing the March decision would require a formal motion.

World.title: 'Imagine if all of us showed up': Young voters urged to enrol
World.content:
The number of young people enrolled to vote has increased over the past month, but almost 188,000 18- to 24-year-olds remain unenrolled ahead of this year's general election.

The youth enrolment rate rose from 53.89 percent at the end of July to 57.45 percent at the end of August. There are currently 253,158 18- to 24-year-olds enrolled to vote.

On A Roll, a rangatahi-led non-partisan campaign, is now urging young people to get on the roll before the 25 October deadline.

Ethan Reille (Kāi Tahu), 22, is one of the rangatahi behind the kaupapa and said young people need to see voting as something bigger than political parties.

"This shouldn't be about political parties. It should be about our communities, the kind of future we want to inherit, and also just ensuring that we have a seat at the table."

Reille said young people's low participation could become a cycle, with a lack of trust in politicians making young people feel disconnected from the political system.

"We know that young people don't feel prioritised by politicians. Therefore, they don't see themselves in the system, and therefore they don't vote. And because they don't vote, politicians will continue to not prioritise those very young people."

Reille was Labour's candidate for Waitaki at the 2023 general election and is a former president of Young Labour. He was only 18 when he put his name forward to contest the seat, and has had a keen interest in politics since he was a 15-year-old, acting as a student rep on his school's board of trustees, as well as a member of the Waitaki District Youth Council.

VNP / Daniela Maoate-Cox

Barriers to voting

On A Roll was created in response to changes made through the Electoral Amendment Act, including the removal of same-day enrolment.

"By virtue of that, there are more barriers for young people to be voting in this year's general election," Reille said.

"We know that young people, particularly 18- to 24-year-olds, are the least likely to be enrolling and voting, and that's by virtue of the statistics."

Reille said 16,000 more young people had enrolled in the past month, which he described as "really good" progress.

"That shows that we're making moves."

But he said there was still a long way to go.

"Imagine if all of us showed up," he said.

"Imagine what kind of future Aotearoa would look like if all of us showed up and enrolled to vote for this year's general election."

22-year-old Ethan Reille (Kāi Tahu) wants rangatahi to imagine an Aotearoa where every young person turned up to vote. Supplied / Ethan Reille

Why are young people less likely to be enrolled?

Reille said young people's disengagement was not necessarily about indifference, but a lack of confidence that voting would make a difference.

"I think the goalposts keep on shifting. For a long time now, young people have been excluded from the system and the way our election cycles are set up. There's the sense of a self-reinforcing cycle."

He said the campaign wanted to make the process easier to understand, while moving the focus away from political parties.

"The conversations we're having on the ground is voting does seem hard.

"Our job in Aotearoa is to make voting as seamlessly easy as possible and to be able to demystify and break down those barriers."

He said their kaupapa was focused on encouraging young people to think about the issues and future they cared about, rather than telling them who to vote for.

"As a non-partisan campaign, we really want to depoliticise the idea of enrolling and voting. This has everything to do about young people and the kind of future they want, no matter their beliefs or the issues they care about."

Reille said cost of living was one issue young people were consistently raising.

But he said the campaign wanted to reach young people before they even got to the question of which party or candidate they might support.

"It's having a real honest conversation about how enrolling and voting brings a sense of community.

"And it's, again, taking away this idea that voting is about an individual, it's about a collective.

World.title: Fake parking QR codes discovered in Wellington
World.content:
Fake parking QR codes have been found across Wellington, with police urging residents of the capital to be vigilant over potential scams.

Wellington City Council said parking staff had removed about a dozen fake stickers from parking meters around the city over the past couple of days.

Scanning the QR code directs the user to a site that requests information such as the anticipated parking time and licence plate number, before asking for credit card details.

Do you know more? Email mary.argue@rnz.co.nz

In July, Christchurch City Council sounded the alarm over a similar scam, after finding fake QR code stickers on several council-owned and privately-owned parking meters

In a post on social media on Thursday, Wellington District Police said it had received complaints about the scam and warned people not to fall for it.

"They might look legitimate but aren't and are scamming people parking on the roads through their payment system.

"Council staff are pulling down these stickers when they see them, but we would appreciate information from the public on where they've been placed."

World.title: Boyd 'extremely honoured' after signing two-year deal as Maroons coach
World.content:
Queensland great Darius Boyd has been unveiled as the next Maroons coach after Billy Slater's exit.

Boyd, who represented the Maroons 28 times in the State of Origin arena as a player, has signed a two-year deal. He is second on Queensland's all-time tryscorers list behind Greg Inglis.

Boyd, 39, said he is "extremely honoured" at receiving the chance to lead his state in the Origin arena.

"It's a privileged position, and I'm very grateful for the opportunity," he said.

Boyd (right) was a long-time Origin teammate of Slater (left) during his 28-game career for the Maroons. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"I understand the responsibility that comes with the role as well. My job is to build on the legacy created by the many great Queensland players and coaches who have come before us."

Boyd's signing comes after Slater departed from the Maroons coaching role last month following a five-year stint at the helm.

Since his retirement as a player at the end of 2020, Boyd has coached Queensland's under-19 team to consecutive series wins over NSW.

Like Slater before him, Boyd joins Queensland with no prior NRL head coaching experience, although he has served as an assistant under Kevin Walters at the Broncos.

Slater ended his stint as Queensland's coach last month after three Origin series wins in five years. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Queensland Rugby League (QRL) chair Brian Canavan said Boyd had "lived and breathed what it means to represent Queensland" as a player.

"His playing achievements speak for themselves, but what has impressed us just as much is the work he has done since retirement to develop as a coach and leader.

"He has built strong relationships throughout our pathways system, earned the respect of players and staff, and demonstrated a genuine commitment to helping young people reach their potential.

"Darius understands the responsibility that comes with the Maroons jersey. He knows our culture, our history and the standards required to succeed at the highest level."

World.title: Cox says Swans five will remain banned regardless of police probe result
World.content:
Sydney's five exiled players will remain stood down until the end of the AFL season, regardless of how an ongoing police investigation unfolds.

Victoria Police has interviewed four Sydney men as part of an investigation into sexual assault allegations during a post-AFL match party at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel.

Swans players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon were suspended for the remainder of the season for "breaching club standards" and will not be at the SCG for the club's qualifying final against Brisbane on Saturday.

Police speak with four men over Sydney Swans scandal Victoria Police detectives confirm they have spoken with four Sydney men as part of their sexual assault investigation linked to the Sydney Swans.

Those suspensions are separate to the police investigation.

Swans coach Dean Cox reiterated those sanctions would remain unchanged despite police interviewing only four men.

Detectives confirmed they travelled to NSW this week to interview a 30-year-old Maroubra man, a 25-year-old Paddington man and two Randwick men aged 25 and 26.

No charges have been laid and the ABC is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

"All five will remain stood down from the football club," Cox said on Thursday.

"That's one thing that we spoke about at the start, the police investigation and then the behavioural nature of it.

The Swans kick off their finals campaign with a clash against reigning premiers Brisbane this weekend. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

"We're going to be separated, and that will still remain."

Police have flagged that an update to the investigation is not expected for at least eight weeks.

Cox, who has remained in contact with the five players over their wellbeing, said the timeframe was out of the club's control as it wrestled with making a call on the group's playing future.

The eight-week period takes in the free agency and trade period from October 2 to October 14.

"That's part of the investigation of the way they do it. I just focus on what we can control and what I can control," Cox said.

Andrew Pridham (right) said the suspensions would "torpedo" Sydney's premiership chances this year. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Asked about potential impacts on the club's trade period, the Swans coach was short: "There are so many things that we need to talk about, so not for today."

While Sydney club chairman Andrew Pridham claimed the suspensions would "torpedo" the second-placed Swans' premiership hopes, Cox was adamant the playing group still had drive.

The Swans return to the SCG after a bye weekend following their emotional 53-point win over North Melbourne, where Cox and captain Callum Mills were in tears after the siren.

"There's still an expectation. You're hosting a qualifying final at home with a chance to go into a prelim, so there's still a hell of a lot at stake," Cox said.

"That's one thing that I want to make sure our players are aware of: the magnitude of this game for our football club and what we've spent so long trying to get to."

AAP

World.title: Season uncertainty 'challenging' for AFLW community
World.content:
The 2026 men's AFL season is still being contested and we already know when next year's grand final is set to be.

Compare that to the AFLW, where this season's decider was announced just before the start of round three, 13 weeks before the date.

Key dates for the men's season are announced well in advance, with possible season start dates, Gather Round weekend and the grand final for next year already known to fans.

This gives clubs and players heading on their off-season breaks clarity when planning for personnel to return to the club. One benefit of this is being able to time pre-season training in order to be in peak condition when the season begins in March.

Former AFLW player and senior coach Lauren Arnell says more certainty would allow clubs to plan their pre-season to get the best performance out of the playing group.

"It's challenging when you don't have absolute security on that because one week more or less in your preseason has a significant impact on all planning, not just high performance, but on what you can educate as a footy program as well," Arnell told ABC Sport.

More certainty around the fixture would allow teams to optimise their pre-season training. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

The AFLW grand final will be played on November 27, after a 12-round home and away season.

The AFLW grand-final announcement came at half time of the men's Wildcard final between Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs, which the league said was a deliberate decision to get more coverage of the announcement.

Despite this, the broadcast on Foxtel/Kayo did not mention the announcement in the half-time break.

Men's players have 196 days from the key dates announcement to March 17, the earliest proposed date for the 2027 season to begin, and 395 days until next year's season decider. At the time of writing there are still 23 days until the 2026 grand final.

In a statement from the AFL accompanying the release, CEO Andrew Dillon highlighted the need for fans and clubs to be informed ahead of time.

"We're really pleased to be able to provide fans and clubs with this clarity well ahead of the 2027 season," Dillon said.

The AFL announced the women's fixture on May 21 of this year, giving clubs 80 days' notice, less than half the time their male counterparts have to prepare for the season.

Many AFLW players are still working full-time jobs outside their football careers and Arnell says more certainty would benefit them as well.

"There are still players in the competition working day jobs, and so those players letting their employers know has become more and more challenging," she said.

Rebecca Miller, who plays for the Richmond Tigers AFLW side, says an earlier fixture would also allow the league more time to promote the competition to fans.

"There's been times we've gone to community camps early in preseason or we've done appearances at a men's game early in the season and people are like, 'When are you playing?' And you're like, 'I don't know. I don't have a draw' so you just feel a bit silly in that regard," Miller told ABC Sport.

The last three AFLW grand finals have been sold out at Princes Park. (Getty: Josh Chadwick/AFL Photos)

Most AFL fans will know that the men's grand final is typically held in the last week of September and occasionally, like in 2027, in the first weekend of October. The AFLW grand final is yet to have that level of certainty, having been held in March, April, November and December across nine editions.

"It probably just goes back to that preparation; if we know the grand final, when and where it is before the season starts, again that marketing and promotion piece can really ramp up and make sure that our centrepiece is well attended and well watched and get the attendance they deserve," Miller said.

Conversely, the NRL announced its 2026 men's and women's fixtures on November 14, 2025, which gave NRLW clubs 230 days to prepare for their season to launch and allowed fans time to plan which games they want to attend the following season.

"They [the NRL] have the draw out for the men's and the women's team so at Christmas I can talk to my family about which games they're gonna go to and plan for it months in advance," Miller said, "to be able to go into the Christmas period and know your draw and be able to set yourself as a player but also as a fan and a member".

Richmond Tigers fans in Darwin celebrating a comeback win in their round three Dreamtime match against Essendon. (Getty: Celina Whan)

NRLW matches this year have had an average attendance of 4,915 after seven rounds. Round three of AFLW had an average crowd of 4,806 fans, which includes five double-headers with men's matches. If you count only standalone matches the average attendance is 2,293 for matches that provided a crowd number.

Miller believes that more notice would not just allow more time for promotion, it could also give players more motivation during a long preseason.

"It's so exciting and it just makes it all real. You circle a few games in particular from an individual point of view because you like playing that opposition or you have some beef against that opposition," she said.

"Your family and your friends can decide 'I want to come down to this game, come to that game' so it just makes it all real in your mind and you know why you're training, you know what you're training for".

Arnell believes the announcement of key dates is important but the next steps should come around fixturing.

"I think a priority for AFLW needs to be that all teams play each other once and then you start to land on where your season begins in a calendar and where your grand final sits," she said.

World.title: Fagan lashes Kangaroos over 'unfair' comments after Clarkson axing
World.content:
A shocked Chris Fagan has labelled North Melbourne's public explanation of coach Alastair Clarkson's axing "unfair" and hopes his old friend was given a chance to act on any feedback before the rug was pulled.

Clarkson, who coached Hawthorn to four premierships in an era-defining stint from 2005 to 2021, arrived at North as head coach amid great fanfare after being appointed in August 2022.

Yesterday, with a year to run on his contract, he was unceremoniously axed by football boss Todd Viney, a close friend, and club president Sonja Hood.

Clarkson sacked as Kangaroos hunt 'coach for the modern game' North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney explain why the club is parting ways with Alastair Clarkson with a year to run on his deal.

Asked what type of coach the Kangaroos wanted, Hood, who declared Clarkson's appointment had not been an error, said: "This club needs a coach who can coach for the modern game.

"It'll be a coach who knows what they're doing, and it'll be a coach who's the best fit for this football club."

Viney said there were "still some gaping holes in our game plan" and Clarkson's efforts to fill them only led to "more meetings, more information and players … becoming a bit more confused".

The pair said a canvassing of the club, including players, revealed he no longer had the belief of enough people that he was the right coach to take the group forward.

"I hope he's okay," Brisbane Lions coach Fagan, who first worked with Clarkson at Melbourne in the late 90s before they joined forces at Hawthorn, said.

"I just hope that the feedback that was given at the press conference yesterday about him was given to him in person at some stage during this year, so that he had a chance to act on it.

" It was a pretty fierce press conference. The way that he was spoken about. I reckon probably an unfair description of the man that's done awful lot for footy. "

The 58-year-old's departure comes despite the Kangaroos's improved season in 2026, when they finished 14th and claimed nine wins.

"It was a big shock to me. I actually thought, 'That can't be right,'" Fagan said of the call.

"Under his guidance, North really started to improve. It just reminded me of how tough coaching can be.

"That when a bloke that's been as successful as him as a coach can be jettisoned as quickly as that."

Alastair Clarkson (left) and Chris Fagan were central figures in the investigation into racism at Hawthorn during their time at the club. (Getty Images: Adam Trafford/AFL Media)

The pair were central figures in Hawthorn's racism saga that was settled after two years of legal turmoil in 2024.

Clarkson took a mental health break in 2023 while Fagan, who has the Brisbane Lions in sight of a third-straight flag, admitted he came close to doing the same before opting to coach on.

Fagan, who has yet to speak to Clarkson, hopes his old mate is not lost to the game, and chuckled at the thought of him in a media role, given his typically frosty relationship with that industry.

"We go back a long way and we'll still be friends and still talk a lot about footy, and I'll still seek his advice, no doubt," Fagan said.

AAP

World.title: Current cricket schedule could hurt women's game, says Perry
World.content:
Ellyse Perry has called for Australia's women to be given regular cricket in the peak of summer, fearing the current schedule could stunt the game.

Australia will play nine white-ball matches at home this summer against Bangladesh and New Zealand, with all confined to October and March.

The Australian team has not played a game at home during the summer school holidays since January 2025, while the WBBL also now falls entirely during the school term.

Part of the issue for officials has been India's WPL moving to the January window, with a common fear it will eventually extend into most of February.

Australia's only home matches in the middle of summer under the current program, which runs until the end of 2029, are white-ball ones against Ireland in the first half of December 2028.

Ellyse Perry feels that the lack of cricket in the school holidays will hurt the women's team. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Australian players have long pushed for a regular spot in the summer, much like the Boxing Day Test in Melbourne and New Year's Test in Sydney are part of the national calendar.

"It's the best time of year to play across that school-holiday window," Perry said.

"People are at home, everyone's head is in cricket too. There is a lot on the schedule in both the men's and women's game. It's a nice time to go out and watch.

"But also for them to be inspired to play themselves and be involved in cricket, it's really important.

"I don't know what the perfect window is, but I think somewhere in the peak of the Australian summer is important to carve out.

"Where and how you do that is more of a strategic planning opportunity that will take some time to find. But we should be prioritising that for the Australian team."

None of the WBBL games are being played in the school holidays this summer. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

There is the view that being pushed to the outskirts of summer also has the potential to stunt any momentum around the team after its dominant T20 World Cup.

The timing of the WPL means the only real window during the school holidays would be in the second half of December, perhaps in the lead-up to Christmas.

"It's not just for Australia and all the southern-hemisphere countries … to make sure we're encouraging people to come along to matches," Perry said.

"It's a really tricky one; the scheduling and planning is a matrix I would never want to look at.

"But it would be really nice for us to preserve a window there where people know the Australian women's team is playing so they have the means and opportunity to come watch.

"That's really important in terms of continuing to grow the game for young boys and girls. But also we want to play in front of a home crowd with good opposition each year."

AAP

World.title: Medvedev puts bird disruption aside to claim win at US Open
World.content:
Daniil Medvedev overcame an unusual interruption from two birds to fly into the third round of the US Open as he flattened American wildcard Sebastian Gorzny 6-1 6-3 7-5 at Louis Armstrong Stadium on Wednesday, local time.

The 2021 champion fired off 14 aces in a lopsided affair, where a mid-match avian distraction served up an odd bit of drama. Medvedev next plays either Spain's Jaume Munar or Frenchman Arthur Rinderknech.

"Being on the court, I was happy with my level," the Russian said.

"I love this court and I love you guys."

The Russian broke his opponent from the baseline in the opening game and needed only 21 minutes to get through the first set, firing off 10 winners to just two from Gorzny, who was outmatched in only his second major main draw match.

Medvedev has kept a calm demeanour in New York — in contrast to his dramatic first-round exit last year — but had his patience tested when a pair of birds appeared on the net during a rally midway through the second set, prompting the umpire to replay the point.

"I saw them straight away and thought the point would stop straight away," said Medvedev, who estimated that they continued to play for 45 seconds before the umpire intervened.

"The moment I hit the winner, we stop, and I say, 'Why?'"

Daniil Medvedev was unhappy that the umpire paused the game. (Reuters: Shannon Stapleton)

He got over it pretty quickly, keeping the demolition job going in the third set, where he briefly sniped at the chair umpire, calling him "crazy," during the changeover after the third game and survived a 33-shot rally in the sixth.

Gorzny improved his level in the third set, saving four break points in the ninth game, but it was too little too late as Medvedev harnessed his powerful forehand to break the American in the 11th game and sealed it with an unreturnable serve.

The bird incident joined a growing list of odd moments in Flushing Meadows for Medvedev, who has endured a love-hate relationship with the New York crowd since his memorable turn as pantomime villain in 2019.

He overcame a booing crowd to beat Spaniard Feliciano Lopez en route to the final that year, losing to Rafa Nadal in the championship match but earning the fans' begrudging respect.

"This would definitely be in the top five [unusual moments]," Medvedev told reporters.

"It's OK. It happens."

Reuters

World.title: LA Clippers fined $40m over 'flagrant' rules breaches
World.content:
The NBA has imposed a sweeping punishment against the Los Angeles Clippers for violating salary cap circumvention rules, suspending owner Steve Ballmer for one year, fining the team $US30 million ($41.5 million) and forcing it to forfeit five draft picks.

Two-time NBA Finals MVP Kawhi Leonard was also hit with a $US700,000 ($977,000) penalty, president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank was banned for six months and team president of business operations Gillian Zucker was suspended for one year.

The league came down hard on the organisation on Wednesday after a nearly year-long investigation led by an outside law firm.

The Clippers had said multiple times that they had done nothing wrong and expected to be exonerated.

"I think that we're going to be in the clear," Leonard said in April, "so I'm not stressing it."

At the same time, Frank said: "If you know Steve and know Steve's integrity, you know there's nothing to it. We believe and we've very confident we're on the right side of this."

The team maintained that stance on Wednesday.

Steve Ballmer (left) will sit out the next 12 months as part of his punishment for the breaches. (Getty Images: Katelyn Mulcahy)

"We vehemently reject the NBA's findings, which are the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence," the team said in a statement.

"What the league told us privately differs from what it announced today publicly, and they have not held themselves close to the standard Commissioner [Adam] Silver set at the start of this investigation to ensure its fairness and accuracy."

The Clippers said they will "now fight just as hard to demonstrate our innocence. We intend to vigorously challenge these findings and penalties through every avenue available to us and look forward to an ethical and impartial arbitration process."

The league said it and the players' union agreed to confirm the penalties as final and binding on all parties. It said the outside law firm continued to receive information involving the investigation, and the league "will consider further action as appropriate".

"I am deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers' institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct," Silver said in a statement.

"The severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations."

Adam Silver says he is "deeply disappointed" in the Clippers' breaches. (Getty Images: Elsa)

The NBA began investigating in September 2025 whether a $28 million endorsement contract between Leonard and Aspiration Fund Adviser LLC — a company that filed for bankruptcy last year — broke league rules, following a report by journalist Pablo Torre.

Earlier this year, Aspiration co-founder Joseph Sanberg was sentenced to 14 years in federal prison after pleading guilty to defrauding investors and lenders of at least $248 million.

The Clippers released a letter from Ballmer's attorney David Kelley to Silver, in which he described the investigation as "a witch hunt" and the subsequent penalties as a "gross injustice".

Kelley accused Silver of not keeping his promises that the investigation would be governed by due process and fundamental fairness, as well as the burden being on the league to prove any violations through evidence.

"League counsel has acknowledged in our discussions that the league does not believe there was an agreement between the Clippers and Aspiration to funnel money to Kawhi Leonard. League counsel also agreed with the Department of Justice, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and a federal judge that Mr. Ballmer was a victim of Joe Sanberg's fraud — not a participant," wrote Kelley, a partner in the firm O'Melveny and Myers.

"Mr Ballmer's reputation has been irreparably damaged as he now finds himself embroiled not only in this heavily biased investigation, but in civil litigation, the Aspiration bankruptcy proceeding, and more," Kelley wrote.

Kelley wrote that no league rule prohibits team personnel from making introductions to both sponsors and vendors in response to player requests.

"Retroactively punishing the Clippers for violating a rule that never existed is hardly consistent with due process," Kelley wrote.

The league said Ballmer knowingly sought to help Leonard obtain off-court income deals, approved a business deal that he knew was a precondition for Aspiration to enter into an endorsement contract with Leonard, and for failing to create conditions under which his team followed league rules.

"I accept full responsibility for lapses in judgement by people within my inner circle and regret the distraction this situation has caused the fans and my family," Leonard said in a statement issued through his new agent, Harrison Gaines.

The NBA said Leonard, through his former business manager and uncle Dennis Robertson, "violated the circumvention rules by pressuring the Clippers to assist him in obtaining off-court income opportunities, successfully obtaining those opportunities, and failing to reimburse payments by the Clippers for personal expenses."

"I entered into my contract with the Clippers as well as the agreements in question in good faith, fully committed to fulfilling my obligations and with no knowledge of any intent on anyone's part to circumvent the salary cap," Leonard said in his statement.

The league said Ballmer was suspended for "knowingly seeking to help Mr Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities," among other issues.

Kawhi Leonard is set to return to Toronto for the upcoming season. (Getty Images: Patrick McDermott)

Leonard's trade to the Toronto Raptors has been on hold pending the outcome of the investigation. The Raptors had said they still want Leonard, and he apparently is just as eager to return to the team where he won an NBA title and was Finals MVP in 2019.

"As I return to Toronto, I am focused on what I can control, closing this chapter, and moving forward with a clean slate," Leonard said in his statement.

The Clippers and their personnel will be under a compliance and monitoring program by the league for five years and Robertson was banned from doing business with NBA teams for five years.

The league penalised Frank for his involvement with the impermissible endorsement arrangements and for approving impermissible expenses incurred by Leonard and his family.

Zucker was banned for being primarily and directly culpable for the illegal endorsement arrangements and for lying to investigators. Both will lose their salaries during their bans.

It is not the first time the Clippers have run afoul of NBA rules under Ballmer, who bought the team for $2 billion in August 2014.

They were fined $250,000 a year later for violating rules against offering unauthorised business or investment opportunities to players during their courting of free agent DeAndre Jordan. A presentation to him improperly included a $200,000-per-year deal with luxury car maker Lexus.

Ballmer, 70, was CEO of Microsoft from 2000 to 2014.

AP

World.title: Hampshire ditches New Zealand all-rounder after fan backlash
World.content:
Hampshire Cricket has cancelled the contract of Kiwi international Scott Kuggeleijn minutes before he was set to take the field after backlash from supporters.

The 34-year-old fast bowler was named in a social media post as part of the 15-man squad to take on Warwickshire in the County Championship match.

The club had not announced the three-Test player's signing on their social channels.

The presence of the New Zealand international bowler in the squad was met with furious resistance from the club's supporters and some staff members, with reaction including comments of "disgraceful" and "shameful" on social media.

"Having reflected and listened to feedback from our staff and supporters, Hampshire Cricket can confirm that Scott Kuggeleijn will not represent the club," a statement from the club read.

"We value the passion of our fanbase and thank everyone who took the time to share their views."

Kuggeleijn had been signed for the final four games of Hampshire's County Championship season as a replacement for South African Delano Potgieter, who was called up for the South Africa A series against Bangladesh last month.

Kuggeleijn faced a rape charge in 2015 and was acquitted in 2017 after the first trial resulted in a hung jury.

The Hamilton-born player made his international debut after his acquittal in an ODI series against Ireland in Dublin in 2017.

There was backlash in New Zealand when Kuggeleijn was initially selected in the squad, with then-coach Gary Stead forced to defend the call-up.

In addition to his three Test matches, Kuggeleijn has played two one-day matches and 18 T20 games for the Black Caps.

He has not played for New Zealand in any format since the second Test against Australia at Hagley Oval, Christchurch in March 2024, which the Aussies won by three wickets.

Prior to his signing for Hampshire, Kuggeleijn was playing for the Kingsmen in a Darwin T20 league.

He is a regular player in first-class cricket for Northern Districts in New Zealand.

Tech.title: Uber beats Waymo as first to launch robotaxis in London
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Uber beat out Waymo in launching a commercial robotaxi service in London, the city’s first. The vehicles use autonomous driving tech developed by Wayve, a UK-based startup, and will initially feature safety drivers behind the wheel.

The launch is a milestone for Uber, which has been plotting a UK launch with Wayve for several years. In beating Waymo to the punch, it allows Uber to set the standard for the robotaxi experience for thousands of Londoners. It’s also an early test of whether there’s appetite for driverless ridehailing beyond the US and China, where most of the world’s robotaxis are currently clustered. (There’s a smattering in the Middle East, too.)

London-based Uber customers who want to try out these new robot-controlled cars can indicate their preference in the app’s settings. When booking a ride through UberX, Uber Comfort, or Uber Electric, riders may be paired with a Wayve-developed autonomous vehicle, but it’s not a guarantee. Wayve is using Ford Mustang Mach-Es for its fleet, followed by the Nissan Leaf in the future.

Safety drivers will monitor the driving from the front seat, though Uber says they won’t control the driving and will gradually be phased out in favor of fully driverless vehicles. Safety drivers are licensed by Transport for London, the city’s transit authority.

Uber says there will be no geofence — the virtual boundary within which robotaxis are programed to operate — because Wayve’s AV2.0 system is designed to move “beyond the constraints of traditional AV systems.” Wayve describes AV2.0 thusly:

The traditional AV1.0 approach relies on hand-engineered stacks, HD maps and a rule-based approach – this limits scalability and the ability to rapidly generalize to new environments or complex scenarios. Wayve’s AV2.0 takes a different path – a single, learned AI driver trained to understand the world, anticipate risk, and adapt to new environments.

The robotaxis will be maintained and serviced by Uber in partnership with UK fleet operator Otto Car. Wayve will stay in charge of the autonomous driving system.

Wayve, which was founded in 2017 by a pair of machine learning PhD students from the University of Cambridge, says its autonomous driving system can learn on the go, adapting to new roads, weather, or driving scenarios much like a human driver. The vehicles use cameras and radar as part of their perception system — but notably do not use lidar, the laser sensor that Waymo and many other robotaxi operators rely on. This puts Wayve in a similar camp as Tesla, which also doesn’t use lidar for its robotaxis.

Still, Wayve claims its system is hardware agnostic, thanks to a software stack that can run on whatever sensors and chips an automaker uses for its vehicles. While additional sensors like lidar can theoretically be integrated if a car manufacturer prefers them, Wayve’s AV2.0 is built to operate autonomously without HD maps or expensive sensors, the company says. In addition to Uber, Wayve is also working with Stellantis on hands-free driving tech. And earlier this year, the startup raised $1.2 billion from Uber, Nvidia, and Stellantis, as well as Nissan and Mercedes-Benz, according to TechCrunch.

Waymo has said it will launch its robotaxis in London before the end of the year. In addition, Lyft is working with China’s Baidu on its own robotaxi service in the city, starting with the neighborhood of Brent.

Uber has been lobbying for a hybrid network made up of human drivers and robotaxis, which clashes with Waymo’s vision of a driver-free, rider-only system. Waymo and Uber still work together in several cities, including Austin and Atlanta, but the companies have increasingly found themselves on opposite sides of the debate — prompting rumors of an imminent breakup. Meanwhile, Uber has made a big to-do about linking up with a variety of AV partners, including Zoox, Avride, Nuro, Motional, Waabi, and of course, Wayve. The company has said it plans on spending upwards of $10 billion to build out its robotaxi business over time.

Tech.title: Google says its new Gemini 3.8 Flash model ‘works harder’ but might cost more
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google launched Gemini 3.8 Flash, arriving just a few weeks after its predecessor. The company claims the new model “works harder” than Gemini 3.7 Flash by performing more reasoning steps on complex tasks and “calling tools iteratively.” It has the same introductory pricing as 3.7 Flash, $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens, but could still end up costing users more. Google warns that “the model might use more tokens to maximize performance, especially at higher effort levels.” Developers can keep using Gemini 3.7 Flash if they want to minimize token usage.

Gemini 3.8 Flash’s launch was followed by some early impressions online. Artificial Analysis highlighted the model’s pricing, saying Gemini 3.8 Flash is “the cheapest we’ve measured at this level of intelligence. This is up ~40% from Gemini 3.7 Flash despite unchanged per-token pricing, driven by a 30% increase in output tokens per task and more turns on agentic evaluations.”

Aigora.ai CEO John Ennis compared Gemini 3.8 Flash to Anthropic’s models, saying it offers “Opus 5 coding quality but at a fraction of the cost and super fast,” adding, “This is going to be so awesome for things like making remotion videos.”

Google says Gemini 3.8 Flash offers “significant improvements” for software engineering and autonomous AI agents. It outperforms its predecessor and other frontier models on the DeepSWE v1.1 software engineering benchmark, including Anthropic’s Fable 5, which got an upgrade earlier this week that also promises stronger performance at a lower price, by cutting the price to use cached data.

Google’s new model also outperformed its competitors on the Vals Finance Agent V2 benchmark and Harvey’s Legal Agent benchmark. However, the new model also “ships with safeguards against misuse in the domains of Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) and cyber offense.”

Google also released Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber alongside its new Fairwind Program, which is limited to governments and “trusted partners.” The program, whose 650 members include CrowdStrike and the Center for Internet Security, offers access to 3.8 Flash Cyber and Google’s CodeMender agent, which Google says can help “autonomously find and fix vulnerabilities, protecting critical infrastructure, public services, and national security.” Gemini 3.8 Flash is available now for consumers with a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription, as well as developers and enterprise users.
