Tech.title: 1Password wades into a right-wing mess after funding a Linux project
Tech.content:
1Password faced immediate backlash from customers this week over a $300,000 pledge in support of a Linux distro created by David Heinemeier Hansson, who has regularly published overtly racist blog posts that include comments calling for deportation of ethnic minorities in Europe. The popular password manager is now a “distinguished corporate patron” of Omacom, the nonprofit foundation that oversees a popular Linux distribution known as Omarchy.

One viral blog post declared that 1Password “Supports the Ethnic Cleansing of Europe” because of the donation. Others on social media asked for suggestions for alternative password managers so they would not support the funding of a project from Heinemeier Hansson, better known as DHH.

The donation has also resulted in internal pushback from employees of 1Password who are disappointed by the affiliation, The Verge has learned. 1Password CEO David Faugno and cofounder Roustem Karimov have since posted internal messages addressing what Faugno describes as “concerns, both internally and externally” that have been raised “due to the polarizing nature” of DHH.

DHH is a Danish entrepreneur best known for creating Ruby on Rails, Basecamp, and the Hey email client. Omarchy is DHH’s “opinionated” version of Linux, meaning it’s Linux the way he likes to use it. It’s based on Arch Linux, with certain apps that install by default. It’s also, apparently, one of 1Password’s big customer environments.

The backlash to 1Password’s funding should have been predictable; DHH’s reactionary comments aren’t new. Way back in 2023, Duke University Libraries dropped one of DHH’s products, Basecamp, citing “harms we see perpetuated by the leadership of Basecamp’s parent company, 37signals,” which is co-owned by DHH. At the time, Duke noted DHH’s attack on DEI programs and The Verge’s reporting on Basecamp banning “societal and political discussions” at work.

This year, DHH has published rants that appear to call for ethnic cleansing in Europe. In his July 21st blog post titled “Wolves, sheep, and gypsies,” DHH implies that immigrants are “wolves.” His solution? “When wolves get out of control, you shoot them. When gypsies take over public spaces, you deport them.”

In an internal Slack message obtained by The Verge, 1Password’s Karimov downplayed the overtly racist comments from DHH, telling staff the following:

As I said, people have different personal opinions. You believe in your heart that DHH is evil, that you have the moral high ground, and that nothing will change your mind. However, not everyone believes that. It is not fair to claim a monopoly and ostracize team members who might disagree with you. There are people who are afraid to speak up simply because they will be personally attacked.

1Password CEO Faugno took a different approach, trying to reassure staff that “1Password does not endorse hateful, dehumanizing, or exclusionary views, including those shared publicly by DHH.”

Nonetheless, it seems the company has sacrificed a moral position for a “mission-driven” position. In the same message to staff, Faugno says “the scale and growth of [Omarchy’s] use among our customers is significant - Omarchy has grown to be the second most used Linux distribution among 1Password users.”

Faugno then tries to create distance, telling staff that its contribution is “to the Omacom Foundation, not an individual.” Still, he says “we recognize that Omarchy is associated with DHH, its founder. Our donation is not in any way an endorsement of his personal views or conduct.”

We asked 1Password for comment on its funding of the Omacom Foundation on August 31st, and again today. We did not receive a response in time for publication.

The Omacom Foundation is also funded by 12 “founding patrons” who each contributed $1 million, including Stripe’s CEO Patrick Collison, Michael Dell, Jack Dorsey, and Shopify’s Tobias Lütke — who recently endorsed the idea that wealthy Canadians should have more voting power in democracy than poorer people. Even before 1Password contributed, this page looked like a rogues’ gallery of tech. (DHH himself also gave $1 million to the project.)

1Password employees don’t seem impressed by its leaders’ comments based on dozens of emoji reactions we saw in their internal Slack conversations. 1Password’s CEO says the company will speak more about it internally at an all-hands meeting.

Tech.title: Amazon’s AI assistant can now spot fake emails from the company
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon is trying to combat impersonation scams with a new feature that allows you to use its AI assistant to determine whether an email, text message, or phone call actually came from the company. With the update, you can ask Alexa for Shopping about a message you received, and it will use AI to compare it “against a record of every message Amazon has sent,” while also analyzing its contents, formatting, and the sender.

As noted by Amazon, the assistant will only confirm that a message is real if it’s “completely certain.” An example shared by Amazon shows a customer asking, “Did Amazon just text me an OTP from 98626? Message came around 4:50pm.” Alexa for Shopping responds by confirming that Amazon actually did send the message, saying, “This was a genuine One Time Password from Amazon.”

If Alexa for Shopping determines a message isn’t from Amazon, it will instruct customers to check their orders in the app and contact Amazon’s support team directly. The company launched a similar feature earlier this year that lets you forward suspicious messages to “verify@amazon.com” to check if they’re real.

This isn’t the only recent update Amazon has launched for Alexa for Shopping, as it added an “Update Me When” feature that can now help you track new product releases as well.

Tech.title: Range Rover’s new EV looks just like a regular Range Rover — that’s refreshing
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

I think automakers are finally getting the memo. Rather than try to reinvent the wheel with its new electric vehicle, Range Rover just made one that looks nearly identical to its lineup of gas-powered SUVs. They didn’t try to pass off some sleek, spaceship-looking pod as a Range Rover. Sometimes familiar designs are the way to go.

Of course, under the surface the Range Rover Electric is nothing like its internal combustion engine sporting brethren. Twin permanent magnet 260kW electric motors are powered by a double-stacked 118.5 kWh lithium-ion battery, with an estimated range of 330 real-world miles.

The all-wheel drive system puts out 542 horsepower and 627 lb.-ft. of torque, which Range Rover describes as “V8 levels of power.” An 800-volt architecture enables DC fast charging from 10–80 percent in just 22 minutes, or about 137 miles in 10 minutes, when plugged into a 350 kW charger. A zero to 60 mph time of 4.3 seconds won’t win it any awards, especially compared to EV rivals like Lucid and Rivian. But this Range Rover probably doesn’t need to blow up any records to make its mark. With a familiar design and decent enough specs, it should be more than sufficient for anyone who has been pining for a touch of British sophistication in their EV shopping.

Previous Next



















1 / 11

The wait has certainly stretched on longer than it should have. Range Rover first announced it was working on an electric model over five years ago. It first opened preorders in 2023, promising that customer deliveries would begin a year later. The Jaguar Land Rover–owned brand took its sweet time fulfilling these promises, but now that the cover has been lifted, the automaker is taking orders at a starting price of £154,070 in the UK (or about $140,450 in the US).

JLR says it will produce the Range Rover Electric at its Solihull factory, alongside gas and hybrid models. It’s also touting the number of patents submitted for this EV — 300 — making it the most technologically custom-built Range Rover ever.

How technologically advanced? Try lightning-fast grip control. Instead of waiting for mechanical gears to adjust when tires slip, the electric motors adjust power in 50 milliseconds — 100 times faster than a gas car. This gives instant control on ice, mud, or loose gravel. The one-pedal drive system is tuned for super steep slopes of up to 45 degrees, so you can climb mountains or crawl over obstacles using just the accelerator. And the battery and motors are fully sealed, allowing you to drive through nearly 3 feet of water (900mm) without damaging the vehicle. Lastly, a built-in heat pump reuses waste heat to warm the cabin and keep the battery at the right temperature, preserving up to 25 extra miles of driving range in freezing weather.

All of this sounds great on paper. Stacked up against rivals like the Porsche Macan EV or the Lotus Eletre, the SUV may look even better — especially for those car buyers who still prefer a familiar face on their electric vehicle.

Images by Range Rover

Tech.title: The best tech and gadgets announced at IFA so far
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

The doors to Europe’s largest consumer tech show haven’t opened to the public yet, but there’s already plenty of news coming out of IFA 2026 in Berlin, Germany. If you’re already struggling to keep up with what has been announced, here are some of the best new gadgets and upgrades from the show — including more competition for Apple’s MacBook Neo, an excellent portable controller for gaming-on-the-go, and a concept handheld designed to balance work and play.

To catch up on everything announced at IFA 2026 you can follow The Verge’s complete coverage right here.

Image: Acer

Flipping the gaming laptop script, Acer’s latest concept is a Windows-based gaming handheld, similar to its Predator Atlas 8, that can transform into a tiny portable PC thanks to a swiveling design that repositions its screen atop a mini keyboard. The DualPlay Mini’s display is just 8-inches in size, which could make productivity a challenge if work involves sprawling spreadsheets, but the concept could be used for answering emails during a daily commute and then connected to a larger display at work for more demanding tasks.

Image: Dell

The Dell 14S isn’t as thin or light as its recently launched XPS 13, but the company is looking to make this model even more accessible for students or others on a tighter budget. The laptop starts with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, and those specs can be bumped to 16GB/1TB. It features a 1080P webcam with face unlock support, two USB-C ports, a headphone jack, and like Apple’s MacBook Neo, will be available in four bright color options: linen, dusty rose, washed denim, and velvet green.

Image: iRobot

The $1,199 Roomba Max 875 Combo is iRobot’s latest flagship floor cleaner and introduces a new feature the company calls “SealForce.” When it detects it’s cleaning carpeting, the robovac lowers a skirt around the cleaning head to create a better seal that increases suction for a deeper clean. The Max 875 also offers up to 35,000 Pa of suction power, mopping capabilities, lidar and camera-based autonomous navigation, and the ability to climb over obstacles and thresholds up to 3.5cm tall.

Image: Jsaux

Released under Jsaux’s new Voidjoy brand, the $49.99 SkyLark S1 Pro is a compact portable controller that appears to do a lot of things right. It’s got drift-resistant TMR thumbsticks that are recessed so they won’t get snagged on other devices in your bag, a pair of analog triggers ideal for racing games, and three different ways to connect to devices and consoles: Bluetooth, USB-C, and 2.4GHz. If you opt for a 2.4GHz connection, you can also pair two S1 Pros to a single transmitter and swap back-and-forth between what character you’re controlling in a multiplayer game, making it useful for parents playing with a kid who may struggle with some challenges.

Image: Acer

Is Framework’s approach to easily repairable and upgradeable laptops finally rubbing off on other companies? Acer’s 16-inch Vero 16 offers tool-free access to several internal components including its user-replaceable SSD and battery. The company says the laptop’s processor can also be upgraded down the line, but that will require it to be sent in to an Acer service center. Pricing is still unknown, but the Vero 16 is expected to launch early next year outside North America.

Image: Jsaux

If you’re lucky enough to have an original Nintendo Switch Pro controller that hasn’t succumbed to joystick drift and want to expand its capabilities, Jsaux’s new Elite Extender is an easy aftermarket upgrade. For $39.99 it attaches to the back of the controller and adds four mappable buttons that can be programmed to reproduce multiple button presses. It’s got its own rechargeable battery, but does hinder Amiibo functionality while it’s piggybacking.

Tech.title: Researchers fear safety disaster ahead of OpenAI’s Astra release
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is on the cusp of releasing its most powerful AI model yet, Astra, following weeks of delays to shore up safety protocols after its agents attacked real targets during testing. As details about the model trickle out, researchers are warning it “may be the single worst development for AI security/safety to date.”

Shortly after OpenAI said on Tuesday that it had delayed Astra’s release to work on safety issues, The Information reported that Astra shows far less of its “thinking” than other frontier AI models, sparking concern it could be dangerously hard to monitor.

Most top AI systems today are built using a technology known as a transformer, which processes some types of information linearly through layers before producing an answer. Models can be made to show their reasoning as they go, essentially “thinking out loud.” This “chain of thought” allows researchers and automated safety systems to monitor what AI models are doing and potentially spot undesirable behavior, such as lying or plans to circumvent safety guardrails, before they act.

According to The Information, citing an unnamed person familiar with the unreleased model’s development, Astra uses a more opaque technique known as a recurrent depth or looped transformer, which cycles information through internal layers before producing an output. This would mean much more of the model’s “thinking” happens inside the system, and in a form that looks a lot less like natural human language, rather than being expressed in a way that researchers can easily monitor. This can boost model performance, but makes potential threats and unwanted behavior harder to detect.

OpenAI has limited its use of the looped transformer / recurrent depth technique with Astra so researchers can continue to monitor the model’s reasoning, according to The Information’s unnamed source.

In a blog post published Tuesday, OpenAI said it is “deploying Astra with additional chain-of-thought monitoring to rapidly detect and contain potentially misaligned actions.” It did not mention if the model has a different technical foundation.

The Information’s report sparked widespread concern among AI safety researchers on social media. It was Redwood Research’s chief scientist Ryan Greenblatt, one of three outsiders OpenAI permitted to research the Hugging Face hack, who said a decision to use a more opaque architecture for Astra “may be the single worst development for AI security/safety to date.”

Greenblatt said the investigation into the Hugging Face incident relied heavily on the models’ chain-of-thought, warning that less visible reasoning could allow AI systems to devise and execute strategies that would be far harder for researchers to detect.

Greenblatt’s primary concern, echoed by other safety experts, is that competition to develop more advanced AI systems could lead to “a race to the bottom on architectures that could be catastrophic for our ability to oversee/monitor AIs” — with developers adopting increasingly opaque systems to gain an edge until models become difficult, or even impossible, to monitor. He added that OpenAI’s communications left him concerned that the company “plans on being extremely reliant on chain-of-thought monitoring for safety.”

OpenAI bigwigs responded to the criticism in a series of social media posts that do not explicitly deny the company’s use of the technique. Several expressed concerns about the possibility of unmonitorable AI or a race to the bottom in terms of transparency, including OpenAI safety researchers Micah Carroll and Tomek Korbak, head of strategic futures Dean Ball, and chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, who voiced fears of “a race into unmonitorability kicked off by confused reporting.” He said the depth of Astra’s computation — a measure of how many steps it can perform internally — “is within a factor of two of GPT-4,” indicating that if the technique was used, the increased opacity is less dramatic than some reactions imply. OpenAI did not respond to The Verge’s request to confirm or deny whether looped transformers were used for Astra and directed us to Pachocki’s X post.

“OpenAI has worked to preserve and utilize chain-of-thought monitoring since our very first reasoning models,” Pachocki wrote, adding that such monitoring “is fragile and unfortunately trending in a negative direction, for reasons not contingent on architecture changes that I will write about soon.”

Tech.title: Palo Alto Networks paid $500M for Thrive-backed Console, sources say
Tech.content:
Palo Alto Networks paid $500 million in cash and stock to acquire Console, a two-year-old startup that uses AI agents to automate routine IT help desk tasks, according to two people with knowledge of the deal.

The companies officially announced the acquisition on Tuesday but didn’t reveal terms of the deal. Since its founding in 2024, Console has raised $29 million across two rounds: a $6.2 million seed led by Thrive Capital and a $23 million Series A co-led by DST Global and Thrive.

Before the sale, Console was valued at $157 million, according to PitchBook, delivering a rapid return for investors including SV Angel, Abstract Ventures, and notably Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, who participated as an angel investor. Palo Alto Networks declined to comment.

The cybersecurity giant said that it will integrate Console into Cortex, its platform that uses AI to automatically detect and neutralize threats. Console’s agentic functionality will allow security teams to investigate and resolve alerts using natural language, giving Cortex “the arms and legs to deliver autonomous security outcomes across the entire enterprise,” as Arora described in a statement.

Console was founded by Andrei Serban, coming shortly after his previous startup — code-security platform Fuzzbuzz — was acquired by Rippling. The startup, whose customers included Ramp, Flock Safety, and Scale AI, automated tasks like password resets, granted access to apps like Figma and Miro, and performed routine troubleshooting without direct human involvement.

As a startup, Console competed primarily with Serval, another ServiceNow challenger that hit a $1 billion valuation after raising a $75 million Series B round led by Sequoia last December. Serval started as an AI tech support tool and quickly expanded to provide AI assistance for human resources, legal, and finance departments. Console’s acquisition leaves Serval as the category-leader-to-watch among startups automating IT service management, one investor, who is not a backer of Serval, told TechCrunch.

Console is Palo Alto Networks’ seventh acquisition in 2026, according to PitchBook. Other VC-backed companies scooped up by the cybersecurity behemoth this year include Greylock and Lux Capital-backed observability platform Chronosphere, at a valuation of $3.35 billion, and Koi, a cyber startup backed by Battery and Team8, for $400 million.

Tech.title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026’s new Real World AI Stage features Nvidia, robots, and extinct animals
Tech.content:
At our past TechCrunch Disrupt events, AI has taken center stage, both throughout our programming and in a stage of its own. This year, the technology, implications, and players are so rapidly developing and widespread that we’re expanding the single AI stage into two!

The AI Stage will continue as you’d expect, with a rundown of sessions and speakers available for review right here. But the Real World AI Stage is brand-new for TechCrunch Disrupt 2026.

On this stage, we’ll be focusing on that intersection between the digital and physical, and all the ways we’ll continue to see a blending of the two, as autonomous hardware goes beyond self-driving cars and enters public spaces, battlefields, our homes, and even potentially helps extinct species reenter Earth.

It’s a packed lineup featuring speakers from Shield AI, Colossal Biosciences, FieldAI, Foxglove, and more still to come. You can join in on all the excitement October 13 to 15 at San Francisco’s Moscone West, so register to attend right here.

But in the meantime, here’s the breakdown of our Real World AI Stage lineup:

Robots Are Waiting for Their ChatGPT Moment. Here Is What Is Standing in the Way

Large language models had the internet. Self-driving cars have millions of hours of road data. Robots have neither. That data gap is the single biggest reason most experts believe general-purpose robotic intelligence is still years away, despite the breakthroughs happening everywhere else in AI. A new wave of startups is racing to close it, building the data pipelines, simulation environments, and foundation models that could trigger the same capability explosion we saw with LLMs. This session asks the hard question: what does the ChatGPT moment for physical AI actually require, and how close are we really?

With Les Karpas, Head of Physical AI, Nvidia

When AI enters the physical world, the consequences of failure change. A mistake could lead to a grounded aircraft, a vehicle crash, or a compromised mission.

In this session, leaders who are building autonomous vehicles, defense technologies, and industrial systems will talk about one of the toughest questions that every hard tech founder must face: How do you know when your system is ready to be safely deployed?

We’ll dig into how founders can create a safety culture, test and validate AI, navigate regulatory hurdles, and build companies that can earn trust when the stakes are high.

With Ben Lamm, CEO, Colossal Biosciences

This session brings together leaders from defense, space, and industrial AI who will share how they have tackled the challenge of making AI work at the edge — where latency matters, connectivity is limited, and failure isn’t an option. With Dr. Ali Agha, CEO and founder of FieldAI; Michelle Lee, CEO and founder, Medra; and Aidan Madigan-Curtis, partner, Eclipse Ventures

From Prototype to Production: Can it scale in reality?

A prototype that works is not a product. A product that ships is not a scaled business. The gap between each of those stages is where most deep tech startups die. Founders might have the right team and tech, but they fail to understand what it takes to bring a prototype into production and eventually scale to higher, profitable volumes.

This session brings together founders who have crossed that gap in space hardware, humanoid robotics, and autonomous systems. They’ll share what they got wrong, what they’d do earlier, and what the prototype-to-production journey looks like when supply chains and manufacturing realities replace lab conditions.

Tech.title: Google spared from ad-business breakup, but judge orders changes to how it operates
Tech.content:
The Justice Department has spent years attempting to break up Google’s gargantuan advertising business across two separate antitrust lawsuits: one filed in 2020 focused on Google’s dominance in search, and a second filed in 2023 that specifically targeted Google’s ad-technology business. Both cases argued that the search giant’s grip on the digital ad economy represents an illegal monopoly.

Courts have largely sided with the government in both cases. In 2024, a court determined that Google’s search business, including its exceedingly lucrative search-ad operation, was an illegal monopoly, claiming that the tech giant had “exercised its monopoly power” to dominate the search industry and search ads. Last April, a second court case — this one focused specifically on Google’s ad-tech business — also came to the same conclusion.

Following the 2024 ruling, Justice Department officials suggested a variety of ways Google’s search business could be broken up, including divesting its Chrome browser and Android operating system. But in September 2025, the judge overseeing that case, Amit Mehta, rejected those divestiture requests, ruling that Google could keep both Chrome and Android. He did order the company to end exclusive default-placement deals and share certain search data with competitors (remedies that Google is currently appealing).

That same pattern held this week. In a ruling handed down on Wednesday, federal judge Leonie M. Brinkema of the Eastern District of Virginia, who oversaw the ad-tech case, said that Google would be able to keep its advertising business. Instead of selling it, the search giant will instead be required to adjust its business practices to favor competitors, Brinkema said. The New York Times notes that the judge’s ruling “did not provide specifics” as to how Google should go about doing that.

Brinkema’s full written ruling will remain under seal for 14 days to allow those involved to issue necessary redactions. Her finding that Google had acted illegally in maintaining its ad-tech business dates back to April of last year; this week’s decision addressed only the remedy.

Unsurprisingly, Google framed the outcome as a win. Lee-Anne Mulholland, Google’s vice president for regulatory affairs, told TechCrunch: “We’re very pleased the Court rejected the DOJ’s proposal to break apart tools that help small businesses reach new customers and grow.”

The online advertising ecosystem is notoriously opaque and byzantine and, for most people unfamiliar with its complexities, difficult to grasp. Much of the government’s ad-tech case against Google revolved around the company’s tactics to ensure that its search engine was the default engine in devices across the world, which in turn helped its ad business dominate as well.

To do this, Google used exclusive agreements with device manufacturers, which made it the default search engine across huge swaths of the mobile phone market, the government has argued. Google also entered into revenue sharing agreements with mobile carriers — deals where carriers earned a cut of ad revenue in exchange for keeping Google as the default — that further cemented its position as the de facto search engine across phone markets.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s new reasoning technique alarms AI safety experts
Tech.content:
OpenAI’s new Astra model will use a reasoning technique called “recurrent depth” that allows it to operate outside of the sequential thinking that characterizes most reasoning models, The Information reported on Tuesday. This technique, also called “opaque recurrence,” will likely make the model’s chain of thought more difficult to monitor — and that has AI safety experts rattled.

While Astra’s use of the technique is reportedly limited, its emergence has still raised significant concerns among AI safety experts.

“I am extremely concerned by the reporting that Astra uses opaque recurrence,” wrote Redwood CEO Buck Shlegeris in a post after the news broke. “I don’t know whether Astra is much less CoT monitorable than previous models. But if OpenAI pushes this technique further, they’ll have the option to massively increase the recurrence and totally destroys CoT monitorability.”

Longtime AI safety advocate Zvi Mowshowitz also weighed in and wrote that laws might be necessary to prevent a “race to the bottom” among AI labs.

“The technique is playing with fire, risking a taboo that OpenAI and Anthropic have fought to establish that we work hard to maintain Chain of Thought faithfulness and monitorability for as long as we can,” Mowshowitz wrote. “More intensive use of such techniques would probably damage monitorability.”

Under normal circumstances, a reasoning model’s chain of thought provides the sequential steps taken by the model as it attempts to solve a problem. While the representation is imperfect, it still serves as a valuable tool for monitoring misbehavior or misalignment. In the case of OpenAI’s recent rogue agent activity, chain-of-thought records were an important tool in teasing out why agents behaved the way they did.

In opaque recurrence, the model takes a less linear approach, processing the same query several times in a loop. The result leaves fewer legible traces, effectively side-stepping a conventional chain-of-thought record.

Crucially, Astra’s use of the technique appears to be limited. The model’s chain of thought is still expected to be legible, and the company pushed back against any suggestion that it would shift to “neuralese.” OpenAI has already announced plans for extensive chain-of-thought monitoring systems as part of its forward-looking safety plans.

In a post on X, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki emphasized the lab’s commitment to legible chains of thought. “OpenAI has worked to preserve and utilize chain-of-thought monitoring since our very first reasoning models,” Pachocki wrote. “It’s a core goal of our current research program.

All AI models do some quantity of opaque reasoning, and few researchers take chain-of-thought logs as a direct representation of a model’s reasoning. Still, those caveats don’t dispel the concern that opaque recurrence may make AI reasoning harder to monitor, particularly as it grows in use across different models. In a follow-up report Wednesday morning, The Information reported that both Anthropic and Google DeepMind were already discussing the technique.

In a post responding to the news, Redwood Research chief scientist Ryan Greenblatt said opaque reasoning could easily scale faster than conventional chain-of-thought reasoning, effectively removing all reasoning from visible channels.

“My biggest concern is that a natural progression from here would involve scaling up the opaque reasoning to the point where the model reasons entirely or almost entirely in latent space,” Greenblatt wrote. “I hope it isn’t too late to avoid the most concerning architectures and that OpenAI will stop here.”

Tech.title: MapQuest is now the No. 1 US app after bucking Trump’s ‘Lake America’ renaming
Tech.content:
MapQuest’s unlikely comeback just got even bigger. On Tuesday, the “OG” mapping application (and one that many thought no longer existed!) became the No. 1 overall app on the U.S. App Store, up from No. 8 on Monday.

The surge in new downloads was inspired by MapQuest’s refusal to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” after President Trump’s executive order directed the U.S. geographic naming service to adopt the new name amid his ongoing trade push.

After the August 27 order, MapQuest announced on X that it would not change the lake’s name, while both Google Maps and, later, Apple Maps, capitulated. As a result, MapQuest’s U.S. App Store ranking steadily climbed, as consumers downloaded the app to show their support for the company’s stance.

The people have spoken. We are working. pic.twitter.com/WeO7OAJ2T7 — MapQuest (@MapQuest) September 1, 2026

MapQuest’s rank climbed from No. 128 on August 28 to No. 92 the following day, and then hit No. 3 this Monday, August 31, when it was also No. 1 in the Navigation category. By Tuesday of this week, MapQuest had reached the No. 1 spot across both apps and games on the U.S. App Store.

Since the executive order was issued, the app has been downloaded an estimated 632,000 times in the U.S., according to data from market intelligence provider Sensor Tower. Reached for comment, MapQuest said the app had actually seen over 1.5 million installs across the U.S. and Canada combined.

MapQuest also said many of these new users aren’t just casual downloaders; they’re actively engaging with the app.

“What’s been incredible is that people aren’t just installing our app — they care enough to communicate directly with us — making feature requests and submitting bug reports on social, and in our app reviews,” MapQuest GM Doug Berger told TechCrunch via email. “Our small team has been working around the clock to build features people are asking for. We are aiming for everyone to have a great experience with the app,” he said.

The surge has come quickly for the company. More than half of MapQuest’s year-to-date U.S. downloads —56% — have occurred from August 27 through September 1, Sensor Tower’s estimates show. During this time period, the app’s U.S. downloads increased by 123% day-over-day and were up more than 50 times compared to the same period last year, its data indicates.

Part of what made MapQuest’s stance resonate with consumers was its contrast with its much larger Big Tech rivals.

Google last week explained its decision to rename the lake, saying that it updates names to reflect changes in official government sources such as the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) in the U.S. Apple didn’t provide a comment, but likely follows the same guidelines.

As a much smaller player, MapQuest has more freedom to take a stand and buck the typical conventions.

Screenshot Image Credits:MapQuest

This isn’t the first time it’s done so, either. It still calls the Gulf of Mexico by its original name, instead of Gulf of America. It even released a fun online tool that lets you jokingly rename Lake Ontario to whatever you want it to be, then share the results on social media.

Though it was once the original mapping application, MapQuest ceded its crown to Google Maps over the years. It’s now owned by the internet advertising company System1, which acquired the property from Verizon in 2019. The telco had bought MapQuest’s initial acquirer, AOL, in 2015.

Tech.title: It sure looks like hackers breached a major ID card verification service
Tech.content:
If you have handed over your driver’s license, passport, or other form of identity document to verify your information in the real world, like at a bar, a weed store, or when booking a car rental, there’s a good chance it’s now been stolen in a suspected massive data breach.

That’s according to a jaw-dropping report by independent security journalist Brian Krebs, who says a company used to verify government-issued identity documents in the real world was likely hacked and its vast stores of people’s ID cards were exfiltrated.

Krebs reports that an identity theft site called Nexus, which launched on the dark web this week, claimed to allow users to search through more than 150 million driver’s licenses and passports belonging to people who live in the United States and Canada. A post advertising the site on a known Russian cybercrime forum said Nexus added about half a million new documents daily, sourced from a “major identity verification company,” implying that the hackers had near real-time access to the identity verification company’s systems.

The advert claims that “customer photos are displayed if available.” Krebs found that his own driver’s license was among the searchable records in the database, confirming that the data was authentic. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was also among the people whose photos were listed on the identity search site.

A spokesperson for the Department of Defense told TechCrunch that it is “aware of these reports and is evaluating them.”

Working with security researcher Zach Edwards, whose ID card was also stolen in the breach, Krebs identified the likely source as the identity verification service IDScan. The Louisiana-based company is relied on by major tech and consumer brands to verify tens of millions of people’s IDs around the world each month.

IDScan chief executive Jimmy Roussel did not return TechCrunch’s request for comment, but the company’s chief operating officer Jillian Kossman told Krebs that the company was investigating. Krebs said the FBI’s field office in New Orleans is also probing the breach. A spokesperson for the FBI did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the breach.

Nexus went offline shortly after Krebs’ report went live.

This data breach comes as governments are increasingly rolling out age-verification laws, which largely rely on requiring adults to upload their identity documents to verify that they are old enough to enter a website or app. Security experts and privacy advocates have long warned that companies storing vast amounts of people’s identity documents for long periods of time put that data at risk of theft by hackers.

By all accounts, this would be the largest known single breach of identity documents in some time.

Tech.title: Delivery Hero board backs Uber’s $15B takeover bid
Tech.content:
In Brief

Delivery Hero’s board has signed off on Uber’s $15 billion takeover offer and recommended shareholders approve the deal, which would create one of the largest on-demand food delivery platforms in the world.

After reviewing the offer, Delivery Hero’s supervisory and management boards said it was in the best interests of the company, its shareholders, employees, and other stakeholders. The boards also deemed that the price was “fair and adequate” and said the deal had the “potential to accelerate product innovation.”

The deal, if approved, would double Uber’s global footprint and make its delivery platform one of the largest in the world outside of China. It could also put Uber in a better position to compete with DoorDash and Just Eat Takeaway.

Uber, which was already the largest shareholder in Delivery Hero, set a minimum acceptance threshold of 50%, plus one share of Delivery Hero’s outstanding share capital.

Prosus, another major shareholder, has agreed to sell its 17% stake in Delivery Hero as well, according to the announcement. Delivery Hero previously agreed to sell its businesses in 14 markets where Uber Eats already operates to New York-based investment firm SSW Partners for $1.6 billion.

The tie-up is the latest example of consolidation in the on-demand delivery industry. In the past 18 months, Uber agreed to acquire Turkey-based Getir for $335 million, Grab said it would buy Delivery Hero’s Foodpanda business in Taiwan for $600 million in cash, and DoorDash said it would pay $3.87 billion for the U.K.’s Deliveroo.

Tech.title: We Need to Talk About Wednesday’s Doggone Connections Puzzle
Tech.content:
Players are barking about the Connections puzzle, for good reason. Oscar Wong/Getty Images

Long ago, the New York Times Connections puzzle replaced Wordle as my favorite online puzzle. But the Connections puzzle for Wednesday is a real dog fight to solve. Spoilers ahead, so if you haven’t played Connections yet, do that now.

In Connections, you sort 16 words into four related categories. And in Wednesday’s puzzle, fully half of the words can precede the word “dog.”

Here come those spoilers.

Corn dog. Hunting dog. Sheep dog. Rescue dog. Salty dog, Prairie dog. Top dog. And even though this one is a bit of a stretch, “sausage dog.”

Also, the unsorted grid begins with the words BOW and WOW, which fall into different categories.

Good luck sorting those eight dog words into the two groups that the Times puzzle editors intended! Here’s the answer grid filled out properly.

The completed NYT Connections puzzle for Sept. 2, 2026. NYT/Screenshot by CNET

So the puzzle-makers first divided the “dog” words into a category relating to real, four-legged canines: hunting, rescue, sheep and that questionable “sausage,” which I guess means dachshund.

And then the remaining four dog words went into the purple category, where they fit alongside other words that aren’t real canines at all, including one food (corn dog), one animal (prairie dog), and two slangy expressions (salty dog and top dog).

Players who complained about the puzzle on Reddit made some good points.

“I was like, “there’s 7 answers???” one player wrote, punctuating their response so aggressively that I could almost hear them groaning. “Well, wait, some of these are like dog dogs and the others are like, well, they aren’t…”

“After I lost today, my next Google search was ‘TF is a sausage dog,'” wrote another player.

I’m not unfamiliar with the dachshund breed. At one point, my brother owned five of these little wiggly pups. But if I called them anything other than “dachshunds,” it was “wiener dog,” not “sausage dog.”

Some Reddit users point out that “sausage dog” is a term used in Australia and the UK. (Viewers of Australian animated dog show Bluey, a true TV treasure, might have known it from there.) Some players likely threw the word sausage into one of the dog groups out of desperation, too. (Dogs…eat sausage?)

And a few Reddit commenters pointed out that this puzzle is training players to “presolve,” meaning you can’t just pick a group of four similar words and hope you’re right, but need to sort all 16 words out on paper or elsewhere before trying to solve.

Regardless, I’m guessing more than a few Connections streaks got chewed up today.

Thanks “fur” nothing, New York Times puzzle people.

Tech.title: Hate AI Data Centers? Big Tech’s New Ad Campaign Aims to Change Your Mind
Tech.content:
If you’re part of the growing majority of Americans who oppose AI data centers, the US government and Big Tech have a message for you: Get over it.

The backlash against these massive AI server farms — notorious for guzzling energy and water — has been countered in recent days by aggressive public statements by President Donald Trump. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said that local communities that don’t want data centers will end up “backwards and poor.” He went on to liken opposition to data centers to killing the “Golden Goose,” implying that we’re all to blame for blocking economic growth.

And billionaire tech leaders, who have been especially cozy with the current administration, are taking to the field with a massive advertising blitz to sway public opinion, especially as November’s midterm elections approach. A group called Build American AI, funded by the pro-AI political action committee Leading the Future, is launching a multimillion-dollar campaign to try to counter the tide and promote the construction of AI data centers. The campaign’s initial rollout targets key election battleground states, starting with Kansas, Ohio and Wisconsin.

Opposition to data centers isn’t just about residents facing spiking electricity and water bills, though that would certainly be reason enough after five years of steadily high inflation. There’s also an array of environmental and health concerns, as well as general ambivalence or hatred of AI technology. Grassroots efforts, such as a nationwide map of data centers and proposed projects launched by activist Erin Brockovich, have helped communities organize and stay informed, while several cities have approved bans or moratoriums on new data center projects.

The sentiment against data centers shifted so quickly and sharply this year that a newly published Annenberg Public Policy Center study finds that around two-thirds (61%) of US adults oppose new data center builds near them. And that negative sentiment is across party lines, shared by Democrats (69%), Republicans (54%) and independents (53%).

Could a powerful network of political action committees and a barrage of expensive digital ads sway public opinion? Marketing experts told CNET it’ll be incredibly difficult to put that genie back in the bottle.

The main challenge is that society is incredibly polarized on AI-related issues right now, said Ari Lightman, professor of digital media and marketing at Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy. Tech companies are “trying to create an argument that local communities are going to benefit from the data center,” but those communities are “saying, no, we don’t believe you.”

According to Lightman, campaigns that attempt to shift public opinion on data centers must build a strong case for local benefits — and especially overcome deep-seated skepticism toward tech companies and AI.

Big Tech’s backers

The Build American AI campaign is part of the super-PAC network Leading the Future, which is bankrolled and organized by a coalition of powerful Silicon Valley investors, tech executives and veteran political operatives. The PR strategy is pretty straightforward: Rebrand data centers so they’re no longer seen as local nuisances but vital economic lifelines.

Key backers include billionaire venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, as well as Greg Brockman, the president of OpenAI. According to filings, Build American AI initially raised $100 million just from those parties. Other financial backers include Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale, who has been a donor and supporter of Trump; AI search engine Perplexity and investor Ron Conway.

The ad campaign would be a major influx of money toward pro-data center messaging. Advertising insights company AdImpact told CNET that, after tracking about 15,000 broadcast airings of data center-related ads, total spend is just $7.6 million this year, and most of it is directed against data centers.

About 73% of the spending is from Democratic candidates, said John Link, VP of data at the firm. Most of the ads go after data centers directly or link opponents to their development, often due to rising energy costs or environmental concerns, Link said.

Earlier this year, Wired reported that Build American AI used a “dark money” campaign to pay TikTok and Instagram influencers to promote scripted messaging to frame aggressive AI development as a critical US national security priority against China. The new campaign could also rely on similar tactics and talking points.

Trump’s recent Truth Social post said: “China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement.”

Persuading is a long road

Build American AI seems poised to hypertarget its ad buys to local news websites, streaming platforms and social media feeds — that way, the campaign reaches nearby residents and zoning decision-makers. In late July, Build American AI previewed its advertising materials to potential vendors and political strategy firms. Internal documents revealed that the campaign’s main thrust will be to portray data centers as engines of economic growth and job creation.

Given the widespread distrust of Big Tech, the ads are likely to avoid mentioning specific companies like Amazon, Google or Microsoft. Another tactic would be to reframe data centers as critical national infrastructure, treating them like public highways, water systems or the electrical grid.

Marketing experts CNET spoke with stressed that for the pro-AI messaging to work, it will have to thread the needle by addressing local concerns like energy and water usage while extolling the benefits data centers bring, such as employment and improved technologies that make people’s lives easier. The employment claim, however, has been met with skepticism. Most jobs created by data centers are construction-related and not long-term positions.

The other central issues to address would be resources, pollution and the lack of transparency around data center projects. Elie Barreby, head of SEO and AI search at Adorama, said that messaging in favor of data centers may fly directly in the face of what people are actually experiencing, such as noise pollution or rising utility bills.

“Nobody can advertise their way out of a bad user experience,” Barreby said. Communities are facing “too many real-world negatives to be fooled by any marketing campaign, no matter how good!”

There’s been a heated debate over how many jobs data centers create beyond their initial construction phase. Stephen Shankland/CNET

According to said Joe Szynkowski, founder of PR company The UpWrite Group, “the only way a national campaign can bring down the temperature will be tying the benefits of data centers to the everyday life of people in the affected communities.”

Any PR or marketing campaign requires making people feel something positive, but Szynkowski said tech companies haven’t done a great job with that kind of messaging so far.

Lightman said there’ll need to be grassroots campaigning and boots on the ground to answer questions and remain consistent. Word spreads fast online if a data center’s promises aren’t met or if incentives are being offered in one location, but not in another.

Lightman isn’t very optimistic that these campaigns will effectively connect with and convince people who already feel misled or skeptical about AI and data centers.

“I don’t think the folks that are building the data centers frankly have the capability and wherewithal to do that,” he said.

Tech.title: Uber and Wayve Launch London’s First Public Robotaxi Service
Tech.content:
London’s first public robotaxi service is now live. Starting today, UK riders can hail a self-driving vehicle via the Uber app, through a partnership with autonomous driving company Wayve – though a safety operator will initially remain in the driver’s seat.

At launch, the rides will take place aboard the all-electric Ford Mustang Mach-E. The vehicles are outfitted with cameras and radar, allowing Wayve’s AI Driver to navigate with “full 360-degree visibility around the car at all times,” the companies said in a press release.

Eventually, rides can expand to other vehicles equipped with Wayve’s driverless tech. In fact, Wayve and Uber plan to open up self-driving trips aboard the Nissan Leaf in Tokyo later this year.

Wayve is one of a handful of autonomous vehicle (AV) companies looking to revolutionize urban transportation around the world. Competitors include Waymo, Zoox, Nuro, Avride and May Mobility – which all have partnerships with either Lyft, Uber or both. Waymo aims to launch its robotaxi service in London sometime this year, pending regulatory approval.

Unlike AV systems that rely on high-definition maps and hand-coded rules for perception and navigation, Wayve says it uses foundational AI models that allow its AI Driver to learn from real-world environments and then apply those driving skills “to unexpected scenarios, even without prior training exposure.” That means the tech can “adapt to new roads, vehicles, weather conditions and cities with unprecedented speed and efficiency,” according to the company.

The launch of the robotaxi service comes as Uber on Wednesday said it’s laying off around 10% of its staff. The cuts involve “simplifying team structures” by eliminating several management roles, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi noted in a message to employees, which the company later shared in a newsroom post. Uber plans to invest more in ride-hailing, delivery and robotaxi operations.

The Mach-E robotaxi is equipped with cameras and radar, allowing Wayve’s AI Driver to navigate with “full 360-degree visibility around the car at all times,” Uber and Wayve said. Uber/Wayve

Navigating the challenges ahead

Wayve was founded in 2017, and began operating on London’s public roads in 2020. That’s around the time Uber abandoned its own self-driving ambitions, opting to instead team up with more established players in the space.

In 2024, Uber and Wayve announced their collaboration, agreeing to bring Wayve-powered vehicles to the Uber network. That was followed by plans the following year to launch self-driving trials on public streets in London.

As driverless cars expand into more cities, they face a unique set of challenges shaped by distinct local cultures, roads and regulations. London may prove especially challenging, with its narrow, one-way routes and free-wheeling (and assertive) pedestrians. Additionally, the city’s iconic black-cab culture has endured even as ride-hailing apps transformed how people get around. Now, autonomous vehicles could trigger another seismic shift in the city’s transportation landscape – and potentially provoke fierce resistance from an industry that’s already weathered one tech-fueled wave of disruption.

At launch, Wayve will manage its fleet, while Otto Car, which provides private car rental services, will oversee the trained onboard safety drivers. Uber will eventually take over day-to-day fleet operations alongside Otto Car. The two companies will run a depot in London, which will serve as a hub for everything from vehicle maintenance to servicing and charging. There will also be charging pitstops throughout the operating area to boost vehicle uptime (and maximize profits).

From the start, Uber will handle rider support, while Wayve will oversee its driverless tech.

“We’re proud to introduce the Wayve AI Driver to the public for the first time right here in London, our home city and one of the most complex driving environments in the world,” Alex Kendall, CEO and co-founder of Wayve, said in a statement. “Autonomous driving technology will complement the city’s rich transport network, and we’re excited for Londoners to experience it first as we begin our global rollout with Uber.”

Riders will be notified when they’re matched with a robotaxi in the Uber app, and have the option to accept or select a standard ride instead. Uber/Wayve

How to hail a Wayve robotaxi ride on Uber

Starting today, if you request an UberX, Uber Comfort or Uber Electric ride in London, you could be matched with a Wayve-powered Mach-E vehicle. There is no additional cost and you’ll see the pricing up front.

The vehicles will drive autonomously, though initially, a safety operator will oversee the trip and offer support or take the wheel if needed. “This is part of our phased introduction, before fully driverless operations begin in the future,” Uber and Wayve said in a release.

Riders will get a notification each time they’re matched with an AV, with the option to accept the ride or switch to a non-autonomous vehicle. So if you’re not thrilled about having an AI-powered driver, you won’t be forced to take one of these vehicles.

On the flip side, if you’re eager to get in an AV, you can boost your chances of being matched with one by opting in via the Uber app. Go to Account > Settings > Autonomous Vehicles (under Ride Preferences) and hit the toggle next to “Get more autonomous rides.”

Once the car arrives, you can unlock it and begin the trip from the Uber app. There’s also a touchscreen in the vehicle for starting the ride and seeing the planned route – similar to what you’ll find in other self-driving vehicles from companies like Waymo. Riders can access human support in the Uber app, or from the safety operator in the vehicle.

You’ll be able to rate the trip afterward, but won’t be prompted to tip.

Tech.title: I Was Disappointed by Miele’s Last Vacuums, but the New IFA Lineup Changed My Mind
Tech.content:
With this in mind, when Miele showed me its new HX3 and HX3 Plus Aqua, I was skeptical it would be more than an incremental jump, but after spending some time using it at the Miele Experience Center in Manhattan prior to the IFA 2026 show in Berlin, I came away impressed by several of the changes.

Miele is known as one of the most reputable brands for home appliances and cleaning, but when we lab tested the Miele HX2 cordless vacuum last year, we were a little let down by it — it performed poorly in sand tests for low and midpile carpet, and the design was a little finicky to use compared to lightweight competition from Dyson and Shark. It also cost $1,100 at full price, making it a hard sell.

To start with, while there hasn’t been a complete redesign, one of the big changes is rebalancing the weight distribution so that more of it is at the bottom, reducing the strain up top when you’re vacuuming. You can also change out where the motor and waste bin are, depending on how you attach the nozzles, so it’s up to you how you want the weight to fall.

A Miele representative showed me an example of how you might want it more top-heavy when you’re using it to clean the corners of ceilings and higher-up spots. You can also convert it fairly easily back into the self-standing vacuum mode, a traditional stick vac or a handheld.

There are also other quality-of-life tweaks, like push-button controls, easier dustbin emptying, finer particle capture, automatic flooring-type detection and the ability to stand upright. It offers 70 minutes of running time, which Miele says should be good enough to clean 1,700 square feet in a single charge, and some models have an extended battery included for even more juice. All key things that I value when vacuuming.

Miele

The big improvements come in performance. The HX3 has notably better pickup on both carpet and hard flooring. The Miele representatives even helpfully provided me with some condiments to imitate sand and pet hair to try to suction up from the carpet. While it wasn’t quite the same as CNET’s rigorous lab testing, the outcome of my vacuuming session offered solid results. The HX3 was able to remove most or all of the pet hair with a single back-and-forth motion, while the imitation sand was no challenge at all on hardwood (though that’s true of most vacuums and robot vacuums we test).

Overall, the HX3 seemed to do a great job of picking up dirt and debris from different floor types. There’s also a powerful Boost mode that can give you extra suction beyond even the highest setting, but it drains the battery the fastest, so it’s limited to just 10 seconds.

The HX3 Plus Aqua is basically the same as the regular HX3; it just comes with Miele’s first mopping attachment, the Aqua Twister Floorhead. It consists of dual spinning mop pads that are machine washable, a 300-milliliter water tank and a 360-degree light. I also took the mopping attachment for a spin, trying out its different modes on hard flooring to clean stains and dirt. Again, the results were impressive, with the amount of water being dispensed fully adjustable, allowing you to tackle bigger messes and spills. When the mopping head is attached, Boost mode also dispenses more water for 30 seconds, so it’s good to see the feature has been integrated into both cleaning heads.

Miele

While there are two distinct models, the HX3 and HX3 Plus Aqua, there’s a somewhat more consumer-friendly price spread: The base HX3 starts at $849, while the top-tier HX3 Aqua Plus, with all the accessories, including the mopping head, runs $1,249. There are a number of models in between, each with its own price and array of attachments, so I’m just going to lay them out in a list below, pulled from the specs sheet.

Triflex HX3 ($849) Included: MultiFloor XXL (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), 1 Lithium-Ion Battery by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

($849) Triflex HX3 Hardfloor (Amazon exclusive) ($949) Included: MultiFloor XXL (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), Hardfloor Roller (HX-HC10), 1 Lithium-Ion Battery by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

($949) Triflex HX3 Cat & Dog ($999) Included: MultiFloor XXL with headlight (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), Electro Compact (HX-EC10), 1 Lithium-Ion Battery by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

($999) Triflex HX3 Plus ($1,099) Included: MultiFloor XXL with headlight (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), Hardfloor Roller (HX-HC10), 2 Lithium-Ion Batteries by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

($1,099) Triflex HX3 Aqua ($1,049) Included: MultiFloor XXL with headlight (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), AquaTwister Pro with 360 Light, Drip Mat, 2 Washable pads, FloorClean (17 fl.oz. bottle), 1 Lithium-Ion Battery by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

($1,049) Triflex HX3 Aqua Plus ($1,249) Included: MultiFloor XXL with headlight (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), Harfloor Roller (HX-HC10), AquaTwister Pro with 360 Light, Drip Mat, 2 Washable pads, FloorClean (17 fl.oz. bottle), 2 Lithium-Ion Batteries by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

($1,249)

Miele also pointed out to me that the base specs and capabilities of each model are the same, so even if you buy the most basic model, you can pick up other attachments separately over time to build the vacuum you want. I’m looking forward to testing these at the CNET Lab, and we already have the Aqua Plus in hand for our next batch of tests. Expect to see results soon.

Editors’ note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: You’re Addicted to Your Phone. Admitting That Is the First Step
Tech.content:
You pick up your phone for a quick read, and suddenly an hour has disappeared. Sound familiar?

More than half of adults say they use their phones excessively, according to a Pew Research Center survey conducted earlier this summer. Of the nearly 10,000 respondents, all 18 and older, 53% said they use smartphones too much, and 36% say they use their phones “about the right amount.”

The younger the people were, the more they felt they had overused phone use — 70% among those aged 18 to 29 and 64% among those aged 30 to 49. About 42% of the 18 to 29 group said they were on their phones “almost constantly.”

Digital marketing platform Semrush estimates that people worldwide average 4 hours and 37 minutes per day on the phone — 5 hours, 16 minutes in the US — and check their phones an average of 58 times per day.

Put another way, 5 hours on your phone each day adds up to 76 full 24-hour days a year. Start Jan. 1 at midnight when the new year begins, and you won’t put your phone down until around St. Patrick’s Day.

I’m assuming these numbers aren’t very surprising, considering we use our phones for everything from shopping and reading the news to texting, scrolling social media and playing games. Once we get accustomed to having instant gratification for our finances, communication and work, it’s hard to break the cycle. But as more of us realize the consequences, we’re starting to take action.

Risks of too much device

Excessive phone use can have tragic consequences. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports that 3,208 people were killed in 2024 in auto accidents caused by distracted driving, which includes drivers talking or texting on the phone.

“Sending or reading a text takes your eyes off the road for 5 seconds,” the NHTSA reports. “At 55 mph, that’s like driving the length of an entire football field with your eyes closed.”

First Aid for Life, a UK-based first-aid training provider, said 41% in the UK have suffered some type of accident related to phone use. Wikipedia even has a gruesome list of selfie-related injuries and deaths.

Anxiety, stress, depression, social isolation, feelings of inadequacy, low self-esteem and even thoughts of suicide and self-harm can all arise from being on devices and social media too much, according to research from Columbia University’s department of psychiatry.

The main downside of excessive screen time in the survey was reduced sleep, with 41% reporting that phone use affected how much they slept. And 34% said phone use hurt productivity, as compared to 30% who said it helped.

Try this one trick

In the Pew study, 45% said they had tried to reduce their phone use over the previous year, and 46% had not. Of those trying to cut back, only 25% rated their attempts as extremely or very successful, and 52% said they were somewhat successful.

For people using iPhones, there is a trick you can try to reduce screen time, says CNET senior writer Zachary McAuliffe.

“Try hiding iPhone apps in a folder in your App Library,” McAuliffe said. “This could prevent you from mindlessly opening apps when you’re bored, since there are more roadblocks to get to those apps. I’ve hidden a few apps on my device for this reason, and I forget I have them. Which is a nice reminder that I need to delete a few apps that I don’t use.”

CNET also has a list of five effective tech gadgets and apps to get you off that doomscrolling hamster wheel. Brick, our Editors’ Choice, is a locking device that lets you block certain apps with the press of a button and includes a timer that shows how long you’ve gone without looking at the phone.

You can also check out our recommendations for the best phone settings to stop doomscrolling.

Tech.title: Anthropic’s Content Checker Tool Is Here, With One Big Catch
Tech.content:
Just a couple of weeks after Anthropic announced it would roll out digital watermarks for text generated with its Claude AI tools, the company has introduced a page where you can check files to see if Claude helped make them.

The page, at claude.com/check-content, lets you upload files with a quick spot check and will confirm, “This file shows signs it was processed by Claude,” if it finds content credentials embedded in the file.

But if you’re hoping to prove that someone used Claude for a term paper or want to see if someone’s texts weren’t actually written by the human you’re talking to, you’re going to need to wait. The checker currently works with only a limited number of file types, and none of them are text formats. Instead, the checker accepts multimedia files, including JPEGs, GIFs, MP3s and MOVs — basically image, audio or video files.

A spokesperson for Anthropic told CNET that the tool is specifically to check for Claude’s use through an industry standard called C2PA; a broader AI detection tool is in the works, but not yet available.

“Text checking is via our Detection API (separate tool) and in private preview, and we hope to share more about it in the months ahead,” the spokesperson said. This aligns with a note on the check content tool reads, “To detect watermarks embedded in text we have a Detection API which is currently in private preview to eligible organizations as required under EU law.”

Anthropic has said that its watermarking of text that Claude produces won’t affect the quality, speed or cost of outputs and that these watermarks won’t be visible or affect how text functions or appears. But they will remain with text from Claude even if it’s copied and pasted from one place to another. Anthropic has a sign-up form for businesses or organizations that want to be added to the list for access to the watermark detector.

Anthropic said in its email to CNET that if the C2PA standard expands to include additional file formats, its checker tool will likely adopt them as well.

How does Anthropic’s new checker work?

The free web-based tool has a drag-and-drop option, or you can click to add a file from your device or Google Drive on mobile. According to the website, the file you choose stays on your device or file service, and the checker only reads the file’s credentials, not the file itself.

“Your file is never stored or used for any other purpose,” the page says.

In CNET’s testing of the tool, the detector correctly flagged an image file that was converted in Claude from a PowerPoint presentation. For files that the detector said were not shown to be processed by Claude, a message is shown that reads, “We couldn’t find any signs that this file was processed by Claude. That doesn’t rule it out. Signals like this can be removed when a file is edited, converted, or compressed.”

Tech.title: The New York Times Just Dropped a Brand-New Wordle Spin-Off
Tech.content:
Wordle fans, start marking your calendars for hump day.

On Wednesday, the New York Times introduced a weekly drop of five to six new puzzles created by the newspaper’s puzzle constructors and editors. The new puzzles aren’t daily but will be released every Wednesday in a group and will include twists on current puzzles. They’re only available to people who pay for a New York Times Games or All Access subscription.

The types of bonus puzzles offered may vary from week to week. Other puzzles, including Wordle, Connections, Strands, Pips, and Connections: Sports Edition, remain free, while some others are behind a paywall.

CNET offers daily hints and answers for Wordle, Connections, Strands, Connections: Sports Edition and the Mini Crossword.

Wordle in 1

I played the new batch of games, and I think the most popular game will be Wordle in 1. Regular Wordle gives you six tries to guess a five-letter word, uses specific colors to indicate if you’ve guessed a letter that’s included, and also notes if you put it in the right spot. Wordle in 1 sets up five five-letter grids, each with a different word, and fills them in with some correct and some incorrect letters. You use the letters provided to figure out the answers.

Wordle in 1 provides you with some correct and some incorrect letters, and you take it from there. NYT/Screenshot by CNET

In the example above, the colored letters indicate that the U and T are in the right spaces, that there’s no N at all, and the S and the other T needs to be relocated. (Answer at the bottom of this post if you want a spoiler.)

More games: Connections 3×3, Colorful Strands

Other games in the weekly drop also play off the current New York Times puzzles.

Connections 3×3 is a smaller version of the regular Connections puzzle, offering just nine words or phrases that you have to separate into three groups.

Colorful Strands is exactly the same as regular Strands, but the answers show up in color, which is something the regular puzzle does from time to time.

Mystery Mini is another Mini Crossword, with a creative twist. The first one, for example, uses two answers twice, with different clues, and other answers are also related.

Easy Mode Crossword simply takes the standard Friday crossword and just makes the clues easier. There’s also a monthly Special Crossword, which might be written in collaboration with a famous person or feature a theme. Comedian Rachel Dratch, a former Saturday Night Live cast member, co-constructed a puzzle released Tuesday.

That promised spoiler

Spoiler for the pictured Wordle in 1 puzzle above: The answer is TRUST.

Tech.title: Mario Kart 8 Deluxe’s Surprise Switch 2 Update Brings Multiplayer Mayhem
Tech.content:
Mario Kart 8 Deluxe is seemingly the game that Nintendo refuses to move on from. The racing game, originally released on the Wii U back in 2014 and then updated for the Nintendo Switch in 2017, has received what might be the greatest update for the game that could get players back on the track.

Nintendo on Tuesday unexpectedly dropped the version 4.0.0 update for Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, which adds a new eight-player, split-screen option when playing the game on the Nintendo Switch 2, as well as CameraPlay support and support for higher-resolution TVs. It’s the new multiplayer option that has gone viral on social media, as gamers try to wrap their heads around playing an eight-player race on the Switch 2’s 7.9-inch screen.

While this split-screen mode can work on the Switch 2 in handheld mode, it’s clear that the new multiplayer option is designed for gamers to play with friends on a TV. It expands Mario Kart 8 Deluxe’s multiplayer beyond the four-player limit it has had since launch. Instead, up to eight racers can play together, with each racer able to have their own individual Joy-Con, Switch Pro Controller or Switch 2 Pro Controller. Those who paid the $25 for the Mario Kart 8 Deluxe – Booster Course Pass will also have access to all 96 courses in the VS Race multiplayer mode.

CameraPlay support was also added on Tuesday. This feature, which made its debut on the Switch 2, lets players connect a USB camera to their console during multiplayer and online matches so other players can see their faces while playing. Nintendo sells an official USB camera for the console, but there are many alternatives that work just as well.

Another welcome change in the update is shortened loading times when playing on the Switch 2. Players should notice it takes less time to start races and battles when playing.

This update for Mario Kart 8 Deluxe is part of Nintendo’s initiative to update its Switch games and optimize them for the Switch 2. On Monday, Pikmin 3 Deluxe received a similar update to match the resolution of the newer handheld console.

Tuesday’s update coincided with the Switch 2’s new price tag of $500. Nintendo announced the price jump of its newest console back in May, citing “changes in market conditions.”

Gaming hardware companies such as Nintendo, Sony, Microsoft and Valve have had to deal with the rising costs of components, mainly memory and storage, in what’s been dubbed RAMaggeddon. So far, there’s no sign that the memory shortage driving these price increases will end anytime soon.
